entries.title: The AI cash-flow divide
entries.text: 2026-10-29-us-earnings 2026-10-29 US earnings 08:00 original edition Source-checked historical edition The AI cash-flow divide Microsoft's cloud momentum and cash generation contrast with Alphabet's costly expansion. AI revenue expansion remains strong, but the market is discriminating between self-funded growth and widening cash deficits. MSFT Microsoft positive Higher after-hours Azure rose 48%; free cash flow reached $18.6bn. Reuters reported free cash flow of $18.6bn and Azure growth of 48% for the September quarter. Next-quarter Azure growth guidance was 49%–50%. Figures describe that reporting period, not current market prices. Azure growth 48% Free cash flow +$18.6bn GOOGL Alphabet negative −10% after-hours Google Cloud doubled, but free cash flow turned negative. Reuters reported September-quarter revenue of $127.6bn and negative free cash flow of $9.07bn. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled. Revenue $127.6bn Free cash flow −$9.07bn AMZN Amazon watch Earnings due 29 Oct US AWS growth expected at 38.2%, according to Reuters' pre-earnings preview. Revenue growth expected at 12.3%. Watch AWS growth, capital spending, financing requirements and free cash flow. These are forecasts, not reported results. AWS growth est. 38.2% Total growth est. 12.3% Status Upcoming Market pulse Cloud and AI demand remain firm. Investors are responding more sharply to cash conversion and capital expenditure than to headline revenue growth. Fixed-income lens A sustained rise in debt-funded AI capex would increase refinancing sensitivity. This is an analytical risk scenario, not a verified bond-market price reaction. Portfolio discipline Compare cash flow after capex, pricing power, guidance and balance-sheet headroom rather than relying only on earnings beats. 2026-10-29T15:35:17+08:00

entries.text: credit-2026-11-12 credit 2026-11-12 Global Markets & Credit Research 08:04 SGT cutoff · 12 Nov; selected sources dated 10–11 Nov Alphabet explores Hong Kong- and Singapore-dollar funding. ECB consumer research and a Bank of England speech examine connections between new technologies and financial stability. Global Markets & Credit Research · 12 November 2026 08:04 SGT research cutoff Verified extract from the newest completed scheduled edition. Selected source claims were independently checked. Global coverage is partial. This extract does not reproduce the full briefing, licensed credit-spread series or unverified final bond terms. 1. Alphabet · proposed Asian bond funding Reuters reported on 11 November that Alphabet was considering roughly US$3bn equivalent through its first Hong Kong- and Singapore-dollar bond sales. The proposed maturities included a 30-year Singapore-dollar tranche. Size and pricing remained unsettled in that report. Important distinction: A proposed sale is not completed issuance. No coupon, issue price or issuance yield is inferred here. The existing dated final-terms comparison remains separate. This records the source edition's cutoff, not later bookbuilding developments. 2. ECB · consumer stablecoin exposure Economic Bulletin Issue 7/2026 examines Consumer Expectations Survey responses from August and November 2025. In August 2025, 5% of euro-area consumers reported stablecoin holdings, compared with 13% reporting any crypto-assets. These are historical survey observations, not November 2026 ownership rates. The ECB identifies reserve assets as a link between stablecoins and traditional finance. The paper describes potential spillovers; it does not establish that a systemic run has occurred. 3. Bank of England · AI agents in finance Jonathan Hall's 11 November speech cites a Bank/FCA survey: 80% of responding firms used some form of agentic AI, while 2% of those agents had broad autonomy. The denominators differ. Hall discusses access limits, monitoring and accountability, largely in the context of future risks. Analysis: Funding access, liquidity and operational controls should be evaluated together. Neither a proposed bond sale nor adoption of new technology demonstrates an improvement in an individual borrower's credit quality. Coverage: Other research and borrower claims in the scheduled report are outside this verified extract. There is no new policy/election edition in this publication. Reuters via MarketScreener · Alphabet planned bond sale · 11 November ECB · Who holds stablecoins? · Economic Bulletin 7/2026 Bank of England · Principals and Agents · 11 November Verified extract

Friday Bond & Credit Deep Dive · post-week review Week ended 30 October 2026 · research verified 2 November This newly completed scheduled edition includes final issuance documents and the completed week. It is not a reconstruction of information available at 08:00 Singapore time on Friday. This public extract retains only independently checked material; the earlier 30 October edition is unchanged. 1. Microsoft: final pricing replaces preliminary borrowing context Microsoft's SEC pricing sheet is dated 29 October, with expected settlement on 4 November. Eight fixed-rate tranches total US$23bn; two floating-rate tranches of US$1bn each bring the offering to US$25bn. The following are issue terms, not current market quotes. Maturity · USD principal · coupon · issue price per 100 · issuance YTM · stated benchmark spread 2036 · $4bn · 5.550% · 99.659 · 5.595% · +65bp 2046 · $2bn · 6.150% · 99.624 · 6.183% · +85bp 2056 · $4bn · 6.250% · 99.919 · 6.256% · +95bp 2066 · $2bn · 6.350% · 99.914 · 6.356% · +105bp The 2066 note is benchmarked to the Treasury due May 2056, not a 40-year Treasury. The floating-rate notes use compounded SOFR plus a margin; no fixed YTM is inferred for them. 2. Non-AI corporate issuance P&G's 26 October SEC document specifies four USD tranches totalling US$4bn. Its 2056 tranche has a 5.900% coupon, 99.860 issue price, 5.910% issue YTM and +60bp over its stated Treasury benchmark. Four verified P&G tranches are added to the existing 26–27 October monitor; Microsoft is detailed separately above because it priced on 29 October. 3. Cross-border credit is a dated stock, not delinquency BIS statistics released 29 October place cross-border bank credit at US$40.7tn at end-June 2026, with 11% annual growth. The Q2 increase was US$877bn: US$560bn in loans/deposits and US$317bn in bank-held debt securities. These global banking aggregates are not U.S. household arrears or current November credit losses. 4. Non-bank transmission and AI financing The Bank of England's 23 October Working Paper 1212 models banks and non-bank intermediaries using UK data. Conventional rate-policy transmission changes little with non-bank size in the model, while QE transmission depends on how that sector expands. This is model-based research, not an observed default forecast. The BIS AI-financing bulletin connects long-term borrowing, off-balance-sheet structures and institutional funding. Its event-study findings do not establish a persistent Treasury-yield increase caused by AI issuance. 5. Analysis and coverage limits Separate duration risk, issuer credit risk and funding risk. Review legal borrower, collateral priority, liquidity and cash interest coverage. A downgrade, late payment, nonaccrual and realised investor loss are different events. Existing household-credit metrics retain their Q2 2026 label. New rating-action ratios, private-credit default estimates and unverified financing terms were omitted from this extract; no personal account amounts or borrowing balances are included. entries.title: Friday Bond & Credit Deep Dive
entries.text: credit-2026-10-30 credit Friday Bond & Credit Deep Dive 2026-10-30 08:09 SGT delivery Duration, AI borrowing, new issuance and the path from late payment to default. Friday Bond, Credit & Debt Markets ────•❉᯽❉•──── 30 October 2026 · 8:00 AM SGT Weekly research Research cutoff: 29 October 2026, U.S. market close, subject to source publication availability. Primary focus: 23–29 October. Earlier studies are explicitly labelled as background. Executive market dashboard 10Y U.S. Treasury 4.98% 29 Oct · −2bp vs 23 Oct 30Y U.S. Treasury 5.32% 29 Oct · −1bp vs 23 Oct U.S. IG credit OAS 86bp 5bp tighter vs 23 Oct U.S. HY credit OAS 314bp 24bp tighter vs 23 Oct Treasury par yields as of 29 Oct; ICE BofA credit-index spreads as of 28 Oct, the latest published observations verified. Sources: U.S. Treasury and FRED. U.S. Department of the Treasury +2 The central development this week is the growing scale and complexity of AI debt financing, not a broad collapse in credit markets. Microsoft moved toward a reported US$25 billion bond transaction, banks and Blackstone arranged US$63 billion of AI-equipment financing for Anthropic-related infrastructure, and new BIS research documented how AI borrowing can affect insurers, private-credit funds and potentially Treasury term premiums. Meanwhile, the broad high-yield index spread actually tightened during the week. Investment interpretation: Credit stress is becoming more issuer-specific and structure-specific, while the public market remains receptive to stronger borrowers. That divergence matters. A credit index can improve while an individual leveraged AI borrower suffers a severe financing shock. 1. U.S. Treasury duration and credit spreads Latest verified yield curve Maturity 23 Oct 29 Oct Change 2Y 4.68% 4.61% −7bp 5Y 4.84% 4.78% −6bp 7Y 4.91% 4.87% −4bp 10Y 5.00% 4.98% −2bp 20Y 5.36% 5.35% −1bp 30Y 5.33% 5.32% −1bp Official U.S. Treasury par yield curve. U.S. Department of the Treasury The curve remains relatively steep from 2Y to 30Y, but the far end offers little additional yield over the 20Y point. On 29 October, the 30Y yielded 3bp less than the 20Y. For a long-duration investor, the extra ten years of maturity must therefore be justified by the bond's valuation, convexity and expected yield path, not by assuming that longer maturity necessarily pays more. Credit spreads: the index is not confirming systemic panic U.S. high-yield credit spreads ICE BofA U.S. High Yield Index OAS, basis points. Latest available observation: 28 October 2026. 310bp 320bp 330bp 340bp 350bp 22 Oct 23 Oct 26 Oct 27 Oct 28 Oct 22 Oct: HY option-adjusted spread 340bp 23 Oct: HY option-adjusted spread 338bp 26 Oct: HY option-adjusted spread 330bp 27 Oct: HY option-adjusted spread 318bp 28 Oct: HY option-adjusted spread 314bp Source: FRED high-yield OAS. St. Louis Fed Index 23 Oct 28 Oct Weekly move IG corporate OAS 91bp 86bp −5bp HY corporate OAS 338bp 314bp −24bp HY less IG OAS 247bp 228bp −19bp The difference between the indexes is a simple comparison, not a duration-adjusted relative-value measure. Positioning implication: Broad HY spread tightening suggests risk appetite remained resilient through the week. That is not an invitation to buy every issuer offering a double-digit yield. The more important question is whether default probabilities, collateral coverage and refinancing prospects are diverging faster than index averages reveal. 2. Institutional research deep dive Four substantive studies and data releases were selected, including two from 23–29 October and two earlier October papers retained for their importance. A fifth Fitch credit review is included with its publication-date limitation. Research 1. BIS: Building AI on Credit Building AI on credit: structures and spillovers BIS Bulletin No. 140 · 27 October 2026 · 8-page full PDF Mathias Drehmann and Egemen Eren This is the week's most directly relevant central-bank research. BIS finding Figure Projected 2026 capex by five major U.S. hyperscalers Over US$800bn Gross bond issuance by those five firms through September US$222bn AI-linked off-balance-sheet bonds/ABS reportedly placed during 2026 US$75–100bn Estimated data-centre lease commitments, mid-2026 US$1.2tn Portion related to leases not yet commenced US$820bn These figures represent different financing categories and should not be added together as though they were all outstanding bonds. bis.org How AI borrowing risk can travel through the financial system AI hyperscalers and technology customers Lease commitments · capacity contracts · limited guarantees Data-centre and equipment SPVs Buildings · power infrastructure · GPUs · contracted revenue Banks Senior loans and construction finance Non-bank investors Private credit · insurers · ABS Simplified structure based on BIS Graph 2, not a representation of any one transaction. The BIS analysed 18 AI-financing news days during 2026. It found an estimated 1.5bp increase in the 10-year Treasury term premium on those days, generally fading within two trading days. This is an event-study association, not a demonstrated causal or persistent effect. The paper's Graph 3 and online annex explain the methodology and limitations. bis.org Why it matters: Long-dated AI corporate debt competes for some of the same institutional capital that buys Treasuries and other long-duration bonds. The immediate measured effect is small. Persistent issuance on this scale could still influence how much compensation investors demand for holding duration. Client talking point: AI investment is now large enough to matter to bond markets, even for investors who own no AI shares. Research 2. S&P: North American data-centre debt dashboard S&P Global Ratings launches interactive North America data center dashboard 23 October 2026 · Official research release and rated-transaction dataset S&P's newly published dashboard covers its rated North American data-centre transactions. 32 Rated transactions $105.3bn Total debt issuance 8.7 GW Tenant capacity Debt issuance across S&P's rated universe Corporate finance Project finance Structured-finance ABS Project finance: 58.3% Structured-finance ABS: 26.4% Corporate finance: 15.3% S&P reports 143 supporting properties and warns that power access, permitting and development constraints may affect project delivery. These figures cover S&P-rated transactions, not the entire data-centre financing market. Oct 23, 2026 Implication: The largest part of the measured debt is project finance, where the exact lender claim, sponsor support and project cash flow deserve scrutiny. The important due-diligence distinction is between a bond issued directly by a profitable hyperscaler and a security issued by a separate data-centre company that happens to have that hyperscaler as a tenant. Research 3. BIS: Bank regulation and private-credit growth Bank liquidity regulation and the growth of private credit BIS Working Paper No. 1388 · October 2026, released 20 October · 48-page PDF · Prior-week research Authors: Sebastian Doerr, Gaston Gelos and Vesa Pursiainen. The researchers examined how U.S. bank liquidity regulation changed the provision of credit. Their central finding: A one-standard-deviation higher historical exposure to banks affected by liquidity requirements was associated with nearly 50% greater private-credit lending volume after the regulatory changes, relative to the comparison counties. bis.org This is a historical empirical estimate, not a claim that private credit grew by 50% in 2026. Credit implication: Lending risk did not simply disappear when banks became subject to tougher liquidity requirements. Some financing shifted toward non-bank vehicles. For portfolio analysis, that means reviewing the entire credit intermediation chain, especially when banks also provide leverage to the funds that ultimately hold the loans. Client talking point: Better-regulated banks do not necessarily mean every form of borrowing has become safer. Risk can migrate to institutions with different funding and transparency requirements. Research 4. Fitch: Business development company credit quality Fitch Ratings Completes Peer Review of 8 US BDCs Fitch original page dated 15 October · Research findings redistributed 28 October · Full Fitch access restricted The accessible Fitch-distributed summary states that seven BDC issuer ratings were affirmed, while New Mountain Finance's outlook moved from Stable to Negative. Indicator Finding Average realised loss rate, Fitch-rated BDCs, full-year 2025 1.1% Same group, first half 2026 0.5% First-half 2026 loss rate for the reviewed peer group 0.4% The periods are not the same length. The 0.5% first-half figure should not be compared mechanically with the 1.1% full-year figure as proof that losses have halved. Fitch expects continuing asset-quality pressure and identifies nonaccrual loans as a risk. The Lead Implication: Public BDC filings may reveal stress earlier than headline aggregate private-credit default statistics, but realised losses, nonaccruals, fair-value marks and interest coverage must be considered together. Research 5. Bank of England: Who buys long-duration corporate bonds? Domestic and foreign insurer corporate bond demand and monetary policy Staff Working Paper No. 1,210 · 9 October 2026 · 59-page PDF · Background research The study uses security-level insurer transactions from 2018–2022. It finds that UK and U.S. life insurers can respond very differently to changes in bond yields. For example, in the researchers' historical estimates, a 1 percentage-point rise in the UK 10-year government-bond yield was associated with higher net buying by UK insurers but reduced demand from U.S. insurers for their relevant UK-corporate-bond holdings over subsequent months. bankofengland.co.uk Implication: Long-duration debt demand is segmented by currency, regulatory treatment and liabilities. A 30-year bond may not have the same natural buyer base as a five-year bond. Methodological limit: Historical UK/US insurer evidence is not a forecast of October 2026 U.S. Treasury yields. 3. Latest Reuters debt and borrowing developments Microsoft: reported US$25bn bond offering Reuters · 29 October 2026 Reuters reported a planned sale of approximately US$25bn, with more than US$100bn in orders and up to ten tranches spanning roughly 2–40 years. Its SEC preliminary prospectus confirms the offering structure but leaves final pricing terms blank. Reuters +1 Classification: Announced/marketed offering. Exact coupon and final issuance yield not verified from the reviewed primary filing. Anthropic/Broadcom: US$63bn structured equipment financing Reuters · 26 October, updated 27 October 2026 Banks and Blackstone announced financing for an SPV to purchase AI chips and network equipment. Reuters reported around US$43.5bn first-lien senior debt, with second-lien capital involving Blackstone and residual-value support from Broadcom. Reuters Classification: Financing arrangement, not an ordinary unsecured corporate bond. Coupon, all-in yield and individual loan maturities were not disclosed. Oracle: attempts to cap future funding requirements Reuters · 28 October 2026 Oracle said it expects to need up to US$20bn of additional financing for the remainder of fiscal 2027, split between debt and equity. It reported US$125.34bn in notes payable and other borrowings as of 31 August. Its goal is positive free cash flow in the second half of fiscal 2028. Reuters Classification: Funding plan and management forecast, not a newly issued US$20bn bond. Two additional transactions deserve attention: Reuters reported that SpaceX secured US$40bn of chip-related debt financing with an Apollo affiliate on 26 October, while Argentum AI was only in talks for a proposed US$5bn chip financing deal on 27 October. These must not be counted as equally completed borrowing events. Reuters Moody's also told Reuters on 27 October that 17% of 607 borrowers in its tracked sample used payment-in-kind interest, while the 2027–2029 refinancing period remained a concern for weaker borrowers. Reuters 4. New issuance and borrowing monitor The table below uses actual final pricing term sheets wherever available. These are issue-date terms, not live secondary-market yields. All amounts USD. Issue price is per 100 of face value. UST benchmark yield and issue spread are quoted together. N/V = not verified in the reviewed source. Issuer / pricing date Amount · Maturity Coupon Issue price Issue YTM UST benchmark yield / spread United Rentals · 26 Oct $700m · 15 Oct 2029 5.550% 99.922 5.580% 4.780% / +80bp United Rentals · 26 Oct $800m · 15 Oct 2031 5.750% 99.884 5.778% 4.828% / +95bp United Rentals · 26 Oct $1bn · 15 Oct 2036 6.200% 99.710 6.240% 4.990% / +125bp Texas Instruments · 26 Oct $500m · 9 Nov 2028 5.000% 99.827 5.092% 4.712% / +38bp Texas Instruments · 26 Oct $500m · 9 Nov 2031 5.350% 99.779 5.401% 4.821% / +58bp CBRE Services · 27 Oct $500m · 15 Jan 2032 5.650% 99.424 5.782% 4.832% / +95bp CBRE Services · 27 Oct $500m · 15 Jan 2037 5.900% 97.872 6.186% 4.986% / +120bp Main Street Capital · 27 Oct $500m · 15 Jan 2030 6.550% 99.258 6.800% 4.800% / +200bp KeyCorp · 27 Oct $1bn · 2 Nov 2032 5.889% initially 100.000 5.889% initial fixed pricing 4.839% / +105bp Sources: Original SEC/issuer pricing documents. sec.gov +4 Special point on KeyCorp: Its coupon becomes floating for the final year, at compounded SOFR +130bp. The quoted 5.889% fixed-rate pricing figure is not a guaranteed fixed YTM across the entire note's life. Ratings and financing purposes Issuer Credit ratings verified Borrowing structure / purpose United Rentals Moody's Baa3 / S&P BBB− Senior unsecured; specific proceeds not verified in pricing sheet Texas Instruments N/V in reviewed term sheet Senior notes linked to an acquisition, with special mandatory redemption provisions CBRE Services Moody's Baa1 / S&P BBB+ / Fitch BBB+ Senior unsecured; general corporate purposes, including commercial-paper repayment and acquisition-related uses Main Street Capital S&P BBB− / Fitch BBB− BDC unsecured notes; initially repay revolving-credit borrowing KeyCorp N/V in reviewed term sheet Fixed-to-floating senior bank debt Microsoft N/V in preliminary prospectus Proposed senior unsecured debt; general corporate purposes including capital requirements Anthropic-related SPV N/V Senior and second-lien AI-equipment financing SpaceX-related financing N/V Chip-related debt, as reported by Reuters SEC +4 What the pricing tells us The verified spread dispersion is substantial: Spread on newly priced USD debt Spread above each deal's stated Treasury benchmark. Issue-date spreads, not live OAS. 0bp 55bp 110bp 165bp 220bp Texas Instruments 2… Texas Instruments 2… United Rentals 2029 CBRE 2032 KeyCorp 2032 CBRE 2037 United Rentals 2036 Main Street Capital… Texas Instruments 2028: Issue spread 38bp Texas Instruments 2031: Issue spread 58bp United Rentals 2029: Issue spread 80bp CBRE 2032: Issue spread 95bp KeyCorp 2032: Issue spread 105bp CBRE 2037: Issue spread 120bp United Rentals 2036: Issue spread 125bp Main Street Capital 2030: Issue spread 200bp Selected issuance spreads sourced from final pricing term sheets above. Different maturities, issuer risk, capital structures and investor liquidity make this a descriptive comparison rather than a pure credit-risk ranking. Main Street Capital's +200bp spread is particularly noteworthy beside the relatively small issuance concessions for Texas Instruments. But the higher spread is not simply free income. A BDC owns portfolios of loans to businesses and its own funding conditions reflect both asset quality and financing risk. For context, Main Street says proceeds will initially refinance existing revolving facilities. That illustrates an important distinction between gross debt issuance and net additional borrowing. 5. Loan delinquencies, defaults and late-payment watch Latest verified national household dataset New York Fed Q2 2026, published 11 August 2026. Full 46-page original report: Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit, Q2 2026. The most recent comprehensive quarter verified is June 2026. These numbers should not be labelled October delinquency observations. Total household debt $18.771tn Balances in some stage of delinquency 4.7% New transitions into serious delinquency: 90+ days Loan category Q2 2025 Q2 2026 Change Mortgages 1.29% 1.52% +0.23pp Credit cards 6.93% 6.97% +0.04pp Auto loans 2.93% 3.00% +0.07pp Home-equity lines 1.15% 1.15% 0.00pp Student loans 12.88% 7.83% −5.05pp These are annualised flows into serious delinquency, not percentages of total outstanding balances already 90+ days past due. Student-loan comparisons remain affected by reporting changes associated with payment resumption. FEDERAL RESERVE BANK of NEW YORK Where to inspect earlier warning signals in the full report Indicator New York Fed report Balances 30, 60, 90 and 120+ days late Page 11 Percent of balances 90+ days delinquent by category Page 12 Transitions into 30+ day delinquency Page 13 Transitions into 90+ day delinquency Page 14 Current mortgages becoming 30–60 days late Page 15 Mortgages already 30–60 days late that recover or worsen Page 16 The underlying charts are available, but the retrieved report does not disclose precise current numerical endpoints for every 30- and 60-day series. I have not inferred exact values from a graph. ReportData_template One additional datapoint is important: 10.6% of student-loan balances were already 90+ days overdue in Q2 2026, up from 10.3% in Q1. That is a stock measure, distinct from the annualised transition figure above. ReportData_template Private credit, PIK and defaults Credit stress signal Verified observation Data period / limitation Moody's tracked borrowers using PIK interest 17% of 607 borrowers Reported 27 Oct Fitch-rated BDC realised losses 0.5% First half 2026, not full year Moody's modelled default probability: public BDCs About 0.49% June 2026, forecast probability, not realised default Moody's modelled default probability: Baa corporates About 0.25% June 2026, different credit universe Moody's reported PIK income share of public BDCs Approximately 8% Compared with about 5.5% in 2021 Redemption requests at some non-traded vehicles Approximately 10.5% Spring 2026, limited sample Reuters +2 The 17% figure does not mean 17% have defaulted. PIK is an interest-payment arrangement. It may support liquidity temporarily but can increase outstanding debt and create refinancing pressure. Moody's also estimated a 2025 private-credit default range of 1.6–4.7%, depending on treatment of distressed exchanges and the relevant sample. It is not directly comparable with the modelled BDC probabilities in the table. Moody's Commercial real estate and bank loans The FDIC's Q2 2026 banking profile graph book remains a useful official source for noncurrent loans, past-due and nonaccrual balances, charge-offs, CRE and bank-lending categories. FDIC Q2 2026 Quarterly Banking Profile Graph Book I could verify the underlying Q2 2026 reporting period but not a complete current set of CRE delinquency percentages from the retrieved pages. Consequently, no unsupported point estimates are presented. Distinguishing types of credit deterioration Status What it actually means 30 days late An early contractual payment delay 60 days late A more persistent arrears problem 90+ days late Serious delinquency, not necessarily a completed default event Nonaccrual Lender no longer recognises interest on the usual accrual basis PIK interest Interest added to debt or paid through additional securities Distressed exchange A restructuring that can count as default under rating-agency definitions Payment default A borrower misses a contractual obligation, subject to relevant grace periods Bankruptcy A legal restructuring or insolvency process Charge-off A lender recognises a loan loss in its accounts Watch point: The strongest warning is not one isolated high delinquency rate. It is a sequence in which new arrears rise, cure rates deteriorate, interest capitalisation grows and refinancing becomes less available. 6. Duration, spread and leveraged-margin scenarios All calculations below are hypothetical risk illustrations, not valuations of any client holdings. They exclude coupon accrual, financing interest, fees, FX changes and changes in bank asset recognition. Scenario A: Long Treasury yield shocks Assume a hypothetical 30-year Treasury exposure with modified duration of 16 and convexity of 300. Δ 𝑃 𝑃 ≈ − 𝐷 Δ 𝑦 + 1 2 𝐶 ( Δ 𝑦 ) 2 P ΔP ​ ≈−DΔy+ 2 1 ​ C(Δy) 2 Yield shock Estimated bond price move −100bp +17.500% −50bp +8.375% +50bp −7.625% +100bp −14.500% These are second-order mathematical approximations, not observed security prices. A 2041 Treasury, 2044 Treasury and STRIP maturing in 2054 would have different sensitivities. Scenario B: IG bond exposed to both Treasury and spread shocks Assumptions: hypothetical corporate bond with duration 7 and convexity 60. Treasury change Credit-spread change Total yield change Estimated price move 0bp +100bp +100bp −6.700% +50bp +50bp +100bp −6.700% +50bp +100bp +150bp −9.825% +100bp +100bp +200bp −12.800% For the +150bp scenario: − 7 ( 0.015 ) + 1 2 ( 60 ) ( 0.015 ) 2 = − 0.09825 −7(0.015)+ 2 1 ​ (60)(0.015) 2 =−0.09825 Credit spread and Treasury movements are kept distinct before combining their effect on price. Scenario C: Hypothetical leveraged Treasury investment Assume, for demonstration only: Item Value Initial bond market value US$1,000,000 Loan outstanding US$700,000 Initial investor equity US$300,000 Illustrative maximum LTV 75% Starting borrowing headroom US$50,000 This 75% LTV is not an OCBC lending rule or security-specific recognition rate. Borrowing headroom formula: 𝐻 = 0.75 × Bond Market Value − 700 , 000 H=0.75×Bond Market Value−700,000 Yield shock Bond value Investor equity Borrowing headroom −50bp $1,083,750 $383,750 +$112,812.50 No change $1,000,000 $300,000 +$50,000 +50bp $923,750 $223,750 −$7,187.50 +100bp $855,000 $155,000 −$58,750 At +100bp, the investor has an estimated US$145,000 mark-to-market equity loss and a US$58,750 shortfall against the illustrative LTV threshold. A negative headroom figure is the collateral shortfall under these assumptions. It does not mean the investor's equity is negative. For a CHF-financed portfolio, the actual outcome would also depend on CHF loan balance, accrued interest, collateral-recognition rules and CHF/USD movements. None of those personal inputs have been invented. 7. Strategy, risks and actionable watchlist Risk Current reading Portfolio action Long Treasury duration 30Y yield 5.32% Stage exposure and quantify DV01/convexity IG credit Index OAS 86bp Demand adequate spread for issuer and liquidity risk HY credit Index OAS 314bp Separate broad spread tightening from distressed issuer cases AI infrastructure debt Large SPV and equipment financing Map borrower, guarantor, tenant and collateral separately Private-credit maturity wall Moody's highlights 2027–2029 Review debt maturity ladders and interest coverage PIK / nonaccrual Growing relevance in weaker credit Track cash interest received versus accounting income CRE and consumer late payments Mixed Q2 household trends Monitor progression from 30-day to 90+ delinquency Leveraged portfolios Large downside sensitivity under yield shocks Preserve collateral headroom and unencumbered liquidity For a Singapore private-banking portfolio, the practical priority is to avoid treating yield, coupon, carry, unrealised P&L and borrowing capacity as interchangeable numbers. A bond yielding 6.8% with a 200bp issuance spread is a fundamentally different exposure from a Treasury yielding 5.32%, even if both are USD-denominated. Once funded through a CHF loan, there is a further layer of collateral and FX risk. 8. Infrastructure leasing, tenant quality and long-term debt repayment risks. Final investment assessment Three observations stand out. First, Treasury duration and corporate credit should not be conflated. A 30-year government bond can lose substantial market value without any credit deterioration, while an IG corporate issuer may face additional spread widening. Second, AI debt is increasingly being transformed through project vehicles, equipment collateral and financial guarantees. The borrower, asset owner, customer and ultimate risk-bearer may be different entities. The BIS and S&P research make that distinction particularly important. Third, the credit cycle should be monitored through cash payments, not only ratings and quoted yields. Rising PIK utilisation, weakening loan cures, higher nonaccruals and refinancing dependence can reveal deterioration before headline defaults rise. For bond positioning: Preserve liquidity and collateral headroom, accumulate long duration selectively, favour transparent credit structures, and require meaningful compensation for subordinated or illiquid exposures. For client conversations: A higher coupon is not the same as a safer investment. The relevant question is whether the borrower can continue paying and whether the investor can hold the security through volatility without being forced to sell. entries.text: 2026-11-05 IREN discloses Microsoft-requested network changes and revised deployment timing IREN says Microsoft requested a network design change across its Horizon deployments. entries.text: 2026-11-06 Coverage correction: Microsoft reportedly winds down Oracle AI-capacity rental Late-observed evidence, published by Reuters November 6 at 17:46:46 UTC: Bloomberg, citing unnamed sources, reported Microsoft was winding down Oracle capacity after nonrenewal. entries.text: 2026-11-07 Berkshire steps up buybacks as insurance weakness lowers operating earnings Berkshire's November 7 original release reports Q3 operating earnings of $12.705 billion versus $13.485 billion a year earlier, a calculated decline of 5.8%. It repurchased approximately $9.6 billion of shares during Q3, bringing nine-month repurchases to $14.4 billion. After-tax insurance underwriting earnings fell to $1.352 billion from $2.369 billion, while insurance investment income fell to $2.734 billion from $3.181 billion. BNSF, Berkshire Hathaway Energy and manufacturing/service/retailing earnings increased. GAAP net earnings were $22.112 billion versus $30.796 billion. Operating earnings are a non-GAAP measure excluding investment gains/losses and specified impairments; Berkshire warns that investment valuation movements can make quarterly net earnings misleading. The original 10-Q reports $352.3 billion in cash, equivalents and Treasury bills at insurance and other businesses, net of payables for September purchases settling in October. This is a specifically scoped liquidity measure, not cash alone. Research analysis: Faster repurchases demonstrate capital deployment but do not offset the operating deterioration in insurance. Growth in non-insurance subsidiaries provided a partial earnings cushion. Repurchases alone do not establish that the shares are undervalued. GEICO's Q3 loss ratio rose to 76.6% from 71.5%, with higher claims frequency/severity and lower average earned premiums per policy. Buybacks remain discretionary. The saved November 6 closing price predates this Saturday release and is not an earnings reaction. The next regular US trading session's response, subsequent repurchase disclosures, and whether GEICO claims costs and insurance investment income stabilize. No direction of share-price response is predicted. This is a screenshot-based reconciliation, not a broker statement or independently audited track record. SPY closed-trade review: premium captured and risk released 2026-11-05T06:22:19Z 2026-11-05T07:03:24Z public Historical closed round trips; expiries differ Approved redacted summary of the dated private report. Original account evidence is not published. Summary Seven closed round trips reconciled to US$446 of gross trading P/L in the reviewed order-chain screenshots. The six short-put trades contributed US$417 and the separate short-call trade contributed US$29. This is a screenshot-based reconciliation, not a broker statement or independently audited track record. Visual 1: Profit bridge US$1,376 opening credits - US$930 closing buybacks = US$446 gross P/L. Chart: opening credits in blue, buybacks in amber and gross profit in green. Label 32.41% as the proportion of opening credit retained, not return on account equity or return on margin. Visual 2: Closed-trade ledger All expiries below are in 2026. Prices are per share, with a 100-share contract multiplier. | Option | Contracts | Sold | Bought back | Gross P/L | Opening credit captured | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | US$600 put, 31 December | 2 | US$1.73 | US$1.04 | +US$138 | 39.88% | | US$635 put, 31 December | 2 | US$2.15 | US$1.53 | +US$124 | 28.84% | | US$590 put, 31 December | 1 | US$1.55 | US$0.94 | +US$61 | 39.35% | | US$590 put, 4 December | 1 | US$0.64 | US$0.35 | +US$29 | 45.31% | | US$600 put, 4 December | 1 | US$0.72 | US$0.39 | +US$33 | 45.83% | | US$595 put, 4 December | 1 | US$0.69 | US$0.37 | +US$32 | 46.38% | | US$805 call, 18 December | 1 | US$2.40 | US$2.11 | +US$29 | 12.08% | | Total | 9 contracts across 7 round trips | | | +US$446 | 32.41% overall | Why close early? The six puts captured 28.84% to 46.38% of their starting credit in approximately 27 to 50 hours. Buying them back crystallised US$417 of gross put gains and ended those positions' future assignment exposure. Pursuing the remaining US$719 of put premium would have kept downside and margin risk open. The US$805 call was a separate, later trade and captured only 12.08% of its starting credit. It opened after the puts had closed. It must not be described as part of a simultaneous short-strangle position, and an uncovered short call can have unlimited upside loss. Visual 3: Risk diagram Eight short puts → 800 shares on full assignment → US$484,500 combined strike purchase obligation. A hypothetical additional US$50 fall per assigned share → 800 × US$50 = US$40,000 further share-price loss. Use three separately labelled boxes: assignment purchase obligation, broker margin requirement and discretionary downside reserve. Do not add them together as though they were the same thing. Margin and evidence limits The exact return on margin cannot be established from these screenshots. Historical peak broker buying-power reduction is missing. Do not use the earlier ten-put proposal's buying-power figure for the different executed trades, and do not add the later call's requirement to the puts' peak as though they overlapped. These listed trades were already closed at the review date. Hypothetical hold-to-expiry figures are counterfactuals, not outstanding positions or promises of further income. Visual 1: Three-stage quote and valuation table | Measure | Initial reference | 30 October review | 31 October update | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | QQQ snapshot | US$721.25 | US$715.28 | US$690.53 | | Put premium per share | US$46.50 reconstructed | US$51.96 bid | US$64.27 bid | | Eight-contract value | US$37,200 | US$41,568 | US$51,416 | | Conditional gain | US$0 | +US$4,368 | +US$14,216 | Chart: use three separate labelled observations, not a continuous live-price series. Reference cost is reconstructed; later values are indicative bid-side marks. Purpose and outcome The plan was temporary protection through an earnings window, with an intended exit one week after entry. A longer option expiry was chosen to reduce estimated short-holding-period time decay. The stated purpose was protection against a repricing associated with AI capital spending, cash-flow pressure and debt-service concerns, rather than a claim that a particular company would fail. The later update showed a larger dollar gain but a smaller proportion of the illustrative stock loss offset. The report's QQQ-equivalent portfolio comparison showed 47.68% of the reference loss offset, versus 75.39% in the earlier review. Actual stock holdings and their returns were not established. Visual 2: Normalized hedge comparison Normalize the stock sleeve to 100 reference units. Fund the option premium separately at 5.3143 units, so both cases start with 105.3143 total units. | At the 31 October snapshot | Without hedge | With the assumed puts | | --- | ---: | ---: | | Stock-sleeve change | -4.2593 units | -4.2593 units | | Hedge contribution | 0.0000 units | +2.0309 units | | Combined change | -4.2593 units | -2.2284 units | | Stock loss offset | 0.00% | 47.68% | Chart: two loss bars, with the hedge contribution shown as a green bridge. Label this a normalized hypothetical portfolio, not personal account performance. Costs and limitations Time decay was one component of cost, not a fixed insurance bill. Starting Greeks suggested approximately US$660 of seven-day theta for the eight-put example if price and implied volatility were unchanged. Price moves, volatility changes, bid-ask spreads and execution costs could produce very different results. These snapshots do not establish a completed one-week hedge or a realized return. The latest midpoint would imply a US$14,908 gain, but midpoint is not an assured fill. Fees, financing, dividends, tax and slippage are excluded, and a QQQ proxy cannot establish the performance of a different stock portfolio. entries.title: Three questions before any market headline
entries.text: starting-point Three questions before any market headline Start here Ask what is happening in the economy, what is already priced into investments, and what reaches your own pocket. These reports become easier to understand once the three questions are kept separate. The economy describes activity, jobs and prices. Markets put a price today on an uncertain future. Your personal outcome also depends on the price you paid, the currency you spend, fees, financing and when you need your money back. Strong growth can coexist with a disappointing investment return if buyers already paid for even better growth. A highly rated borrower can issue a bond whose market price swings sharply. An overseas portfolio can gain in its own currency yet deliver a much smaller gain in SGD. These are different mechanisms, so a single green or red headline is usually inadequate. Use the MAS October review to understand Singapore’s current growth, inflation and policy backdrop. Use JPMorgan to explain global markets and investment mechanics. Use MAS, GIC and Temasek annual reports to understand institutional roles and measurement. The three supplied written reports are secondary analyses: their claims need the underlying official sources. The reading order in this briefing follows those links. It moves from growth and inflation to equities, rates and credit, then currency, public finances, institutions and private markets. All quoted numbers retain the source’s own displayed precision. A source-published rounded figure is not converted into a falsely exact economic measurement. A useful market update explains a cause, a possible consequence and a decision to monitor. It should help the reader ask a better question. The review date of this briefing is 31 October 2026. The charts are dated snapshots, not live prices or a claim that all figures describe the same day. Begin each client discussion with spending currency, time horizon, cash needs and ability to withstand a temporary loss. mas-macro jpm-markets jpm-alternatives Explanation with dated evidence

entries.title: Why strong Singapore growth can still feel uneven
entries.text: singapore-growth Why strong Singapore growth can still feel uneven Singapore Technology is doing much of the heavy lifting; a strong national figure does not mean every sector is thriving. The MAS October review reports Q3 2026 GDP growth of 5.4% year on year and 1.1% quarter on quarter after seasonal adjustment. These are advance estimates. The two figures answer different questions: the first compares with the same quarter a year earlier; the second compares with the immediately preceding quarter after removing recurring seasonal patterns. Technology-related industries accounted for around 75% of year-on-year growth in Q3, according to MAS. That is a share of the increase in output, not a claim that technology is 75% of Singapore’s economy. The same page identifies technology-related industries as 22.1% of nominal value added in 2025. Confusing the level of activity with its contribution to growth would substantially overstate the sector’s size. The practical picture is an uneven expansion. Electronics, machinery, related trade and information services benefit from AI investment. Other parts of the economy face different demand and cost conditions. MAS describes weakness in some consumer-facing businesses and pressure on oil-related industries even while the headline economy expands. MAS expects the technology expansion to continue into 2027 at a more measured pace. This is its baseline assessment, not a promise. A slowdown in growth means output is rising less quickly; it does not automatically mean a recession. The vulnerability is that a narrower engine leaves the economy more exposed if AI spending or its financing disappoints. Think of a company whose best division generates most of the additional profit. The company can be growing strongly while other divisions struggle. Do not treat strong GDP as a buy signal for every Singapore company, property or fund. Sector earnings, balance sheets and prices still differ. Watch whether growth broadens beyond technology, whether semiconductor orders hold up, and whether jobs and household spending follow. mas-macro mas-oct2026-p21 Published observations and MAS outlook

entries.title: Why MAS cares about the SGD basket
entries.text: inflation-sgd Why MAS cares about the SGD basket Singapore Singapore uses the exchange rate to help control imported inflation; USD/SGD is only one part of that policy picture. MAS Core Inflation rose from 1.5% in Q2 2026 to 2.1% in July–August. The October review forecasts core inflation of 1.5–2.0% for 2026 and 1.5–2.5% for 2027. These are forecasts for annual averages, not a ceiling on every monthly reading. Core inflation excludes accommodation and private transport; it is not identical to a particular household’s cost-of-living change. Inflation describes how fast prices rise. If inflation slows, prices can still be increasing. It is the difference between climbing stairs more slowly and going back downstairs. Energy, food, transport, wages, subsidies and competition can move differently, so the components matter as much as the headline. MAS maintained the prevailing appreciation rate of the S$NEER policy band in October 2026, after tightening in April and July. S$NEER is a trade-weighted currency measure. The bilateral USD/SGD rate is the price of one currency against another. An appreciating basket can coexist with SGD weakness against a particular currency, because the other basket currencies also move. For households, a stronger SGD can soften imported costs. For an investor with unhedged overseas assets, it can reduce the value translated back into SGD. Those effects can occur together. MAS’s policy objective concerns price stability in Singapore; maximising the SGD accounting return on foreign reserves is a different objective. The review’s inflation research separates external demand, external supply and domestic forces. It estimates that external factors explain about 68% of the inflation variation captured by its model over the sample. That is a model-based historical decomposition, not a statement that 68% of each household bill is imported. The policy implications depend on the source and persistence of the shock. The same stronger dollar that makes some imported goods cheaper can make an overseas investment look smaller on an SGD statement. A fall in USD/SGD alone does not measure the full MAS policy stance. Neither the basket path nor the inflation forecast guarantees a particular future FX rate. Separate a household’s SGD cash requirements from long-term foreign assets. Read the latest policy decision alongside inflation components and actual bilateral rates. mas-macro mas-oct2026-p10 mas-oct2026-p29 Published data and labelled forecasts

entries.title: Who pays for the AI buildout
entries.text: ai-financing Who pays for the AI buildout Equities Demand can be strong while the bill for future capacity rises even faster than cash generation. JPMorgan’s page 22 groups Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle. It shows total company capital expenditure of US$416 billion in 2025, with consensus forecasts of US$799 billion in 2026, US$1,093 billion in 2027 and US$1,200 billion in 2028. The last three are forecasts. The measure is total company capex, not a directly measured AI-only spending total. Operating cash flow is cash generated from running a business. Capital expenditure pays for long-lived assets such as equipment and buildings. On the slide, free cash flow is operating cash flow minus capex. A company can report accounting profit while free cash flow is weak because it is spending heavily on future capacity. That does not by itself prove insolvency, but it changes the funding question. MAS provides a useful second view. Page 23 compares semiconductor production conditions with a composite indicator of hyperscalers’ capacity to sustain capex. The latter considers cash-flow margins, leverage and investment intensity. Its company universe differs from JPMorgan’s and includes CoreWeave. These are analytical indices, not an observable default probability or a reproducible bank credit score. The connection is straightforward: suppliers can enjoy strong orders today while customers take on larger financing commitments. If future AI revenue justifies the spending, the expansion may endure. If monetisation disappoints, buyers may reduce capex, lenders may demand better terms and suppliers may face weaker orders. MAS describes this as a downside risk, while judging near-term backlogs and commitments supportive. For a portfolio, inspect the shared economic exposure. Technology equities, semiconductor suppliers, data-centre property, power infrastructure and private credit to the same ecosystem may all respond to one investment cycle. Different product labels do not ensure different underlying risks. A restaurant can be busy and profitable while borrowing heavily to open many new outlets. The question is whether the new outlets eventually earn enough to justify the cost. Large capex is neither proof of a bubble nor proof of an attractive investment. Aggregate cash-flow charts cannot establish whether an individual borrower can service its debts. Track cash generation against capex, debt and lease commitments, refinancing needs, customer contracts and actual monetisation. entries.title: Does owning hundreds of shares spread risk evenly
entries.text: equity-concentration Does owning hundreds of shares spread risk evenly Equities An index can own many names while a small group still drives much of its value. At 30 September 2026, JPMorgan shows the ten largest S&P 500 constituents at 40.6% of market capitalisation and 36.1% of trailing earnings. A market-cap-weighted index puts more money into larger companies. Counting the number of holdings therefore does not tell you how evenly the risk is spread. The earnings share also matters. The largest companies contribute substantial profits as well as substantial market value. Concentration alone does not prove prices are irrational. It tells you which companies and business drivers can most influence results, and where earnings disappointment could be consequential. JPMorgan’s valuation page reports a forward P/E of 19.0 times against its 30-year average of 17.2 times. Forward P/E is price divided by forecast earnings. A higher ratio means paying more for each unit of expected profit. If the earnings forecast changes, the valuation can change even without a move in the share price. CAPE, also shown in the guide, uses a long historical average of inflation-adjusted earnings. It is a different measurement, so its number should not be compared directly with forward P/E as if one were an alternative price quote. Valuation measures help frame expectations; they do not provide a date for a market correction. For a Singapore investor, add a currency lens. A U.S. index chart generally describes the U.S. market in USD. The return in SGD depends on the exchange rate and any hedging. Owning an S&P 500 fund, a technology fund and several megacap shares may add overlapping exposure rather than meaningful new diversification. A supermarket basket with hundreds of items can still be dominated by a few expensive purchases. The number of items does not determine where most of the money went. A historical average is not a fair-value guarantee. Concentration can persist, and expensive markets can keep rising. Review the largest underlying holdings across all funds and direct shares. Compare business drivers, regions, currencies and valuation assumptions before adding another product. jpm-markets jpm-gtm-p8 jpm-gtm-p5 30 September 2026 snapshot

entries.title: Why a strong borrower can have a volatile bond
entries.text: bond-duration Why a strong borrower can have a volatile bond Bonds Credit quality concerns repayment; duration concerns how much the price moves when required yields change. A fixed-rate bond promises a stream of payments. If comparable new bonds offer a higher yield, buyers usually pay less for the old payment stream. If required yields fall, the old stream becomes more attractive. The issuer can remain financially sound throughout this repricing. Maturity is the date principal is due. Duration measures sensitivity to a change in yield. A long maturity and low coupon often leave more of a bond’s value dependent on distant payments, increasing its rate sensitivity. Convexity describes the bend in the price–yield relationship; it explains why a simple straight-line estimate becomes less accurate for larger moves. JPMorgan page 34 illustrates total-return scenarios under a parallel shift in the yield curve. The printed figures below show how the range widens at longer maturities. The slide does not explicitly state the scenario horizon, so these should be described as the publisher’s illustrations, not independently verified one-year forecasts. Long yields are influenced by more than the next central-bank meeting. Inflation expectations, the compensation for holding long debt, government borrowing needs and supply can all matter. MAS’s October financial-conditions chapter describes rising long government yields even alongside resilient equity markets. Holding to maturity changes the decision if contractual payments are met and the investor can hold. It does not remove inflation, currency, funding or collateral risk. A financed investor might be forced to sell before maturity, turning an interim price fall into a realised loss. This is why duration must be assessed together with liquidity and borrowing terms. A reliable tenant does not make the resale price of a long rental contract stable when market rents and interest rates change. These publisher illustrations are not prices or P&L forecasts for a specific Temasek or Treasury holding. They exclude the investor’s own FX, fees, financing and margin arrangements. Compare duration and maturity separately. Stress the relevant part of the curve, and check the cash and collateral available to survive the path. jpm-markets mas-macro jpm-gtm-p34 mas-oct2026-p9 Treasury maturity Yield falls 1 percentage point No yield change Yield rises 1 percentage point 2 years 6.8% 4.9% 3.0% 10 years 13.1% 5.3% −2.5% 30 years 20.3% 5.6% −9.0% Exact displayed scenario values from JPMorgan page 34. entries.title: Is a high bond yield good compensation for risk
entries.text: credit-spread Is a high bond yield good compensation for risk Bonds A bond can offer a high total yield while paying only a small extra amount for the company’s credit risk. A useful breakdown is a government or near-risk-free reference yield plus compensation for credit, liquidity and other bond features. This is a pricing guide, not an exact universal identity. Credit spread is not the coupon and not the entire yield. One basis point equals 0.01 percentage point. JPMorgan page 36 shows investment-grade option-adjusted spreads of 80 basis points versus a 144 basis-point long-run average in its chart. High-yield spreads are 311 basis points versus 498. Yet displayed yields to worst are 6.0% and 8.3%. Much of the attractive-looking yield therefore comes from the wider interest-rate environment, while the extra credit compensation is relatively narrow. This distinction matters when deciding between taking more duration and taking weaker credit. They expose the portfolio to different problems. Government yields can rise even if an issuer’s business is healthy. Credit spreads can widen even if government yields are unchanged. Both can happen together. An average spread does not establish the value of an individual bond. Seniority, covenants, cash flows, refinancing dates, liquidity and recovery prospects differ. The default chart on the same JPMorgan slide also uses different treatment of distressed exchanges across some categories. A reader should retain that methodology rather than turning the chart into a simple ranking of all default risks. The base rental market can be expensive even when the extra rent for accepting a troublesome tenant is small. Total income and compensation for a particular risk are different questions. Tight spreads do not prove an imminent sell-off. High yield does not guarantee a sufficient cushion against defaults or spread widening. Compare the extra yield with the specific risk being accepted. For each issuer, examine cash coverage, maturity schedule, debt structure and the liquidity available to exit. jpm-markets jpm-gtm-p36 30 September 2026 snapshot Investment grade High yield Option-adjusted spread 80 bps 311 bps Long-run average in chart 144 bps 498 bps Displayed yield to worst 6.0% 8.3% Figures retain the source’s displayed precision. The long-run averages use the chart’s historical window, not a promised normal level. Dated credit-market observations

entries.title: Why a USD gain can shrink in SGD
entries.text: fx-return Why a USD gain can shrink in SGD Currency The investment return and the currency conversion multiply; they do not simply subtract. Define the exchange rate as SGD received for one USD. If an investment’s USD value changes by r and this exchange rate changes by f over the same measurement period, a simplified return with no intermediate external flows is (1 + r) × (1 + f) − 1 in SGD. This convention matters: quoting the inverse exchange rate changes the calculation. The supplied USD sensitivity report uses a 5.60% USD return and a 3.00% annual USD decline against SGD over a matched annualised horizon. The exact arithmetic is 1.056 × 0.97 − 1 = 0.02432 = 2.432%. The original report displayed 2.43% because it explicitly rounded to two decimal places. This briefing preserves the exact computed value. There is a major interpretation limit. GIC’s 5.6% is a historical twenty-year annualised USD return, not a next-year forecast. Pairing it with assumed future FX weakness is a conditional illustration. It does not reveal GIC’s direct net USD position, currency hedges or an expected future SGD return. Changing the reporting currency of a diversified global portfolio is also different from measuring how much the portfolio is economically exposed to one currency. Non-USD assets can themselves rise in USD terms when USD weakens. Company revenues, costs, borrowing and hedging can pull in different directions. For an actual bond portfolio, coupon payment dates, conversion rates, fees and financing cash flows require their own dated ledger. A simple terminal-return identity should not be used to silently approximate those flows. For a household, the relevant question remains what purchasing power is available in the currency of future spending. The investment can grow in dollars while each dollar buys fewer Singapore dollars. Both steps affect the final SGD result. The 3% FX move is a stated scenario from the supplied analysis, not a forecast by MAS. The institutional reports do not disclose enough to estimate a precise common USD sensitivity for MAS, GIC and Temasek. Show investment P&L, income, FX effects, fees and financing separately, then reconcile them. Match the currency and horizon before comparing returns. gic-2026 mas-2026 temasek-2026 Assumed annual USD weakening USD return assumption Exact converted SGD return 0% 5.60% 5.6% 1% 5.60% 4.544% 2% 5.60% 3.488% 3% 5.60% 2.432% 4% 5.60% 1.376% 5% 5.60% 0.32% Derived from inputs already shown in supplied Report 2. entries.title: Where Singapore’s government revenue comes from
entries.text: public-finances Where Singapore’s government revenue comes from Singapore Taxes and other operating revenue are one stream; the permitted investment-return contribution is another. A household analogy helps: recurring earnings fund spending, while accumulated savings can also generate income. Singapore’s system has a specific constitutional framework, so the analogy should not be taken as an exact household budget. The important distinction is between the reserve principal, investment returns and the amount available for annual spending. The audited FY2025/26 government accounts show operating revenue of S$130,049,822,095.34 and Net Investment Returns Contribution of S$27,522,875,864.50. Adding those two reported values gives S$157,572,697,959.84. This sum describes revenue before deducting expenditure; it is not the fiscal surplus or a measure of total reserves. IRAS collections are already inside government operating revenue. IRAS’s 4 September 2026 release reports S$97.3 billion collected in FY2025/26, up 9.4%, representing 74.8% of government operating revenue at the release’s published precision. Adding that S$97.3 billion again would count much of the same revenue twice. NIRC includes up to 50% of expected long-term real returns on relevant net assets invested by GIC, MAS and Temasek, plus up to 50% of net investment income on remaining past reserves. Real means after inflation. Relevant net assets account for government liabilities. It is not simply half of this year’s combined accounting profit or dividends. This approach helps smooth spending across market cycles. A weak investment year does not mechanically cut the budget by the same amount. Persistent changes in asset values or expected long-term returns can still affect resources over time, so smoothing does not mean markets are irrelevant. Land-sale proceeds add to reserves rather than ordinary spendable operating revenue. The supplied revenue report was prepared in August 2026. Its statement that the latest IRAS series ends at FY2024/25 is now outdated. Its FY2026/27 total of approximately S$163.23 billion is derived using rounded components; MOF’s own published total is S$163.24 billion. Use the publisher’s aggregate at its stated precision and retain the rounding caveat. Keep FY2026/27 budget estimates separate from FY2025/26 audited actuals. The spending allowance from a long-term investment pool is not the same as the pool’s market gain in one year. Do not add IRAS to operating revenue, treat land-sale receipts as ordinary tax revenue, or add MAS, GIC and Temasek totals into a national-wealth figure. Internal claims and different measurement bases would need reconciliation. Use AGD for audited actuals, MOF for the current budget and NIRC rules, and IRAS for agency collections. Preserve fiscal-year labels and classification changes. budget-actual budget-estimate iras-2026 nirc reserves FY2025/26 audited values SGD Operating revenue 130,049,822,095.34 NIRC 27,522,875,864.50 Sum of the two revenue components 157,572,697,959.84 AGD Statement of Budget Outturn, physical PDF page 17 / printed page 9. Sum is calculated exactly from the displayed audited amounts; it is not the budget surplus. Audited actuals with separately labelled estimates

entries.title: How MAS can have an FX drag and still make a profit
entries.text: mas-accounts How MAS can have an FX drag and still make a profit Currency Currency translation is one part of the result; investment gains, liquidity-management costs and other expenses also matter. MAS holds foreign reserves for central-bank purposes while reporting its accounts in SGD. A foreign-currency asset can be unchanged in its own units yet translate into fewer SGD when SGD strengthens. That alone does not remove the foreign currency available for policy operations. The supplied FY2024/25 infographic is an accessible example: investment gains of S$31.4 billion, negative currency translation of S$3.4 billion and net money-market-operation and other costs of S$8.3 billion produce reported net profit of S$19.7 billion at the infographic’s displayed precision. It is a historical year, not the October 2026 result. The separately verified FY2025/26 MAS speech reports investment gains of S$39.8 billion, translation drag of S$16.4 billion, net money-market-operation and other costs of S$2.4 billion and a S$1.0 billion Consolidated Fund contribution. The reported net profit is S$20.0 billion. Showing only the S$16.4 billion drag would give an incomplete picture. The FY2021/22 statements provide the opposite historical example: an overall loss despite positive investment gains. That year’s main translation effects involved EUR, JPY and GBP. FY2025/26’s explanation principally involves USD and JPY. It would be inaccurate to describe all three years as simply USD losses. There are further measurement distinctions. MAS’s accounts have Group and Authority columns; its accounting investment result is not a fully comparable fund NAV total return. Liquidity operations incur interest costs and have policy objectives. A Consolidated Fund contribution, a later distribution of profit and NIRC are different fiscal concepts. For an individual who needs SGD to pay a mortgage or school fees, an FX translation reduction can be economically important. The fact that MAS can continue to conduct policy with its foreign assets does not imply a household should ignore its own currency mismatch. Read the whole income statement. A large deduction can coexist with a positive final result when other gains are larger. Headline amounts use issuer rounding. The FY2021/22 cost definition differs from later net-cost figures, so do not force those rounded components into a common exact waterfall. Net USD exposures and full hedges are not disclosed. Pair FX effects with the total result, state the affected currencies and period, and distinguish institutional policy capacity from personal SGD purchasing power. mas-2025-info mas-2025-accounts mas-2022-accounts mas-2022-info mas-2022-speech mas-2026 mas-fy2025-results mas-fy2022-highlights Financial year Investment gains Negative FX translation Reported net result 2021/22 S$4.0bn S$8.7bn −S$7.4bn 2024/25 S$31.4bn S$3.4bn +S$19.7bn 2025/26 update S$39.8bn S$16.4bn +S$20.0bn Published headline precision. Other costs and contributions affect the net result; these three columns alone are not a complete reconciliation. Historical uploaded evidence plus verified newer update

entries.title: Why MAS, GIC and Temasek need different scorecards
entries.text: gic-temasek Why MAS, GIC and Temasek need different scorecards Singapore They have different jobs, portfolios and measurement systems; their headline results are not a league table. MAS is a central bank and needs liquid foreign reserves for monetary policy and financial stability. GIC manages government assets for long-term global purchasing power. Temasek is an investment company that owns its portfolio assets and reports shareholder returns. Their objectives, funding arrangements and investment flexibility differ. GIC’s uploaded FY2024/25 report explains its rolling twenty-year horizon. The separately verified FY2025/26 release reports 5.6% annualised nominal USD return and 3.4% annualised real return for the twenty years ended 31 March 2026. These are compounded annualised results over twenty years, not returns earned in just FY2025/26. A rolling figure can change because an old year drops out as well as because a new year enters. The historical GIC asset mix on page 14 is useful for explaining diversification. It is not a prescription for a client. GIC’s funding horizon and ability to hold private investments are different from a household’s. Its 2026 release also announces a Strategic Portfolio framework, so the older Reference Portfolio description should not be presented as the unqualified current framework. Temasek’s uploaded 2025 highlights reported S$434 billion net portfolio value, with a further S$35 billion uplift if the remaining unlisted investments were marked to market. The same-date comparable value was S$469 billion. The 2026 release reports S$518 billion after the full transition to mark-to-market reporting. The comparable increase is S$49 billion, not S$84 billion. Keep the bridge in sequence: S$434 billion plus S$35 billion equals S$469 billion at 31 March 2025; S$469 billion plus S$49 billion equals S$518 billion at 31 March 2026. The first step changes valuation basis at the same date. The second is the change between dates. Net portfolio value movements are not automatically identical to an investment return because capital flows and shareholder distributions can matter. Temasek’s 2026 one-year TSR was 10.5% in SGD, 12.9% at constant currency and 14.8% in USD. The arithmetic constant-currency gap is 2.4 percentage points. It reflects foreign-currency exposures collectively, not a disclosed USD-only loss. Headquarters, underlying business geography and currency exposure are also different classifications. Judge a hospital, an insurer and an investment fund against their own jobs. Comparing one headline number without its mandate and measurement would miss the purpose. Do not infer full government reserves, an undisclosed GIC asset base, or each entity’s NIRC allocation from these reports. Do not treat a valuation-method change as an investment gain. Compare like periods, like currencies and like valuation methods. Use institutions to learn process and discipline, then adapt to the client’s actual liabilities and liquidity needs. gic-2025 gic-2026 temasek-2025 temasek-2026 mas-2025-accounts nirc gic-fy2025-horizon gic-fy2025-allocation temasek-fy2025-overview Historical framework with current source corrections

entries.title: Why Temasek USD and SGD bonds have different prices
entries.text: temasek-bonds Why Temasek USD and SGD bonds have different prices Bonds The payment currency, coupon and discount curve can create very different prices even with the same guarantor. The issuer’s official register confirms the four bonds below. They are issued by Temasek Financial (I) Limited and guaranteed by Temasek Holdings (Private) Limited. Temasek explicitly states that its bonds are not guaranteed by the Singapore Government. The guarantee concerns contractual payments, not a stable market price or ready resale liquidity. A USD cash flow is valued against the USD interest-rate environment and relevant issuer spread. An SGD cash flow is valued against the SGD environment. A low fixed coupon becomes less competitive when the market requires a higher yield, so the price may fall well below face value. A higher-coupon bond can trade above face value and still offer a lower yield than its coupon. The supplied bilingual report uses two snapshot dates: 14 August 2026 for the 2039 examples, and 7 August 2026 for the 2070/2071 examples. These can illustrate the mechanism but must not appear as live dealing levels. The 2039 ask prices of 118.040 in SGD and 104.092 in USD are above par, not below par. Their location below an earlier chart high is a different claim. The report’s displayed yield-gap calculations are arithmetically consistent: 2.588% − 2.313% = 0.275 percentage point = 27.5 basis points, and 4.950% − 4.890% = 0.060 percentage point = 6 basis points. These are illustrative comparisons with particular government bonds. Maturity and cash-flow mismatches mean they are not precise option-adjusted or interpolated credit spreads. Pair each price with its own quote side. In the 2070 example, 5.475% is the bid yield paired with the 50.664 bid price, not the 51.076 ask price. The 2071 example likewise shows a 2.975% bid yield. An investor buying at an ask price needs the corresponding ask yield; this cannot be inferred by relabelling the bid yield. Compare total settlement cost and expected cash flows rather than the clean price alone. Clean price excludes accrued interest; the settlement amount normally includes it. Accrued interest paid to the seller should be reconciled with the next coupon in a dated cash-flow calculation. It should not be counted twice or mistaken for a permanent change to the coupon rate. If the starting clean price is already an executable ask, do not add the bid-ask spread again; add accrued interest and only separately charged fees or costs. A financed holding has additional moving parts: borrowing rates, loan currency, recognition ratios, collateral requirements and refinancing. These must use the actual facility terms. No advance ratio or margin-call threshold can be established from these public reports alone. The same company can issue two long-term payment promises in different currencies. Their values depend on what investors require for each currency and payment schedule. A low price alone is not proof of a bargain. High credit quality does not remove duration, FX, liquidity or leverage risks, and the Singapore Government does not guarantee these bonds. Obtain current executable bid/ask prices, settlement dates and terms. Compare yield, duration, spread, spending-currency exposure and ability to hold through volatility. temasek-bonds temasek-guarantee sgs treasury Bond currency and maturity Coupon Regulation S / local ISIN USD · 23 November 2039 5.3750% US87973RAB69 SGD · 7 December 2039 4.2000% SG7U77951360 USD · 6 October 2070 2.5000% US87973RAW07 SGD · 17 August 2071 2.8000% SGXF69044257 Official issue terms, checked 31 October 2026. These are distinct bonds; do not merge a USD issue with the SGD issue sharing a similar maturity year. Verified issue terms; historical price examples only

entries.title: When a statement value is not cash you can withdraw
entries.text: alternatives-liquidity When a statement value is not cash you can withdraw Alternatives Private investments may earn returns while still limiting when, and at what price, you can recover your money. Alternatives is a broad label. Private equity owns companies; private credit lends to borrowers; real estate owns property; infrastructure owns or operates physical assets; hedge funds use varied trading strategies. Their risks are not interchangeable. The useful starting point is the economic source of return and the conditions for turning it back into cash. Private assets are often valued less frequently than exchange-traded securities. A smoother reported line may reflect the valuation process as well as the economics. It does not prove the asset would hold its value if sold immediately. Historical comparisons can also mix private-fund internal rates of return with public-market annual returns, making simple rankings misleading. JPMorgan’s page 58 shows a 4Q 2025 private-equity capital-call rate of 31% of beginning dry powder and a distribution rate of 14% of beginning NAV. These are preliminary rolling twelve-month rates with different denominators. Subtracting 14% from 31% would not calculate a valid net funding gap. A capital call asks an investor to deliver money already committed. A distribution returns cash. A fund can call capital before much cash comes back. An investor’s liquidity plan therefore needs to allow for commitment schedules and delays in exits, rather than assuming a stated annual return is spendable cash. Page 59 shows 2Q 2026 LP-led secondary pricing at 91% of NAV for buyout, 89% for credit, 79% for venture capital and 68% for real estate. These are market aggregates, not firm offers for a particular fund. A discount may reflect illiquidity, uncertainty or an out-of-date NAV; it is not automatically a bargain. Institutional portfolios can offer useful lessons about diversification and manager selection. Copying their allocation without matching their ability to meet future cash needs can create a very different risk. Liquidity is a portfolio property: even attractive long-term holdings can be unsuitable for money needed on a fixed near-term date. Owning a valuable apartment is different from having the sale proceeds in your bank account today. Timing and selling price both matter. Reported volatility, NAV, IRR, cash distributions and executable exit prices are different measures. Do not rank private products using a single yield or past-return figure. Before allocating, map capital commitments, redemption windows, gates, notice periods, valuation methods, fees and the cash reserve needed outside the investment. jpm-alternatives gic-2025 jpm-gta-p58 jpm-gta-p59 Lagged private-market observations with methodology

entries.title: Is all reported interest paid in cash
entries.text: private-credit Is all reported interest paid in cash Alternatives Some interest can be added to debt rather than received in cash, so reported income needs a cash-quality check. Payment in kind, or PIK, is a form of non-cash payment. In a loan context it often adds interest to the outstanding amount instead of paying it immediately. It can be a contractual feature rather than a default. It can also become more relevant when a borrower is conserving cash. JPMorgan page 69 shows PIK at 8.0% of interest and dividend income, on average for the Fitch-rated business development company sample, in 1Q 2026. This does not mean 8.0% of all private loans defaulted. It does not mean 8.0% of a particular fund’s assets are impaired. The population and denominator are essential to understanding the statistic. The same page compares public and private default trends with differing definitions and denominators. Private-credit defaults use counts of defaulted loans relative to loans; the public series uses issuer-based measures. Distressed exchanges also change the apparent default rate. A rewrite that strips away these differences can make a precise-looking chart misleading. For income-oriented clients, ask where the distribution comes from: cash interest, asset sales, borrowing, accumulated income or other sources permitted by the fund structure. A stated distribution rate is not necessarily a sustainable economic return. Asset-level yield and the investor’s net return can also diverge after fees, leverage and losses. The AI connection is worth monitoring, but it should be established issuer by issuer. Private financing can support productive investment; it can also concentrate financing risk in businesses whose revenues arrive later than their interest and capital spending. Aggregate charts identify questions for due diligence, not verdicts on every private-credit fund. Being told that someone owes you more is different from receiving more cash this month. Both may have value, but they fund your spending differently. PIK is not automatically default, and a lower reported default rate is not automatically evidence of a safer market if definitions differ. Review cash interest coverage, PIK share, non-accruals, amendments, leverage, covenants, recoveries and actual cash distributions at the specific fund or borrower level. jpm-alternatives jpm-gta-p69 1Q 2026 income-quality observation; not a default rate
