entries.title: Understanding Creditworthiness | Research Explained
entries.text: Understanding Creditworthiness | Research Explained ← Research Explained INDEPENDENT EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH · 5 NOVEMBER 2026 Can the company pay you back? Understanding creditworthiness, default, recovery and the price of risk. Corrected research edition. Debt generally ranks ahead of common equity. Operating income is not EBITDA. Buybacks are a cash use, not debt. This report uses defined calculations, dated primary sources and no speculative issuer ratings. Company comparisons intentionally use historical FY2025 data, not current ratings or live quotations. Download the complete PDF Check the evidence Read the report Can the company pay you back? How credit analysis is built The six calculations worth learning Default risk: probability is not certainty Recovery: who gets paid first? Credit spread: separate the two prices A bond can lose money without default Read Morningstar beside the 10-K Apple: follow the cash, not just profit Apple: reconcile the denominator Apple: maturities and a cash stress test Peer comparison: investment absorbs cash Five-issuer cash-flow ratio comparison AI infrastructure: find the real obligor Read a financing headline precisely Your repeatable survival checklist Source register AUDITED PUBLIC PRESENTATIONS · 5 NOVEMBER 2026 Two ways to present the research Each PowerPoint has exactly five slides, editable charts and tables, and formatted speaker notes with dated public sources. Financial briefing (PPTX, 45 KB) Clear visual story (PPTX, 52 KB) Historical FY2025 educational examples, not current credit ratings or live quotations. Cash-stress cases are illustrations, not forecasts; the five issuers have different fiscal year ends. Meta’s issue-source access limitation is retained on slide 5 and in its notes. Original explanatory material and public financial snapshots only. Publication details, file hashes and limitations . CHAPTER 01 Can the company pay you back? Creditworthiness is about meeting obligations on time, including when the business disappoints. A practical guide to company survival, bond recovery, default risk and credit spreads. Learn the method, work through Apple, then apply it to AI infrastructure financing. The question The evidence The investor decision Will it pay? Cash generation, liquidity, debt maturities and stress scenarios. Choose an issuer and a maturity you can defend. What if it does not? Collateral, creditor priority, guarantees and enterprise value in distress. Estimate loss severity for the exact instrument. Am I paid enough? Yield, benchmark spread, duration, liquidity and embedded options. Compare compensation against expected loss and uncertainty. Three ideas to carry through the report 1. A profitable company can run out of cash. A low-margin company can survive if its cash flows and funding are resilient. 2. A strong company can issue a risky long-duration bond. Bond price losses do not require default. 3. A wide moat or attractive stock valuation is not a promise that a particular bond is safe. Scope: completed educational analysis, not a personalized recommendation, a rating-agency opinion, or a live bond-price service. Research checked 5 November 2026. Company comparison uses explicitly dated FY2025 statements, not the latest available TTM. Historical data and scenarios are kept separate. Navigation: Use the PDF bookmarks or web contents for navigation. Sources [1-18] are linked in the register. CHAPTER 02 How credit analysis is built There is no single universal creditworthiness formula. Layer Ask this Evidence that changes the answer Business resilience Will customers keep paying through a downturn? Revenue concentration; switching costs; pricing power; cyclicality; regulation. Cash conversion Does accounting profit become spendable cash? Operating cash flow; receivables; inventories; supplier terms; recurring vs one-off effects. Debt burden How much has already been promised? Borrowings; leases; guarantees; pensions; purchase commitments; debt at subsidiaries. Liquidity and time Can the next payment be made without a friendly market? Unrestricted cash; committed facilities; covenant headroom; maturity calendar. Financial policy Who receives surplus cash? Buybacks; dividends; acquisitions; willingness to preserve ratings or deleverage. Instrument protection Where does this bond stand in a failure? Issuer entity; guarantors; collateral; seniority; covenants; governing law. Analysts combine historical ratios with forecasts and judgment. Agency methods differ by sector and adjust accounting data differently. A bank, a property company and a software issuer cannot be ranked fairly using one unadjusted debt/EBITDA threshold. Do not invent an agency grade. Record the actual agency, issuer or instrument, publication date, outlook and watch status. A rating outlook is not an additional notch. A rating is an opinion, not insurance. Basis: independent teaching framework; rating-process distinction supported by Morningstar DBRS [5] . Credit ratings are forward-looking committee opinions, not mechanical scores. CHAPTER 03 The six calculations worth learning Ratios are questions to investigate, not pass/fail rules. Metric / formula What it tells you Main trap Net debt = borrowings - eligible cash Debt after a realistic liquidity offset. Restricted cash, overseas taxes and securities haircuts matter. State whether leases are included. Debt / EBITDA Debt relative to operating earnings before D&A. Adjusted EBITDA can exclude recurring costs; EBITDA is not cash available for principal. EBIT / gross interest expense Operating earnings buffer over financing expense. Do not divide by net interest income. Capitalized interest and leases complicate coverage. CFO - cash capex Simple cash left after investment in fixed assets. Not standardized FCF. Lease principal, acquisitions and shareholder payouts may be additional uses. CFO / debt Annual cash generation relative to borrowings. Working-capital timing and one-off taxes can distort a single year. 12-month sources / uses Near-term funding buffer under a specified scenario. CFO already includes some uses, such as cash interest under US GAAP. Avoid double counting. Build the bridge: cash from operations minus capex minus dividends minus buybacks minus acquisitions minus debt principal, plus new funding and asset sales. Track starting and ending cash separately. For a simple liquidity forecast using CFO, do not subtract the same cash interest or working-capital outflow a second time. If starting from EBITDA instead, explicitly deduct interest, taxes, working-capital needs and capex. Definitions here are classroom definitions, not agency-adjusted measures. There are no universal healthy cutoffs. Use consistent periods, currency, accounting basis and peer business models. CHAPTER 04 Default risk: probability is not certainty Expected loss combines the chance of default with the loss if default occurs. Expected loss = probability of default (PD) x loss given default (LGD) x exposure. If recovery is 40% of face value, LGD is 60%. For a $1,000 claim and a one-year PD of 2%, expected credit loss is $12. This is an average across uncertain outcomes, not a guaranteed $12 deduction. One-year PD 20% recovery 40% recovery 60% recovery 1% $8 $6 $4 2% $16 $12 $8 5% $40 $30 $20 10% $80 $60 $40 Illustrative sensitivity table. Exposure $1,000; expected loss = PD x (1 - recovery) x $1,000. No issuer estimate or historical default-rate forecast. Recoveries ignore discounting and expenses here. Time matters. With a constant independent annual default probability of 2%, five-year cumulative default probability is 1 - 0.98^5 = 9.61%, not exactly 10%. Real conditional probabilities change with the economic cycle and the company. A rating-based historical default rate, a model estimate and a market-implied probability are different objects. Historical averages depend on rating category, cohort, horizon and default definition. A market-implied probability embeds risk pricing and should not be presented as the actual chance of bankruptcy. What counts as default? Missed payments, bankruptcy and some distressed exchanges can qualify, depending on the agency or contract. A covenant breach can cause a funding problem without being identical to a missed coupon. Sources: corporate default basics [1] ; rating opinions [5] . All numerical scenarios and formulas on this page are independently constructed teaching examples. CHAPTER 05 Recovery: who gets paid first? The value left for your claim matters more than the original asset price. Recovery is the value received after default relative to the claim or other stated denominator. It may arrive as cash, new debt, equity or a mix, often after delay. A trading price soon after default and ultimate recovery are not the same measurement. Illustrative waterfall Claim Cash paid Recovery Net distributable value after costs $60m Available pool Not book value Secured creditors $30m $30m 100% Senior unsecured creditors $50m $30m 60% Subordinated creditors $20m $0 0% Common equity Residual $0 0% Stress the asset value. If the distributable pool falls to $40m, the same senior unsecured class receives $10m / $50m = 20%. If it rises to $80m, that class receives 100%. A bond label alone cannot determine recovery. This simplified example assumes secured claims are covered by collateral, the remaining priority rules are as shown, and there are no competing administrative, employee, tax or other priority claims. Real insolvency outcomes depend on law, collateral, guarantees and the specific corporate structure. Structural subordination: a parent-company bond may have access only to the residual value of a subsidiary after that subsidiary pays its own creditors. Consolidated cash does not necessarily belong to the bond issuer. Illustration, not a predicted recovery or legal advice. General creditor-priority concepts: SEC Investor.gov [1] . For an actual bond, read the indenture and guarantee/security documents; do not use this stylized ordering as a legal opinion. CHAPTER 06 Credit spread: separate the two prices A bond yield can rise because Treasury yields rise, spreads widen, or both. Simple benchmark spread = bond yield - comparable benchmark yield. One percentage point equals 100 basis points (bp). A 6.50% yield minus a 4.90% benchmark gives 1.60%, or 160bp. These rounded numbers are illustrative. Measure Use Do not confuse it with Coupon Contractual interest as a percentage of face value. Yield earned at today's purchase price. Yield to maturity Discount rate equating price to promised cash flows under stated conventions. A guaranteed realized return if default, early sale or reinvestment differs. Treasury / G-spread Yield difference to a specified Treasury or interpolated government curve. An option-adjusted spread or a same-day par-curve observation. Z-spread Constant spread added to spot rates to value promised cash flows. A direct standalone probability of default. Option-adjusted spread Model-based spread after accounting for embedded options. The raw spread of a callable bond. Spread compensation reflects expected default losses, uncertainty around them, liquidity, risk appetite, supply-demand and bond-specific features. Tax and benchmark conventions can matter. Comparing a 30-year callable bond with a five-year noncallable bond by raw spread alone is misleading. Useful shortcut, dangerous forecast: spread / LGD is a rough risk-neutral hazard-rate approximation under restrictive assumptions. At 160bp and 60% LGD, it gives about 2.67% per year. It is not a reliable physical default forecast and not a conclusion about Meta. Sources: CFA Institute yield/spread concepts [6] . Numerical examples are independent teaching calculations; no live pricing or OAS estimates are supplied. CHAPTER 07 A bond can lose money without default Longer duration magnifies sensitivity to both interest rates and spreads. First-order price change (%) is approximately -duration x yield change in percentage points. For a credit bond, use rate duration for benchmark changes and spread duration for spread changes. Duration is not the same as maturity. Illustrative shock 3-year duration 7-year duration 15-year duration Yield +0.50 percentage point -1.5% -3.5% -7.5% Yield +1.00 percentage point -3.0% -7.0% -15.0% Yield -0.50 percentage point +1.5% +3.5% +7.5% Hypothetical modified durations; no actual security. Approximation excludes convexity, coupon carry, default, accrued interest and transaction costs. Large moves require full repricing; callable bonds may behave differently. Offsetting forces example: benchmark yield falls 50bp while credit spread widens 100bp. If rate duration and spread duration are both 7, approximate price change is +3.5% - 7.0% = -3.5%, before carry and convexity. Holding a solvent bond to maturity can avoid realizing an interim market-price decline, but it does not remove default risk, inflation, opportunity cost or the risk that you need cash before maturity. A bond fund has a portfolio and no single promise to repay your original purchase price on a specified date. Refinancing channel: a company with fixed-rate debt is not immediately paying more on every bond when yields rise. The higher cost reaches floating-rate debt, new borrowing and maturities that must be refinanced. This is why the maturity ladder matters. Sources: yield and option considerations [6] ; SEC bond basics [1] . All calculations are illustrative and independently constructed. CHAPTER 08 Read Morningstar beside the 10-K Use research to frame questions and filings to verify the numbers. Morningstar lens 10-K evidence to inspect Your credit question Business / moat Item 1: business; segments; customers. How durable is demand and pricing power? Risk and uncertainty Item 1A: risk factors; subsequent updates. Which shock could damage cash flow or financing? Financial strength Item 7 liquidity discussion; Item 8 cash flows and balance sheet. Can it fund operations and obligations under stress? Capital allocation Dividends, repurchases, acquisitions and debt notes. Will management protect creditors or spend the buffer? Stock stars / fair value Stock price and valuation assumptions. This answers an equity valuation question, not bond safety. Practical Apple workflow 1. Open the requested Morningstar AAPL Financials page. Select annual rather than quarterly or TTM, confirm USD units, and note the fiscal end date. 2. Compare cash-flow, balance-sheet and income-statement numbers with the same Apple filing. 3. Read liquidity, debt, leases and commitments notes. Add the latest 10-Q/8-K events before making a current decision. 4. Read the exact bond prospectus and indenture. A stock page is not a bond term sheet. Morningstar equity stars concern valuation relative to estimated fair value and uncertainty. An economic moat concerns durable competitive advantage. Morningstar DBRS credit ratings are a separate credit-opinion process. Do not convert stars or moat labels into default probabilities. Sources [2-5,14]. The live AAPL Financials interface and subscriber-only analyst report were not authenticated or reproduced. This is an original teaching workflow, not a claim to quote Apple's current Morningstar rating or proprietary research. CHAPTER 09 Apple: follow the cash, not just profit FY2025 operating income grew, while cash after capex fell. USD billions FY2024 FY2025 Read it this way Revenue 391.035 416.161 Sales are not cash receipts. Operating income 123.216 133.050 Operating profitability increased. Operating cash flow 118.254 111.482 Cash conversion moved differently. Cash PP&E purchases 9.447 12.715 Investment consumed more cash. CFO minus cash capex 108.807 98.767 Before financing and distributions. Borrowings 106.629 98.657 Not total liabilities. Calculate it yourself: 111.482 - 12.715 = $98.767bn. Cash capex consumed 11.41% of CFO. CFO / borrowings = 1.13x. These are unadjusted classroom ratios, not an agency score. At 27 September 2025, cash and equivalents were $35.934bn. Adding current marketable securities gives $54.697bn; adding noncurrent securities gives $132.420bn. Borrowings were $98.657bn, including $7.979bn commercial paper and $12.350bn current term debt. Interpretation: broad liquid investments exceeded borrowings by $33.763bn, but calling all securities immediate cash would overstate precision. Test availability, maturity, market risk and operating cash needs. The strong cash-generation profile does not establish a numerical default probability or make every Apple bond attractive. Sources: Apple FY2025 release with FY2024 comparatives [8] ; annual filing for reading practice [14] . This intentionally teaches a fixed historical period. It is not Apple's latest financial position as of November 2026. Ratios calculated from displayed unrounded source inputs. CHAPTER 10 Apple: reconcile the denominator Buybacks use cash; they are not a debt balance. USD billions / ratio Calculation Result Borrowings, carrying amount 7.979 CP + 12.350 current term + 78.328 noncurrent term 98.657 Cash-only net debt 98.657 - 35.934 62.723 Simple FCF / borrowings 98.767 / 98.657 1.001x Operating income Gross profit less operating expenses 133.050 Operating income + D&A proxy 133.050 + 11.698 144.748 Debt / proxy above 98.657 / 144.748 0.682x EBITDA caution. The $133.050bn figure is operating income, not EBITDA. Adding disclosed depreciation and amortization produces a defined $144.748bn proxy; this is not a company-reported or agency-adjusted EBITDA measure. Interest coverage is not calculated. A separately verified gross annual interest expense input is not available in this report. The $0.129bn sensitivity to a 100bp rate increase in Item 7A is an incremental hypothetical impact, not the interest expense denominator. No coverage ratio is inferred from it. Priority correction. Debt claims generally rank ahead of common equity in insolvency. The bond’s entity, collateral and governing law determine its position among creditors; consolidated accounting labels alone do not establish recovery. Source: Apple FY2025 Form 10-K [14] , statements pp.29-33, Note 9 pp.43-44 and Item 7A p.27. Debt excludes lease liabilities; net debt here deducts cash and equivalents only. Share repurchases are excluded from the debt denominator. General priority: [1] . CHAPTER 11 Apple: maturities and a cash stress test A maturity calendar turns a balance-sheet number into dated cash needs. FY maturity bucket 2026 2027 2028 2029 2030 Later Term principal, USD bn 12.393 10.078 9.300 5.235 4.972 49.303 As of 27 September 2025; term-note principal totals $91.281bn. Excludes commercial paper and leases. Principal differs from carrying value; do not mix these measures. Source [14] , Note 9 p.44. Not a current November 2026 maturity schedule. Illustrative one-year case, USD bn Base CFO -25% CFO -50% Starting cash and equivalents 35.934 35.934 35.934 Annual CFO assumption 111.482 83.612 55.741 Cash capex assumption (12.715) (12.715) (12.715) 2026 term principal + CP assumed repaid (20.372) (20.372) (20.372) Cash left before other uses 114.329 86.459 58.588 How to read it: this is a transparent cash bridge, not a solvency forecast. It assumes no new borrowing, no securities sales, unchanged cash capex, and repayment of the $7.979bn CP balance alongside 2026 note principal. CFO already includes operating cash uses such as interest under US GAAP. The ending amounts exclude dividends, buybacks, acquisitions, financing-lease principal and any new extraordinary obligations. They do not establish that these cash balances would actually be available. Stress specific business drivers, working capital and minimum operating liquidity before making a real decision. Classroom sensitivity based on historical [14] inputs. Calculations use full precision; the 25% CFO amount is displayed rounded. No independently estimated default probability, rating or forecast is implied. CHAPTER 12 Peer comparison: investment absorbs cash Capex intensity is more revealing than a ranking of revenue alone. Cash capex / CFO: FY2025 (%) Apple 11.4% Microsoft 47.4% Alphabet 55.5% Meta 60.2% Oracle 101.9% Cash capex / operating cash flow, FY2025. A bar above 100% means this cash investment measure exceeded operating cash generated that year. Zero-based scale; exact inputs below. Not a credit rating. USD bn / FY end CFO Cash capex Difference Borrowings Apple 2025-09-27 111.482 12.715 98.767 98.657 Microsoft 2025-06-30 136.162 64.551 71.611 43.151 Alphabet 2025-12-31 164.713 91.447 73.266 48.543 Meta 2025-12-31 115.800 69.691 46.109 58.744 Oracle 2025-05-31 20.821 21.215 -0.394 92.568 Oracle is the useful contrast. FY2025 cash capex of $21.215bn slightly exceeded CFO of $20.821bn. That signals a need for cash reserves or external funding before additional uses; it does not by itself prove imminent default. Cash capex excludes noncash lease additions. Meta also deducted $2.524bn of finance-lease principal in its own FCF, producing $43.585bn rather than the $46.109bn simple difference here. Borrowings exclude leases. Different fiscal ends and business models limit direct ranking. Sources: issuer statements [8-12]. These are five issuers, not the entire AI supply chain. No forecasts, latest TTM figures, current ratings or unsupported R&D rankings are mixed into this table. CHAPTER 13 Five-issuer cash-flow ratio comparison A cash-flow comparison is useful only when definitions and missing inputs remain visible. Issuer / FY end Operating margin CFO / debt CFO-capex / debt Capex / CFO Apple 2025-09-27 31.97% 1.130x 1.001x 11.41% Microsoft 2025-06-30 45.62% 3.155x 1.660x 47.41% Alphabet 2025-12-31 32.03% 3.393x 1.509x 55.52% Meta 2025-12-31 41.44% 1.971x 0.785x 60.18% Oracle 2025-05-31 30.80% 0.225x -0.004x 101.89% Definitions: operating margin = operating income / revenue. Debt = balance-sheet carrying borrowings including current maturities and commercial paper, excluding leases. CFO-capex is the simple measure on the prior page, not a uniform agency FCF definition. Interpretation: a larger annual cash-flow/debt ratio gives more observed cash generation relative to borrowings, but it ignores the maturity distribution and future deterioration. Negative CFO-capex/debt indicates cash investment exceeded operating cash generation; it is not a negative debt balance. No overall credit score or rating is assigned. Interest coverage, lease-adjusted leverage and peer maturity ladders are not reported because those inputs have not been reconciled consistently for this comparison. The completed table covers the five named issuers only, not every company in the original AI universe. Source inputs and fiscal dates [8-12]. Oracle operating income is $17.678bn and revenue $57.399bn, giving a 30.80% operating margin. Annual fiscal periods differ; do not treat this as a synchronized quarter-end ranking. All ratios are this report’s calculations, not agency measures. CHAPTER 14 AI infrastructure: find the real obligor Off-balance-sheet borrowing can still create economic exposure for the sponsor. Funding route Who borrows? What to examine Corporate bonds Operating company or parent. Use of proceeds, maturity, new leverage and cash-flow coverage. Leases / capacity contracts Owner or project vehicle; user promises future payments. Cancellation terms, minimum payments, commencement timing and guarantees. Project / private credit SPV with pledged project assets and contracts. Customer concentration, construction risk, collateral obsolescence and lender priority. Equity or joint venture Shareholders supply risk-bearing capital. Dilution, control, capital calls and whether debt has sponsor recourse. BIS Bulletin 140, published 27 October 2026, describes growing debt funding and complex vehicles for AI infrastructure. Commitments by large firms can support vehicle credit quality, and banks may be exposed both to vehicles and to investors in their debt. Its observed Treasury and investment-grade spillovers on AI-financing news days were small and short-lived; that is not proof of no future risk. [7] Stress the chain: weaker AI demand -> lower utilization -> less project cash -> pressure on fixed contractual payments -> refinancing or collateral-sale risk. A technologically successful sector can still contain overleveraged borrowers. NVIDIA illustrates why models differ: FY2025, ended 26 January 2025, generated $64.089bn CFO versus $3.236bn purchases of PP&E and intangibles. Its fabless design model is not comparable with a data-center owner, and the period largely covers calendar 2024. Low own capex does not eliminate customer concentration or demand risk. [13] R&D is an expense category; capex is investment in long-lived assets; acquisitions and lease commitments are different again. None is a clean, consistently disclosed total for AI spending. Do not add them blindly or call all infrastructure investment AI-only. CHAPTER 15 Read a financing headline precisely Amount, rate, spread and use of proceeds answer different questions. Documented pricing What was priced Correct interpretation Microsoft 29 October 2026 $25bn total notes: $23bn fixed + $2bn floating. The supplied $23bn figure describes the fixed-rate subset, not total issuance. Oracle 2 November 2026 $10bn notes and a separate $10bn equity offering. A $20bn combined financing headline is not $20bn of debt. Meta 3 November 2026 $15bn across five senior-note tranches. Pricing and expected settlement are not proof of completed settlement. Meta maturity Amount ($bn) Coupon (%) Issue YTM (%) Spread (bp) 2031 3.25 5.850 5.850 110 2033 3.25 6.250 6.289 145 2036 4.00 6.550 6.552 160 2046 1.75 7.350 7.359 200 2056 2.75 7.500 7.531 220 Worked decomposition: the 2036 Meta tranche issue yield of 6.552% equals its 4.952% Treasury benchmark plus 160bp. Its coupon was 6.550%. The spread belongs to that benchmark at pricing, not to a Treasury par yield observed the next day. Do not label all corporate proceeds AI-only when the documents state general corporate purposes. A longer tranche's higher yield can reflect duration and term compensation as well as credit concerns; it does not mean that five different bonds imply five simple issuer default forecasts. Sources [15-18]. Meta filing text was rechecked via the StreetInsider reproduction [18] ; direct SEC access was unavailable during final audit. Terms are historical issue-date terms, not current executable quotes. Meta expected settlement 5 November; completion not independently checked. Supplied 4 November Treasury curve and TBAC interpretation were not independently verified and are excluded. CHAPTER 16 Your repeatable survival checklist Finish with a dated, conditional judgment, not a single reassuring ratio. Check Record before deciding Identity and time Exact legal issuer, guarantors, bond identifier, currency, financial period and pricing timestamp. Cash engine Three-year CFO history; working-capital drivers; capex split; leases; recurring vs one-off items. Funding calendar Cash available today; committed facilities; debt due in each year; covenant headroom. Downside case Revenue/margin shock; cash conversion; refinancing rate; capex flexibility; cash after unavoidable payments. Recovery case Priority, collateral value after costs, competing claims, guarantee coverage and recovery delay. Price of risk Comparable maturity and currency; spread definition; duration; call schedule; bid-ask and trading size. Decision and trigger Why compensation is sufficient or not; what new fact changes the conclusion; next filing date. Example decision language: "On the stated historical data, the issuer has substantial cash-generation capacity. I would still need updated liquidity, its maturity schedule and this bond's spread and protections before judging whether the bond offers adequate compensation." Red flags to investigate: persistent CFO weakness despite profit growth; rising receivables; large near-term maturities; aggressive EBITDA adjustments; expensive refinancing; weak covenant headroom; dividends funded with debt; guarantees or purchase commitments outside headline borrowings. Coverage limits: no live bond quotations, current comprehensive ratings table, quantitative issuer PD model, complete AI-company ranking, or proprietary Morningstar report. The supplied margin/R&D lists were not adopted as verified data. Unverified means evidence is insufficient, not that a claim is necessarily false. Source register Checked 5 November 2026. Financial data are historical FY2025 unless another date is explicitly stated. Sources are original issuer, regulatory or institutional pages, plus the explicitly disclosed Meta filing reproduction; calculations and illustrations are independently constructed. SEC Investor.gov - corporate bonds, default and creditor priority SEC - How to Read a 10-K Morningstar - company report sections (search-index extract; direct access restricted) Morningstar - stock ratings (search-index extract; direct access restricted) Morningstar DBRS - credit ratings process and scales CFA Institute - yield and yield spread measures, 2026 curriculum BIS Bulletin 140 - Building AI on credit, 27 October 2026 Apple FY2025 financial statements / results Microsoft FY2025 financial statements / results Alphabet FY2025 financial statements / results Meta FY2025 financial statements / results Oracle FY2025 financial statements / results NVIDIA FY2025 financial statements / results Apple FY2025 Form 10-K, year ended 27 September 2025 Meta new issuance, SEC filing dated 2026-11-03 Microsoft new issuance, Primary company release verified priced 2026-10-29 Oracle new issuance, Primary company release verified priced 2026-11-02 Meta pricing term sheet, 3 November 2026 - SEC filing text rechecked via StreetInsider mirror; direct SEC access unavailable during final audit Design follows the verified Colour & Tagging Standard V1.2 Merged. No private files, personal details, subscriber-only reports or invented issuer ratings are included. Educational analysis, not personalized investment advice or a credit rating. Update financial statements, instrument terms and market prices before an investment decision. Back to Research Explained

Creditworthiness · corrected teaching edition Earlier edition All report editions Research Papers Public teaching package · partial research coverage, not a current bond-buying list. Workbook dashboard ratio axis: 1.0 = 100%. Downloads: PDF XLSX Research explained / Corporate credit ANALYSIS + PRIMARY EVIDENCE Can the business survive and repay its bonds? Creditworthiness, AI borrowing and the evidence behind the numbers Corrected research & teaching edition · 6 November 2026 · Singapore time Historical annual observations are labelled individually. No live market-price snapshot. US corporate credit AI infrastructure Apple / SEC 10-K Evidence coverage: partial 01 · Cash first Repayment depends on cash and timing, not profit headlines. Apple’s FY2026 operating cash flow less cash PP&E was US$136.056bn; it is not cash available after every obligation. 02 · Test the funding gap AI investment can outrun internally generated cash. Oracle’s FY2026 cash PP&E exceeded operating cash flow by US$23.686bn. Financing access and payment timing are therefore central. 03 · Read the claim Creditors rank ahead of equity, but bondholders do not all rank equally. Collateral, issuer entity, guarantees and other priority claims change recovery. 04 · Price separately A resilient issuer can still offer a poorly priced bond. Compare matched instruments and distinguish Treasury-rate, credit-spread, liquidity and FX risks. Business Where cash comes from → Obligations What must be paid, when → Claim Who gets paid first → Price What risk you are paid to bear Evidence boundary. Nine annual financial snapshots, audited teaching calculations and partial primary issuance coverage. No unsupported credit ratings, default forecasts, target prices or composite safety scores. The original broad peer universe and every new-issue field are not fully verified. Sources and dates AAPL (2026-11-03) · ORCL (2026-06-22) · SEC_PRIORITY (Undated; checked 2026-11-06) · FINRA_SPREAD (Page checked 2026-11-06) Home Contents Local edition · 6 Nov 2026 01 / 28 Research explained / Corporate credit READING GUIDE Your route through the evidence Clickable contents · start with the question you need to answer 01 Can the business survive and repay its bonds? 03 Correct the framework before using the numbers 04 Default is only one way a bond can disappoint 05 Six questions turn accounts into a credit view 06 The legal claim can matter as much as the company 07 Use Morningstar to navigate, SEC filings to verify 08 Apple’s FY2026 cash generation is large, but definitions still matter 09 Apple retains US$33.945bn after the selected cash uses 10 Apple can show net debt or net cash, depending on the definition 11 Eight reported annual snapshots cover cash investment; one does not 12 Cash investment absorbs very different shares of operating cash flow 13 A completed diagnostic scorecard is more useful than a fabricated rating 14 Accounting definitions can change the apparent winner 15 Trace who buys, who builds and who carries the obligations 16 AI credit risk follows contracts, not just company logos 17 Oracle’s maturity profile is long, but its cash investment still needs funding 18 Original pricing must not masquerade as a current quote 19 A wider spread is meaningful only after the comparison is controlled 20 A solvent issuer can still produce a negative bond return 21 The corrected waterfall pays both claims in full at US$100 22 Interest coverage can remain positive while liquidity fails 23 Use three separate decisions before buying a bond 24 What was checked, what remains open 25 Sources and evidence trail 1 26 Sources and evidence trail 2 27 Sources and evidence trail 3 28 Sources and evidence trail 4 Read this as a sequence, not a league table The first question is whether cash can meet obligations. Only then ask what your particular bond could recover and whether its market price compensates you. The Excel model keeps assumptions separate from reported inputs. In everyday terms A successful shop, a reliable borrower and a good investment are three different judgments. This report keeps them separate. Home Contents Local edition · 6 Nov 2026 02 / 28 Research explained / Corporate credit CORRECTIONS + AUDIT Correct the framework before using the numbers This edition supersedes the unsupported statements in the earlier draft Earlier problem Correction used here Debt described as below equity Creditors are paid before common equity, subject to applicable legal priorities and claim structures. $100 assets / $80 senior / $20 junior treated as a junior loss $80 + $20 = $100. With no costs or other claims, both classes recover 100%. EBIT described as EBITDA Operating income is an EBIT proxy. An operating EBITDA proxy adds D&A and is not automatically covenant EBITDA. Buybacks included in debt Buybacks are cash distributions to shareholders, not borrowing balances. Unsupported ratings and implied issuer rankings No issuer rating is included without dated agency verification; no weighted safety score is invented. Spread treated as default probability Spreads include risk premia and instrument/market differences. Any PD illustration states its model assumptions. Annual periods and cash-flow definitions mixed Each fiscal year end is shown; gross cash investment, leases and company-defined FCF are separated. Checks that can be reproduced The workbook contains conservation and claim-cap tests. Each recovery scenario reconciles gross assets to costs, creditor payments and equity residual. Scenarios show operating cash flow, principal payments and minimum-cash needs separately. Sources and dates SEC_PRIORITY (Undated; checked 2026-11-06) · NYFED (2026-02-24) Home Contents Local edition · 6 Nov 2026 03 / 28 Research explained / Corporate credit ANALYSIS + PRIMARY EVIDENCE Default is only one way a bond can disappoint Creditworthiness is the capacity and willingness to pay the promised cash flows Risk What can go wrong What to inspect Issuer default Interest or principal is missed, or debt is restructured under distressed conditions. Cash generation, liquidity, payment schedule, covenant terms. Interest rates The benchmark yield rises and the bond’s price falls even if repayment remains credible. Duration, maturity, coupon and holding horizon. Credit spread Required compensation above the benchmark increases. Issuer news, peer spreads, supply, risk appetite, liquidity. Trading liquidity A sale requires a discount or a wide bid-offer spread. Issue size, trade frequency, dealer quotes and settlement. FX and optionality Currency moves reduce home-currency returns; calls change cash-flow timing. Currency exposure, hedges, call schedule, yield-to-worst. Valuation You pay too much for the risks and contractual cash flows. Comparable instruments, market price, fees and alternatives. Default risk versus loss Default probability and loss severity are different. For a common horizon, expected credit loss = exposure at default × probability of default × loss given default. A legal recovery paid years later also has a time value. Ratings are opinions, not insurance A credit rating is not a price target or a guarantee. Agency methods, incentives, timing and issue-specific protections matter. Ratings do not remove market-price or liquidity risk. This report omits unverified issuer ratings. In everyday terms The borrower can keep paying while your bond’s screen price falls. A promise being honoured and a price staying still are not the same thing. Sources and dates SEC_BOND (Undated; checked 2026-11-06) · SEC_RATING (2017-10-12) · FINRA_YIELD (Page checked 2026-11-06) · NYFED (2026-02-24) Home Contents Local edition · 6 Nov 2026 04 / 28 Research explained / Corporate credit ANALYSIS + PRIMARY EVIDENCE Six questions turn accounts into a credit view An original teaching framework, not a Morningstar or rating-agency methodology Earn Durable demand? → Convert Profit into cash? → Fund Cash after investment? → Refinance Maturities covered? → Recover Claim and collateral? → Price Compensation sufficient? Question Calculation / evidence Interpretation and limit Is the business durable? Segments, customer concentration, competition, regulation, supplier dependence. A moat can support future cash flow, but does not establish a credit rating. Does profit become cash? OCF / net income; working capital; taxes; stock compensation. One year can be distorted by timing. OCF is not the same as recurring cash earnings. Can investment be funded? Cash surplus = OCF − cash capex. Add finance-lease principal, other investment and distributions as relevant. How much leverage? Borrowings / EBITDA; net debt = specified debt − specified liquid assets. Use consistent definitions. Do not treat all liabilities as borrowings or all investments as cash. Can interest and maturities be paid? EBIT / gross interest; sources / uses over the next 12–24 months. Interest coverage is not principal coverage. Undrawn lines may be conditional. What changes in stress? Revenue × margin → cash → debt service → closing liquidity. Test cash buffers and refinancing assumptions, not only accounting ratios. No single ratio calculates “survivability” A defensible probability of default requires a calibrated model. Balance-sheet ratios, market signals and qualitative evidence can inform a view; they do not create a precise probability without a defined horizon, historical calibration and validation. A mechanical score is a screening device, not a certified rating. In everyday terms Look at the shop’s earning power, then its bank account, then the bills due. A profitable year does not settle a bill that arrives before the cash. Sources and dates AAPL (2026-11-03) · ORCL (2026-06-22) · ORCL_DEBT (2026-06-22) · SEC_BOND (Undated; checked 2026-11-06) · SEC_RATING (2017-10-12) · NYFED (2026-02-24) Home Contents Local edition · 6 Nov 2026 05 / 28 Research explained / Corporate credit ANALYSIS + PRIMARY EVIDENCE The legal claim can matter as much as the company General teaching framework; actual rights depend on the instrument and applicable law Legal entity Who owes the money? → Collateral Which assets support it? → Priority Which claims rank ahead? → Covenants What can change or accelerate? Structure Plain-English meaning What to check Secured debt Rights over specified collateral, rather than a general promise alone. Collateral ownership, valuation, lien priority, other liens, enforcement costs and shortfall treatment. Senior unsecured debt A general claim without specified collateral; senior within the contractual ranking stated. Other secured or priority claims, guarantees and the legal issuer. Weaker operating performance, less accessible liquidity, large commitments, aggressive distributions or changed debt terms. Microsoft and Alphabet cover the selected annual cash investment from OCF. Faster cash and lease investment, weaker monetisation, working-capital changes or later balance-sheet funding. NVIDIA and AMD hold cash above the selected borrowing balance. A downturn in demand, customer concentration, supply commitments, acquisition spending or changing cash quality. Oracle requires greater attention to financing and investment timing in this snapshot. Equity proceeds, committed financing and durable customer cash flows can offset risk; project delays, spending overruns or financing constraints can intensify it. No bond is declared cheap or suitable from these annual accounts alone. A dated executable quote and matched instrument comparison are required for a relative-value view. Monitor the evidence that can break the thesis. The practical review list is quarterly cash flow and capex, unrestricted liquidity, debt due within 12–24 months, lease and purchase commitments, covenant headroom using the actual definitions, and distributions to shareholders. A watchlist is not an automated task created by this report. In everyday terms A strong company is the starting point. A good bond also needs a sound contract, a sensible price and a place in the investor’s portfolio. entries.text: Global Markets & Credit Research · 7 November 2026 Saved briefings Research register Earlier bond review 7 November 2026 · Verified public extract Employment, bank resilience and the risks behind a bond yield. October U.S. employment, June EU bank credit quality and new BIS banking scenarios: three official-source findings, with rate, credit and liquidity risks kept separate. Public abridgement, not the full briefing. 08:05 SGT original cutoff · 7 Nov; data dates shown separately. Public-source check: 7 November 2026. 1. Employment supports borrowers, but does not promise lower yields Fact: The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported 165,000 additional nonfarm payroll jobs for October and a 4.1% unemployment rate on 6 November 2026. Employment and unemployment come from different surveys. The number working part time for economic reasons increased by 339,000 to 4.8 million. The estimates can be revised. Indicator October 2026 observation Release date Nonfarm payroll change +165,000 jobs 6 Nov 2026 Unemployment rate 4.1% 6 Nov 2026 Part time for economic reasons 4.8 million people 6 Nov 2026 Analysis : Employment income can support debt repayment. Strong hiring can also reduce the case for rapid monetary easing if inflation remains persistent. The increase in involuntary part-time work is a counterweight to the headline strength. None of these observations establishes the next Federal Reserve decision or a bond-price target. Source: BLS Employment Situation, October 2026. 2. European bank loan quality and capital tell different stories Fact: The ECB's 6 November release covers end-June 2026, not November loan performance. EU-headquartered credit institutions had €34.99 trillion of assets, up 5.18% year on year. Their non-performing-loan ratio was 1.99% , compared with 1.96% a year earlier. The CET1 capital ratio was 16.43% . Measure June 2025 June 2026 Total assets €33.27 trillion €34.99 trillion Non-performing-loan ratio 1.96% 1.99% Analysis : The 0.03-percentage-point change equals 3 basis points, not a 3% deterioration. A small increase does not establish a banking crisis. Bank capital, earnings, liquidity and borrower performance need separate assessment. The NPL denominator includes central-bank cash balances and certain demand deposits. First-half return on equity was 5.31% , not annualised. Source: ECB consolidated banking data; figures may be revised. 3. Digital banking changes where income and risk sit Research finding: BIS Working Paper 1391, published 4 November 2026, studies about 9,000 banks across more than 150 jurisdictions. Its four ten-year scenarios assign emerging technology-based models 3– 27% of banking-system assets, versus about 3.5% in the trend baseline. The paper also considers competition for roughly 40% of banking revenue. These are scenario outputs, not forecasts or assigned probabilities. Analysis : A bank can keep loans on its balance sheet while other firms capture distribution or fee income. Digital channels can also speed up deposit withdrawals. Sustainable earnings and dependable funding therefore matter alongside reported capital. The paper expresses its authors' views, not necessarily those of the BIS or its member central banks. No bank failure is predicted here. The original content can be found at the BIS source link below. 4. Separate three bond risks Risk What to examine What does not establish it Interest-rate risk Maturity, duration and yield changes A high coupon alone Credit risk Cash generation, debt terms and repayment A share-price decline alone Funding and liquidity risk Collateral, refinancing and available cash An unchanged credit rating alone Analysis : A bond's yield is compensation for several risks, not a guaranteed realised return. Long-duration prices can fall when yields rise. A borrower may remain current while refinancing becomes harder. A leveraged holder can face collateral pressure without an issuer default. These are general analytical distinctions, not a personalised investment recommendation or a claim that such losses have occurred. 5. What would change the assessment? Employment revisions and future inflation releases could change rate expectations. Later bank data could show whether impaired-loan ratios persistently rise. Issuer filings could reveal weaker cash interest coverage or tighter refinancing terms. Actual missed payments, nonaccruals and realised losses would provide stronger credit evidence than equity volatility alone. Coverage : This abridgement retains three independently rechecked official-source findings and a general risk framework. It excludes the full report's JPMorgan/third-party valuation tables, proprietary credit-index data, Reuters market quotations and issuance totals, issuer pricing tables, the consumer-credit and securities-lending sections that were not fully revalidated in this publication pass, and the original charts and scenario calculations. Omission does not establish that those claims are false. No private holdings, personal examples, names of the owner or colleagues, or account identifiers are included. Earlier published editions remain unchanged. Sources · optional verification BLS · October 2026 Employment Situation, released 6 November ↗ ECB · consolidated banking data for June 2026, released 6 November ↗ BIS Working Paper 1391 · Scenarios for future banking, 4 November 2026. It uses original summaries and public source links without copied publisher charts or images. It retains established readable layout conventions; the current master colour-standard files were not independently rechecked for this edition. entries.text: Howard Marks and the price of conviction Skip to report ← Research Explained Print / save PDF Research reading · 5 November 2026. Independent commentary on Howard Marks’s public Oaktree memos, with separately sourced evidence and original analysis. Not an Oaktree publication or endorsement. The linked memos remain the original sources. Educational research, not personalised investment advice. Two five-slide presentations Independent summary and analysis of Howard Marks’s memos. Both PowerPoint files contain editable charts and speaker notes on every slide, including source dates and qualifications. Download financial briefing · PPTX · 55 KB Download clear visual story · PPTX · 58 KB Investment research 5 November 2026 · Singapore Jump to section 01 · Howard Marks and the price of conviction 02 · Five memos, five different decisions 03 · What can a Treasury buyback change? 04 · The two-year yield moved more 05 · The interest bill Marks anticipated 06 · What a smooth loan valuation can hide 07 · When repurchases overtake new subscriptions 08 · Who else has a claim on the same invoice? 09 · Who keeps the value AI creates? 10 · What changed his mind about AI? 11 · When capex overtakes operating cash 12 · Three clocks inside one data centre 13 · The same AI success can help one borrower and hurt another 14 · The bond matures in USD. The bills arrive in SGD. 15 · What would make you change your mind? 16 · Read the five original memos 17 · The records behind the charts 18 · A reading key for the colour coding Contents Top ↑ RESEARCH NOTE / 05 NOVEMBER 2026 / SINGAPORE Howard Marks and the price of conviction Five Oaktree memos on long bonds , private credit and who earns the return on AI . US Treasuries Private credit AI Singapore Contents · 18 sections 01 Howard Marks and the price of conviction 02 Five memos, five different decisions 03 What can a Treasury buyback change? 04 The two-year yield moved more 05 The interest bill Marks anticipated 06 What a smooth loan valuation can hide 07 When repurchases overtake new subscriptions 08 Who else has a claim on the same invoice? 09 Who keeps the value AI creates? 10 What changed his mind about AI ? 11 When capex overtakes operating cash 12 Three clocks inside one data centre 13 The same AI success can help one borrower and hurt another 14 The bond matures in USD. The bills arrive in SGD. 15 What would make you change your mind? 16 Read the five original memos 17 The records behind the charts 18 A reading key for the colour coding Suppose Marks is right that AI changes the economy. Who gets paid? A software customer might save money, a chip buyer might overspend, and a lender might collect every coupon until its borrower needs to refinance. Believing in the technology tells us little about which of those positions to own. The same question runs through his recent writing on government bonds and private loans. The claim Identify who promises the money. The price Work out what success already costs. The impact Find who absorbs a shortfall. Three findings worth taking into a portfolio review Observed What it changes Observed US Treasuries · 13 bp versus 1 bp What it changes From 22 September to 4 November, the two-year yield fell 13 bp and the 30-year yield fell 1 bp. A short-rate view alone can be a poor reason to extend duration. Observed Private credit · cash exits What it changes Accepted repurchases exceeded new inflows in the Fed ’s Q1 2026 sample of 14 large perpetual BDCs. A fund can face liquidity pressure while borrowers keep paying. Observed Alphabet · −US$9.065bn What it changes Q3 2026 free cash flow was negative as purchases of property and equipment exceeded operating cash. Across four quarters it was still positive US$19.747bn. Both horizons matter. This is an independent reading of five public letters by Howard Marks, Oaktree’s co-chair. The exhibits draw on separate primary records. The portfolio applications are this report’s analysis. The research cutoff is 5 November 2026 in Singapore . Sources A0 · Oaktree · The public archive of written memos T3 · US Treasury Department · September 2026 daily par yield curve T4 · US Treasury Department · November 2026 daily par yield curve CR1 · Federal Reserve · May 2026 Financial Stability Report, Funding Risks E1 · Alphabet · Q3 2026 earnings release , SEC Exhibit 99.1, free cash flow reconciliation READING MAP / FIVE LETTERS 02 / 18 Five memos, five different decisions Oaktree’s latest public written memo at the research cutoff was dated 22 September 2026. US Treasuries Private credit AI Date Written memo Decision it informs Date 22 Sep 2026 Written memo Shall We Repeal the Laws of Economics – Part III Decision it informs Can a buyback change the long-term cost of borrowing? Date 9 Apr 2026 Written memo What’s Going on in Private Credit ? Decision it informs What does a smooth fund valuation conceal about a loan? Date 26 Feb 2026 Written memo AI Hurtles Ahead Decision it informs Which beliefs should change when a technology improves? Date 9 Dec 2025 Written memo Is It a Bubble? Decision it informs Who keeps the value created by an AI buildout? Date 6 Nov 2025 Written memo Cockroaches in the Coal Mine Decision it informs What can two failures tell a lender about other deals? Read the credit letters as a pair. November starts with two troubled borrowers. April follows the money back to the managers who supplied loans and the vehicles that sold access to them. Borrowers can pay their loans on time while the fund holding those loans offers less liquidity than its investors expect. Read the AI letters in publication order. December examines the conduct of investors and builders. February revisits what the tools can actually do. The change in Marks’s confidence about the technology makes his refusal to name a fair price for the whole sector more interesting. Scope The five titles above are the latest five entries in Oaktree’s written-memo archive. In the chapters that follow, related letters are paired so that the change in Marks’s thinking is visible. Sources A0 · Oaktree · The public archive of written memos M1 · 22 Sep 2026 · Shall We Repeal the Laws of Economics – Part III M2 · 9 Apr 2026 · What’s Going on in Private Credit ? M3 · 26 Feb 2026 · AI Hurtles Ahead M4 · 9 Dec 2025 · Is It a Bubble? M5 · 6 Nov 2025 · Cockroaches in the Coal Mine MEMO 01 / 22 SEPTEMBER 2026 03 / 18 What can a Treasury buyback change? Marks asks whether buying long bonds can durably lower the interest rate investors demand. US Treasury Department US Treasuries Fiscal deficit Liquidity The Treasury Department and Marks are asking different questions. On 19 August, Treasury announced larger buybacks in the 10–20 and 20–30 year nominal sectors. The maximum per operation would rise from US$2 billion to at least US$4 billion, effective 9 September for the rest of that refunding quarter. Treasury gave liquidity support as its objective. Marks interpreted the intervention as an effort to bring down long yields. Policy action Treasury bids for older bonds . Market mechanism A dealer gains a buyer for inventory. Investor impact The long yield still reflects the terms buyers require. A bond can become easier to sell while the country’s long-term borrowing cost stays high. Liquidity concerns the ease of trading. A long yield also reflects expected short rates, inflation and compensation for bearing duration. Treasury can help a dealer clear a position today while investors still demand a sizeable return to hold decades of fixed payments. Marks’s deeper concern is about the maturity of the liability. If more bills are issued alongside the purchase of long debt, a portion of government funding must reset sooner. Lower interest expense today then has to be weighed against the future refinancing bill. His proposed remedies address the fiscal balance through revenue , spending discipline and productivity growth. A point of disagreement A November Treasury advisory presentation found no clear evidence that AI -related issuance was crowding out Treasuries or non-tech credit. Marks outlined a plausible competition for capital. The advisory presenter’s reading of the market gives a specific reason to keep that mechanism open to revision. Sources M1 · 22 Sep 2026 · Shall We Repeal the Laws of Economics – Part III T1 · US Treasury Department · 19 Aug 2026 buyback announcement T5 · Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee · 3 Nov 2026 meeting minutes EVIDENCE 01 / US TREASURIES 04 / 18 The two-year yield moved more From the memo date to 4 November, the two-year par yield fell 13 basis points and the 30-year fell one. US Treasuries Yield curve Liquidity Exhibit 01 Two snapshots of the US Treasury par yield curve Two snapshots of the US Treasury par yield curve 22 Sep 2026: 4.71, 4.96, 5.29; 4 Nov 2026: 4.58, 4.9, 5.28. Par yield (%). Exact values and qualifications follow in the report. Par yield (%) 4.4 4.6 4.8 5.0 5.2 5.4 2 years 10 years 30 years 22 Sep 2026 4 Nov 2026 Long and short yields moved by different amounts. Selected maturities, in percent. Lines connect the three observations at each date. A par yield is a benchmark, so a holder’s bond can trade at a different yield. Swipe across for all columns → Observation 2-year 10-year 30-year 30Y less 2Y Observation 22 Sep 2026 2-year 4.71% 10-year 4.96% 30-year 5.29% 30Y less 2Y 58 bp Observation 4 Nov 2026 2-year 4.58% 10-year 4.90% 30-year 5.28% 30Y less 2Y 70 bp Observation Change 2-year −13 bp 10-year −6 bp 30-year −1 bp 30Y less 2Y +12 bp The announcement-day reaction partly reversed the next day. The 30-year yield moved from 5.28% on 18 August to 5.19% on 19 August and 5.23% on 20 August. By 4 November it was back at 5.28%. The path includes other news. These observations cannot isolate the effect of the purchases. Dealers saw a benefit that a chart of benchmark yields would miss. In the November advisory committee minutes, most dealers reported at least modest improvements in trading conditions for older bonds after the increase. Evidence on their ability to intermediate client flows was mixed. That distinction matters to an investor who needs a bid for a specific issue. Sources T1 · US Treasury Department · 19 Aug 2026 buyback announcement T2 · US Treasury Department · August 2026 daily par yield curve T3 · US Treasury Department · September 2026 daily par yield curve T4 · US Treasury Department · November 2026 daily par yield curve T5 · Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee · 3 Nov 2026 meeting minutes EVIDENCE 02 / US FISCAL YEAR 2026 05 / 18 The interest bill Marks anticipated The completed fiscal year gives us one part of the September memo we can check directly. US Fiscal deficit US Treasuries Marks expected annual net interest outlays to exceed US$1 trillion and the defense budget. The fiscal year ended on 30 September. The Joint Economic Committee’s Republican staff, using Treasury data, reported US$1,051.75 billion of net interest and US$916.85 billion of defense outlays. The figures below use the source table’s displayed precision. Swipe across for all columns → US$ billion FY2025 FY2026 Change US$ billion Net interest outlays FY2025 970.66 FY2026 1,051.75 Change +81.09 US$ billion Defense outlays FY2025 868.41 FY2026 916.85 Change +48.44 US$ billion Interest less defense FY2025 102.25 FY2026 134.90 Change +32.65 The yearly financing gap was US$1,992.47 billion on the same presentation. US$7,395.80 billion of net outlays less US$5,403.33 billion of net receipts gives US$1,992.47 billion. Net interest is already inside outlays. Gross Treasury issuance also refinances maturing debt, so its total answers a different question. A growing interest bill works its way through the budget over time. A higher auction yield affects newly issued or refinanced debt first. The cost of previously issued fixed-rate bonds stays contractual. That lag explains how pressure can build without immediately appearing across the entire debt stock. What if the real concern is the value of the dollars received? When a friend asked whether he should sell his US stocks , Marks asked where the proceeds would go. Moving into a USD deposit changes the exposure to share prices but leaves the spending power of those dollars at issue. He also recalls that his own concerns about lasting dollar weakness after the 2008 crisis did not play out as feared. The size of a balance sheet alone gives little guidance about currency timing. Portfolio implication The budget result confirms a fiscal cost, while the next move in long yields remains open. A buyer of a long Treasury needs to judge the yield on offer and the consequences of being early. Recession or falling inflation expectations can still support long bond prices while the deficit remains large. Sources M1 · 22 Sep 2026 · Shall We Repeal the Laws of Economics – Part III F1 · Joint Economic Committee Republican staff · September 2026 fiscal update T3 · US Treasury Department · September 2026 daily par yield curve T4 · US Treasury Department · November 2026 daily par yield curve MEMO 02 / 09 APRIL 2026 06 / 18 What a smooth loan valuation can hide Marks follows the money from private equity sponsors to lenders and then to the investors seeking their cash back. Private credit AI Liquidity The first direct lenders had bargaining power. Private equity sponsors needed acquisition financing after the global financial crisis. Lenders could negotiate both the spread and the conditions under which they could intervene. As more managers competed for deals, borrowers could shop for a cheaper loan or fewer restrictions. A record earned on the early loans says little about the protections in the next one. The Sharpe ratio rewards a quiet valuation history. It divides excess return by the volatility of returns. An infrequently priced loan can show little movement even as its borrower loses customers. For a software borrower exposed to AI competition, ask when customers can cancel or renegotiate, then compare the cash left after operating costs with the interest due. The structure changes what an investor sees when confidence falls. The owner of a listed BDC can sell shares to another investor, potentially at a discount to net asset value. In a non-traded BDC, the investor may instead face a limit on how many shares the vehicle will buy back. A wider listed discount or a limited repurchase can appear before a borrower misses a payment. Borrower Customer renewals support cash interest payments. Lender Covenants determine when a lender can intervene. Fund investor Repurchase terms determine when an investor can exit. Portfolio implication A quarterly exit window still has a capacity limit. A non-traded business development company (BDC) may accept only part of a repurchase request. An investor with a dated cash obligation needs the prospectus terms as well as the loan performance report. Sources M2 · 9 Apr 2026 · What’s Going on in Private Credit ? CR1 · Federal Reserve · May 2026 Financial Stability Report, Funding Risks EVIDENCE 03 / PRIVATE CREDIT 07 / 18 When repurchases overtake new subscriptions The Federal Reserve ’s May 2026 report measures two fund structures that give individuals access to private credit . Federal Reserve Private credit Liquidity Exhibit 02 Two types of semi-liquid private credit funds Two types of semi-liquid private credit funds Federal Reserve, May 2026. Perpetual-life BDCs: gross assets 306, net assets 161. Credit-focused interval funds: gross assets 119, net assets 80. All in US$ billions. Net assets are after liabilities, not a credit-loss measure. Gross assets Net assets US$ billion 0 100 200 300 306 161 Perpetual-life BDCs 119 80 Credit interval funds Net assets are what remains after liabilities. Figures in US$ billions, as reported in May 2026. The difference between gross and net assets does not measure credit losses. Fund structure Gross assets, US$bn Net assets, US$bn Fund structure Perpetual-life BDCs Gross assets, US$bn 306 Net assets, US$bn 161 Fund structure Credit-focused interval funds Gross assets, US$bn 119 Net assets, US$bn 80 Fund structure Combined Gross assets, US$bn 425 Net assets, US$bn 241 In 2026 Q1, accepted repurchases exceeded new subscriptions for the first time in the Fed ’s series. That finding covered the 14 largest perpetual BDCs, representing 86% of segment assets. Most perpetual BDCs disclosed an intended quarterly cap of 5% of net asset value, subject to manager discretion. Repurchases count accepted withdrawals. Investor requests can be higher. A persistent outflow could reach borrowers through fewer new loans. A fund can use cash, collect principal, draw on a bank line or sell liquid assets to meet withdrawals. Keeping more resources available for investors can leave less money for a borrower coming back to refinance. The Fed judged the financial stability risks from further requests manageable at the time. Sources CR1 · Federal Reserve · May 2026 Financial Stability Report, Funding Risks M2 · 9 Apr 2026 · What’s Going on in Private Credit ? MEMO 05 / 06 NOVEMBER 2025 08 / 18 Who else has a claim on the same invoice? First Brands and Tricolor gave Marks a reason to question how lenders verify the collateral behind a loan. Private credit Credit risk Two bankruptcies raised a question about how widely the same weakness might recur. First Brands supplied auto parts and had both public and private debt . Tricolor sold used vehicles and financed subprime buyers. When Marks wrote, allegations included the repeated pledging of First Brands receivables. He saw grounds to revisit underwriting across portfolios. His distinction was between losses clustering after loose lending and one failure transmitting losses through contractual links to others. Two cases can justify wider checks while leaving that second mechanism unproven. The subsequent First Brands indictment made the alleged mechanism more specific. On 29 January 2026, US prosecutors alleged that executives used fictitious or inflated invoices and pledged assets more than once. Marks had already contrasted US$5.9 billion of debt disclosed in July with US$9.3 billion of debt included in US$11.6 billion of total obligations reported in the bankruptcy process. A lender needs the complete list of claims to estimate what reaches its account. The January allegations are later evidence and were unavailable when Marks published the memo. Invoice The receivable must exist. Ownership The lender must have a valid claim. Collection The customer’s payment must reach the lender. Three checks a credit committee can request Question Evidence to inspect Question Does the receivable exist? Evidence to inspect Confirm selected invoices and balances directly with customers. Question Who has the prior claim? Evidence to inspect Reconcile assigned invoices across lenders and factors, then check security filings. Question Where did cash arrive? Evidence to inspect Trace customer remittances to bank statements and the controlled collection account. What would change the conclusion? The same failure at unrelated borrowers would make the pattern more persuasive. Compare lenders , collateral agents and servicing platforms across cases. Shared controls can create a concentration that an industry allocation report misses. Sources M5 · 6 Nov 2025 · Cockroaches in the Coal Mine CR2 · US Department of Justice · First Brands indictment announcement, 29 Jan 2026 AI LETTERS / 9 DECEMBER 2025 09 / 18 Who keeps the value AI creates? In Is It a Bubble?, Marks separates the economics of the buildout from the prices investors pay to join it. AI Equities Private credit Data centres There are two ways to be early and still lose money. An operator can build more capacity than it can profitably rent. An investor can buy a successful operator at a price that assumes even better results. The second mistake remains possible if the first never happens. Marks uses railways and communications infrastructure to show how useful assets can survive the loss of their original investors’ capital. A real advance Computing gets cheaper or more capable. The customer wins Users may capture the savings. The investor’s test Can this particular owner retain enough profit? Marks asks, “Who will be the winners, and what will they be worth?” A shareholder in the eventual winner participates in its growth. A lender who identifies exactly the same winner generally collects the contractual coupon and principal. A spectacular winner in a loan book therefore offers limited help against a failure elsewhere. In assessing a loan, the surviving cash flows and collateral matter more than the size of the industry’s prize. The strongest case for optimism deserves a place in the analysis. The presence of customers and profitable companies financing investment from operations distinguishes parts of this buildout from ventures living entirely on external capital. The harder question concerns the next project, especially if the tenant needs another financing round to honour its commitment. What changes the decision For a data centre, ask who pays the rent if computing prices fall faster than its costs. A tenant with a binding commitment and the capacity to honour it offers different protection from a long demand forecast. The contract, counterparty and price paid determine how much that difference is worth. Sources M4 · 9 Dec 2025 · Is It a Bubble? E2 · Meta Platforms · Q3 2025 Form 10-Q, Note 13, subsequent event AI LETTERS / 26 FEBRUARY 2026 10 / 18 What changed his mind about AI ? In AI Hurtles Ahead, stronger evidence of capability changes Marks’s view of the technology while leaving the valuation question open. AI Software AI capex Equities Marks asked Claude for a tutorial and then challenged its conclusion. The account he published draws on a 10,000-word essay from the model, prepared using prompts developed with advisers. He saw a meaningful difference between a system that answers a question and one that breaks down a task, uses tools and checks its work. He also describes its errors and the difficulty of relying on patterns when a situation has no close precedent. The distinction between training and inference changed the investment question. Training creates the model. Inference runs it when a customer makes a request. Heavy use today provides evidence of demand for inference capacity. When Marks pressed the argument, the missing variable was future supply. A queue today can disappear after multiple operators finish building at the same time. Observed Customers use the tools today. Unresolved Rivals can add capacity together. Impact Future utilisation and margins determine what owners earn. What the observation supports What the investor still needs What the observation supports A tool performs a valuable task. What the investor still needs Who pays, how often and at what price? What the observation supports Customers use today’s available capacity. What the investor still needs How much is being built, and when will it open? What the observation supports A model can compare public data quickly. What the investor still needs Does the resulting judgment retain value once competitors can make the same comparison? For an investor, the tutorial is also a lesson in when to stop delegating. A model can extract debt covenants and compare filings. Someone still has to decide whether a sponsor will support a borrower in distress, and take responsibility for the capital placed at risk. Marks also raises the prospect of dislocated work and lost purpose. He offers these as social concerns rather than measurable labour-market forecasts. What changed His confidence in AI ’s capabilities rose, but the tutorial supplied no valuation of the securities. A revision to the operating thesis warrants a fresh look at price, remaining uncertainties and position size. Sources M3 · 26 Feb 2026 · AI Hurtles Ahead M4 · 9 Dec 2025 · Is It a Bubble? EVIDENCE 04 / ALPHABET CASH FLOWS 11 / 18 When capex overtakes operating cash Alphabet ’s filings show how quickly the timing of investment can change the cash left over for shareholders. Alphabet Capex Free cash flow AI Exhibit 03 Operating cash flow and purchases of property and equipment Operating cash flow and purchases of property and equipment Operating cash flow: 52.402, 45.79, 39.069, 42.29; PP&E cash purchases: 27.851, 35.674, 44.924, 51.355. US$ billion. Exact values and qualifications follow in the report. Purchases are displayed as positive spending amounts. Alphabet defines free cash flow as operating cash flow less capital expenditures.
