entries.text: MAS + SNB | Monetary policy research | 5 Nov 2026 MAS + SNB 5 Nov 2026 Current section / Jump to 01 · Central conclusion 02 · Evidence at the cutoff 03 · Policy frameworks 04 · MAS decisions and projections 05 · Singapore monthly inflation 06 · Why Singapore inflation moved 07 · Singapore employment 08 · Singapore wages and capacity 09 · SNB policy decisions 10 · Swiss monthly inflation 11 · Swiss inflation composition 12 · SNB forecast revisions 13 · Swiss employment 14 · Growth and concentration 15 · CHF/SGD quotation and evidence 16 · CHF/SGD mechanisms 17 · CHF financing implications 18 · Attributed policy assessment summaries 19 · Conditional scenarios 20 · Monitoring priorities 21 · Source and calculation controls 22 · Exact observations 23 · Sources 1 24 · Sources 2 25 · Sources 3 26 · Sources 4 Print ← Research Explained · Market Intelligence Hub · Read the complete report ↓ CHF / SGD research and presentations Dated 5 November 2026. Download either five-slide PowerPoint version with formatted speaker notes and editable native charts. Financial briefing · PowerPoint (.pptx) Clear visual story · PowerPoint (.pptx) Independent factual analysis and attributed paraphrases, not an MAS or SNB publication or endorsement. No blanket commercial licence is claimed. Figures have different observation dates; forecasts and scenarios are labelled separately. No live CHF/SGD price, historical bilateral performance or personalised investment recommendation is provided. 01 / Central conclusion MAS and SNB face the same external shocks through different monetary systems Full comparative research | Monetary policy · employment · inflation · CHF/SGD Policy, inflation composition and capital flows provide a framework for assessing CHF/SGD . Singapore is maintaining an appreciating currency path after two 2026 tightenings. Switzerland retains a 0% policy rate, while its latest inflation acceleration is concentrated in imported energy. This combination can support SGD relative to CHF; it does not determine the next currency move. [S01] [S18] [S24] 2.0% MAS core inflation September 2026, YoY [S12] 0.5% Swiss core 1 inflation October 2026, YoY 0% SNB policy rate 24 September decision Key takeaway What it changes 1. The policy instruments differ Compare the MAS currency band with the SNB interest-rate and FX toolkit. 2. Headline inflation is insufficient Check import costs, domestic prices, core definitions and persistence. 3. Employment is expanding unevenly Distinguish net employment growth from resident outcomes, vacancies and wage pressure. 4. The franc can reverse sharply Funding flows can turn into demand for CHF during risk aversion. 5. Data dates matter A later CPI release cannot explain an earlier policy decision. Research question. Why can Singapore tighten through its currency while Switzerland holds rates, even when both face higher energy costs? The report follows the evidence from prices and employment to policy, then to CHF/SGD and financing risk. Independent monetary-policy research. Information cutoff: 5 November 2026. Official releases supply the policy and economic facts. Figures retain source precision and their observation periods. This is a dated research report, not a live market feed or personalised investment recommendation. Back to overview ↑ 02 / Evidence at the cutoff The latest available figures do not all describe the same month Measure Singapore / MAS Switzerland / SNB Latest policy decision 14 Oct: appreciation slope unchanged after Apr/Jul increases 24 Sep: policy rate held at 0% Headline CPI, latest Sep: 2.2% YoY; +0.2% MoM Oct: 1.5% YoY; +0.2% MoM Headline CPI, common month Sep: 2.2% YoY Sep: 1.0% YoY Core CPI, latest Sep: 2.0% YoY; +0.1% MoM Oct core 1: 0.5% YoY; 0.0% MoM Unemployment, latest Sep: 2.0% overall; 3.0% resident; 3.1% citizen, all SA Oct: 3.0% registered NSA; 3.1% registered SA Recent real GDP growth Q3 advance: +5.4% YoY; +1.1% QoQ SA Q2: +1.5% QoQ SA, sports-adjusted Main analytical report Macroeconomic Review, Oct; cutoff 13 Oct Quarterly Bulletin 3/2026; cutoff 24 Sep Sources: [S01] [S02] [S12] [S16] [S18] [S22] [S24] [S25] [S28] [S31] [S43] . SA = seasonally adjusted; NSA = not seasonally adjusted. Core and labour definitions differ. Use September for a matched headline-inflation comparison. October Swiss CPI is an additional update, not a matched comparison with Singapore . Singapore October inflation was not yet published at this cutoff. The latest observation and the latest comparable observation answer different questions. The equivalent Swiss report is the Monetary policy report within the SNB Quarterly Bulletin. Its Business cycle signals section adds company-level evidence. MAS presents its projections and supporting analysis in the Macroeconomic Review. Later monthly releases update each report's dated information set. [S02] [S22] Read the report in three passes. Sections 3-14 explain the two economies; sections 15-20 translate the findings into CHF/SGD and monitoring decisions; sections 21 onward document the data controls, exact observations and sources. Forecasts are labelled by the date on which they were made. Back to overview ↑ 03 / Policy frameworks MAS manages an exchange-rate path; SNB sets a rate and can use FX intervention Swipe the chart horizontally for the full view. Different instruments aim at domestic price stability Conceptual transmission diagram; not a numerical forecast MAS / Singapore S$NEER path slope, centre, width Import prices and demand conditions Domestic costs and inflation SNB / Switzerland Policy rate + FX when necessary Funding conditions CHF and demand Domestic costs and inflation How to read. Each row shows a policy channel, not a fixed causal coefficient. Exchange-rate changes affect both economies. Sources: MAS framework [S06] - [S09] ; SNB strategy [S29] . Singapore uses its exchange rate because external prices reach the economy quickly. MAS describes a highly open economy in which imports account for almost 40 cents of domestic spending. The relevant policy variable is the trade-weighted S$NEER , not a peg to CHF or USD. Singapore interest rates are influenced by global rates and currency expectations. [S07] Policy feature Correct interpretation MAS slope Rate at which the policy band appreciates; an unchanged positive slope still permits continued strengthening. MAS centre / width The band position and permitted fluctuation range. Exact numerical parameters and basket weights are undisclosed. [S09] SNB price stability CPI inflation below 2%, with sustained deflation also inconsistent with price stability. [S29] MAS price stability No explicit numerical inflation target. Just-under-2% core inflation is described as consistent with price stability over time. [S06] Employment informs both policy assessments. Slack, vacancies, productivity and wages help indicate future price pressure. Neither framework should be relabelled as a simple rule to minimise the unemployment rate regardless of inflation. [S06] [S08] [S29] Back to overview ↑ 04 / MAS decisions and projections MAS tightened in April and July, then preserved that stance in October Decision date Policy action 2026 core forecast 2026 headline forecast 29 Jan 2026 Hold appreciation slope 1.0-2.0% 1.0-2.0% 14 Apr 2026 Increase slope slightly 1.5-2.5% 1.5-2.5% 27 Jul 2026 Increase slope very slightly 1.5-2.5% 1.5-2.5% 14 Oct 2026 Hold appreciation slope 1.5-2.0% Around 2.0% Annual-average forecast ranges, not monthly targets. Width and centre were unchanged at all four decisions. Sources: [S03] - [S05] , [S01] . Swipe the chart horizontally for the full view. The 2026 core-inflation forecast first rose, then narrowed Annual-average MAS core inflation, %; forecast vintage on each row 0 1 2 3 January 1-2% April 1.5-2.5% July 1.5-2.5% October 1.5-2% How to read. Each segment is the published range for the same forecast year. Its length expresses a range, not a probability distribution. Sources: [S03] - [S05] , [S01] . View exact chart values Annual-average MAS core inflation, %; forecast vintage on each row Forecast vintage Published range, % January 1-2 April 1.5-2.5 July 1.5-2.5 October 1.5-2 January was a normalisation assessment; April was an imported-cost response. January raised the inflation forecast but left policy unchanged. April anticipated wider pass-through from the energy disruption and increased the slope. July added a smaller increase as growth proved resilient and external costs remained persistent. [S03] - [S05] The October hold is consistent with earlier tightening still working. The bank retained the appreciating path while narrowing its 2026 core forecast. Its 2027 core and headline forecasts were both 1.5-2.5%. An analyst should distinguish a smaller projected inflation outcome from a reversal in policy. [S01] Back to overview ↑ 05 / Singapore monthly inflation September inflation eased, but prices continued to rise Swipe the chart horizontally for the full view. Core inflation was higher by August, then eased in September Monthly observations of year-on-year inflation, %; January-September 2026 0 1 2 3 Jan Feb Mar Apr May Jun Jul Aug Sep Headline 2.2% MAS core 2% How to read. Each point compares that month with the same month a year earlier. Solid circles = headline; dashed squares = core. These are inflation rates, not price-index levels. Source: MAS September release, Table A.2 [S12] ; June/August releases [S10] [S11] . View exact chart values Monthly observations of year-on-year inflation, %; January-September 2026 Period Headline MAS core Jan 1.4 1 Feb 1.2 1.4 Mar 1.8 1.7 Apr 1.8 1.4 May 1.8 1.4 Jun 1.9 1.6 Jul 2.2 2 Aug 2.3 2.2 Sep 2.2 2 Disinflation means slower price increases, not necessarily falling prices. September headline inflation fell from 2.3% to 2.2% YoY, and core from 2.2% to 2.0%. Yet the monthly price changes were still +0.2% and +0.1%, respectively. A household can therefore experience rising prices while the annual inflation rate declines. [S13] September detail Monthly movement in annual rate Interpretation Services 2.0% to 1.7% Some service-price pressure eased. Retail and other goods 1.8% to 1.2% Goods inflation moderated. Food 2.3% to 2.4% Pressure continued despite lower overall core. Electricity and gas 8.7% to 8.7% Energy-related pressure remained elevated. August to September 2026; component rates are YoY. These components do not have equal weights and cannot be averaged. Source: [S12] , pp.2-4. Policy implication: assess breadth as well as direction. A single softer month is useful evidence, but it cannot establish that imported pressure has ended. Continued food and utility inflation can coexist with cheaper telecommunications and softer discretionary goods. Back to overview ↑ 06 / Why Singapore inflation moved Energy costs reach Singapore through both direct prices and business costs Swipe the chart horizontally for the full view. A supply shock can reach consumers on different timetables Illustrative channels; no contribution shares are implied Direct channel Global fuel costs Tariff reset and transport prices Household bills Indirect channel Freight + inputs Business margins and pricing decisions Broader goods and services prices How to read. The direct and indirect channels can overlap. A policy response aims to contain pass-through and persistence; it cannot create missing fuel. Sources: April statement [S04] ; tariff methodology [S12] . Timing explains why retail inflation can rise after the initial commodity shock. The September CPI report links the Q3 regulated electricity tariff to natural-gas prices observed mainly during April to mid-June. Contracts, inventories and tariff resets can delay pass-through. The exchange rate moderates the domestic-currency cost, but does not cancel the global supply shock. [S12] The Macroeconomic Review supports an external-shock lens. Box B estimates that external factors explain about 68% of inflation variation captured by its model. That is a model-based historical decomposition: it is neither an import weight nor a claim that 68% of today's inflation is imported. [S02] , Box B The more important question is whether the shock spreads. If firms absorb cost increases in margins, the consumer impact is smaller. If demand is strong enough to sustain repeated price rises and workers seek compensating wage increases, the shock can become more persistent. Evidence on wages, productivity and services prices determines which mechanism is more plausible. Policy works before the forecast horizon arrives. MAS cites a modelled peak effect after four to six quarters. That does not mean every import-price effect waits that long; it explains why policy should consider the medium-term path rather than react mechanically to the latest monthly number. [S08] Back to overview ↑ 07 / Singapore employment Employment growth accelerated while restructuring continued Swipe the chart horizontally for the full view. Net employment gains accelerated in Q3 Persons; excludes migrant domestic workers; 2026 quarterly changes 0 10000 20000 30000 9,400 Q1 11,400 Q2 27,700 Q3 advance How to read. Bars start at zero and show changes in employment, not employment levels. Q3 is preliminary. Sources: MOM [S14] - [S16] ; coverage confirmed in [S45] . View exact chart values Persons; excludes migrant domestic workers; 2026 quarterly changes Measure / period Value Q1 9,400 Q2 11,400 Q3 advance 27,700 Labour measure Q1 / March Q2 / June Q3 / September Retrenchments, persons 3,830 4,620 4,800 advance Overall unemployment, SA 2.0% 1.9% 2.0% Resident unemployment, SA 2.9% 2.9% 3.0% Citizen unemployment, SA 3.1% 3.0% 3.1% Unemployment rows are end-quarter snapshots, not averages. Employment additions and retrenchments are different measures; do not subtract retrenchments from net additions. Sources: [S14] - [S16] . Total job growth does not describe every worker's experience. Q3 gains were stronger for both residents and non-residents, but non-residents accounted for most growth, notably in construction and manufacturing. Resident gains were more concentrated in essential and public services. [S16] The inflation signal is mixed. Expanding labour supply can let output grow without an equivalent surge in wage pressure. At the same time, layoffs in outward-oriented industries point to restructuring and skill mismatch. A large net employment gain therefore cannot, by itself, establish a wage-price spiral. Watch matching as well as hiring. More job vacancies than unemployed people can coexist with unemployment if the available skills, location or pay do not match the positions. The relevant policy evidence is whether this mismatch produces persistent aggregate wage and cost pressure. Back to overview ↑ 08 / Singapore wages and capacity Productivity and labour supply can absorb strong output growth Evidence What it says What it does not establish Resident earnings growth: 3.3% in Q1 to 4.0% in Q2 YoY Nominal earnings strengthened. Every sector faced equivalent wage pressure. H1 unit labour cost growth: 0.3% Output per worker helped contain labour cost per unit. Household living costs rose by only 0.3%. June vacancies: 68,600 SA; 1.48 per unemployed person Vacancies exceeded unemployed persons in aggregate. All vacancies were accessible to each unemployed worker. Resident re-entry within six months: 60.7% to 54.9% Some retrenched workers took longer to find work. The whole labour market was contracting. Earnings: October Review [S02] , chapter 4, p.27; ULC: Box B, p.37. Vacancies and re-entry: MOM Q2 [S15] [S44] . Earnings, labour cost and consumer prices use different denominators. Unit labour cost is the bridge between jobs and inflation. In a simplified identity, labour cost per unit of output equals compensation per worker divided by output per worker. Higher pay is easier to absorb when productivity also rises. This is why headline employment or wage growth alone is an incomplete guide to the inflation outlook. Growth concentration matters. A capital-intensive export industry can expand quickly without generating equally large demand for every type of domestic worker. An analyst should therefore examine spillovers into local wages, rent and consumer services rather than assume that strong technology output automatically overheats the entire economy. Subsidies and competition affect measured inflation too. October's policy assessment described healthcare support and telecommunications competition as restraints on services inflation. These can reduce measured household prices even while some underlying business costs remain firm. [S01] Decision rule: look for persistence across indicators. A stronger case for additional tightening would combine sustained import-cost pressure with accelerating unit labour costs and broad service-price increases. A weaker hiring survey or one subdued CPI component would be insufficient on its own. Back to overview ↑ 09 / SNB policy decisions SNB kept the rate unchanged while the balance of risks evolved Decision Policy rate Central concern at that date 19 Jun 2025 Cut to 0% Established the low-rate starting point for the subsequent period. [S48] 11 Dec 2025 Hold at 0% Recent inflation somewhat below expectation; medium-term pressure broadly stable. [S21] 19 Mar 2026 Hold at 0% Higher energy costs alongside a stronger franc; increased willingness to intervene. [S20] 18 Jun 2026 Hold at 0% Energy-driven inflation pickup; heightened intervention readiness retained. [S19] 24 Sep 2026 Hold at 0% Medium-term pressure only slightly higher; weaker CHF and stronger growth. [S18] An unchanged rate can coexist with changing monetary conditions. Borrowers and exporters respond to market yields, credit terms and the exchange rate, not only the policy-rate announcement. The September discussion assessed that CHF depreciation outweighed modest interest-rate increases, easing overall conditions since June. [S23] The economic logic is conditional, not automatic. When underlying inflation is modest, raising interest rates solely to offset a temporary energy shock can unnecessarily weaken demand. Equally, holding rates becomes harder to justify if the shock raises broad wage and price expectations. The relevant issue is medium-term persistence. FX intervention remains available. The removal of heightened intervention language later in the year did not abolish the instrument. The SNB still stated that it could act in the currency market when needed. Such willingness is different from evidence that a specific intervention actually occurred. [S18] [S23] Wage intentions add a domestic-cost check. Companies in the SNB 's regional talks expected wage increases averaging 1.3% in 2027, following 1.5% in 2026. These are surveyed company intentions, not realised national wage growth. [S22] , Business cycle signals Do not backdate later information. The September decision used August CPI. The October inflation release arrived in November; it is new evidence for the next assessment, not an explanation the September policymakers could already have used. Back to overview ↑ 10 / Swiss monthly inflation Swiss inflation accelerated after July, with imported prices leading Swipe the chart horizontally for the full view. Imported-price inflation rose much faster than domestic inflation Year-on-year CPI change, %; May-October 2026 0 1 2 3 4 May Jun Jul Aug Sep Oct Imported 3.7% Headline 1.5% Domestic 0.8% How to read. The same percentage scale is used for all lines. The lines are sub-index inflation rates, not contributions to headline inflation. Exact observations appear in section 22. Sources: SNB Table 4.1 [S22] ; FSO September/October [S25] [S24] . View exact chart values Year-on-year CPI change, %; May-October 2026 Period Imported Headline Domestic May 0.7 0.6 0.6 Jun 0.2 0.5 0.5 Jul 0 0.4 0.5 Aug 1.5 0.8 0.6 Sep 2.1 1 0.7 Oct 3.7 1.5 0.8 The monthly sequence contradicts a simple story of permanently negligible Swiss inflation. Headline inflation rose from 0.4% in July to 0.8% in August, 1.0% in September and 1.5% in October. The acceleration deserves monitoring even though the composition remains comparatively narrow. [S22] [S25] [S24] Separate the change in the annual rate from the monthly price increase. October's YoY rate increased by 0.5 percentage points, from 1.0% to 1.5%. October's price level rose by 0.2% from September. These are different calculations; the former also reflects the year-earlier comparison base. [S24] [S25] A weaker franc can amplify an external cost shock. If an imported item costs more abroad and the franc weakens against the invoicing currency, both changes can lift the CHF price. This is a transmission mechanism, not an estimate of how much of October inflation was caused by exchange rates. The policy question is whether this spreads. Rising imported inflation paired with stable core inflation calls for a different assessment from an economy-wide acceleration in wages and service prices. The next section tests that distinction with the October composition. Back to overview ↑ 11 / Swiss inflation composition Swiss inflation remains concentrated in imports and energy Swipe the chart horizontally for the full view. Imported inflation reached 3.7%; core 1 remained 0.5% October 2026, year-on-year change, %; component rates, not contributions 0 1 2 3 4 1.5 Headline CPI 0.5 Core 1 0.8 Domestic products 3.7 Imported products How to read. Bars share a zero baseline. Core and origin categories overlap, so the bars must not be added. Source: FSO October release, p.1 [S24] . View exact chart values October 2026, year-on-year change, %; component rates, not contributions Measure / period Value Headline CPI 1.5 Core 1 0.5 Domestic products 0.8 Imported products 3.7 Additional FSO detail October 2026 value Why it matters Energy and fuels 15.9% A sharp increase in a relatively small CPI category. Petroleum products 40.3% Oil-product prices were particularly volatile. CPI excluding petroleum 0.6% The broader basket showed much less pressure. Core 1, monthly change 0.0% MoM No monthly increase in this underlying measure. Source: [S24] , p.3. Ex-petroleum CPI is not the same measure as core 1. The evidence favours a concentrated shock over general overheating. This is an interpretation of the distribution of price changes, not a claim that domestic inflation is zero. Domestic inflation and some service prices are positive; imported costs could still feed into them later. Core definitions change the comparison with Singapore . FSO core 1 excludes fresh and seasonal products, energy and fuel. MAS core excludes accommodation and private transport, but retains food and other energy exposure. A higher MAS core number is therefore not a clean measure of stronger wage-driven inflation. [S24] [S06] The next test is persistence. A retreat in energy inflation with stable core would support looking through part of the shock. Broadening services inflation, stronger wage settlements or rising expectations would make that interpretation less comfortable. The October data does not by itself settle the next SNB decision. Back to overview ↑ 12 / SNB forecast revisions SNB 's 2026 inflation forecast rose despite the unchanged rate Forecast vintage 2026 average CPI 2027 average CPI 2028 average CPI 11 Dec 2025 0.3% 0.6% Not published 19 Mar 2026 0.5% 0.5% 0.6% 18 Jun 2026 0.6% 0.6% 0.7% 24 Sep 2026 0.7% 0.8% 0.8% Sources: [S21] [S20] [S19] [S18] . All forecasts assume the policy rate remains 0% over the forecast horizon. These are annual averages, not year-end rates. Swipe the chart horizontally for the full view. A conditional forecast tests a policy setting Forecast logic, not a promise of future interest-rate decisions Assume a rate held constant Project inflation under that assumption Assess whether policy remains suitable How to read. If the inflation outlook changes, the rate assumption can be reconsidered. Source: SNB strategy [S29] . The forecast revision is informative even without a rate move. The 2026 forecast rose by 0.4 percentage points from the December 2025 vintage to September 2026: 0.7% minus 0.3%. Between June and September, the 2027 forecast rose by 0.2 percentage points. Those revisions indicate a changing outlook, not a mechanically fixed reaction function. Do not compare October's 1.5% directly with a 0.7% full-year forecast. A single monthly YoY inflation rate can exceed the calendar-year average. Testing whether a forecast is too low requires the full price-index path, the remaining months and its underlying assumptions. The headline comparison alone cannot prove a forecast error. Conditional forecasts are not rate-path guidance. The SNB 's constant-rate assumption differs from forecasts that embed an expected path of policy changes. Combining the two without adjustment would make a cross-country forecast comparison appear more precise than it is. [S29] September also improved the growth assessment. The SNB raised its 2026 GDP view to 1.5-2.0%, while retaining around 1.5% for 2027. Stronger activity reduced the case for immediate easing, even though underlying inflation remained modest. [S18] Back to overview ↑ 13 / Swiss employment The Swiss labour picture depends on the measure and seasonal adjustment Series Earlier observation Later observation Change ILO unemployment, NSA Q1: 5.2% Q2: 4.9% -0.3 pp ILO unemployment, SA Q1: 5.0% Q2: 5.1% +0.1 pp Employed persons, YoY Q1: +0.2% Q2: +0.8% +0.6 pp Registered unemployment, NSA Sep: 3.0% Oct: 3.0% 0.0 pp Registered unemployment, SA Sep: 3.1% Oct: 3.1% 0.0 pp Quarterly survey: FSO [S26] [S27] ; SA survey rates: SNB September bulletin [S22] , printed p.15. Monthly registered rates: SECO [S28] . pp = percentage points. The apparent quarterly improvement disappears after seasonal adjustment. The unadjusted ILO rate fell between Q1 and Q2, while the adjusted rate edged higher. This is precisely why a monthly or quarterly policy narrative should keep seasonal treatment consistent rather than select whichever measure supports the preferred story. Employment and unemployment can rise together. The number working can increase while the labour force expands faster, or while some workers struggle to move into the new vacancies. The Q2 ILO unemployment rate was also above the 4.6% recorded a year earlier. The data therefore supports growth with residual labour-market slack, rather than a simple boom-or-recession label. [S27] October administrative counts Count Definition Registered unemployed 141,015 Up 535 from September; rate rounded unchanged. Registered jobseekers 230,001 Broader administrative category than unemployed. Registered vacancies 40,462 Positions, not unemployed people or jobseekers. Source: SECO October labour release [S28] . These administrative categories differ in definition and cannot be substituted for one another. Cross-country ranking would be misleading. Singapore 's overall rate combines resident survey evidence with nonresident employment records. Switzerland 's registered rate depends on administrative registration; its ILO survey is a separate measure. The direction within each well-defined series is more informative than comparing 2.0% with 3.0%. [S17] [S28] Back to overview ↑ 14 / Growth and concentration Strong export sectors can lift GDP without overheating every domestic market Latest consistent real GDP vintage Q1 2026 Q2 2026 Q3 2026 Singapore , YoY 6.4% 6.2% 5.4% advance Singapore , QoQ SA 1.4% 1.5% 1.1% advance Switzerland , QoQ SA, sports-adjusted 0.5% 1.5% Not yet released Singapore : 14 Oct release [S43] and its linked tables; Switzerland : 3 Sep SECO release [S31] . Figures are not annualised. Different adjustment conventions are disclosed. Singapore 's growth remains strong but has moderated on this vintage. Technology-related production supports the overall economy, while the latest advance estimate shows slower quarterly growth than Q2. The relevant inflation question is whether export demand spills into domestic wage costs, rents and consumption. [S43] Swiss Q2 strength has a large industry-specific component. SECO reports a 10.5% quarterly expansion in chemicals and pharmaceuticals, against 0.7% in the rest of manufacturing. Domestic final demand grew 0.5%. A large export-sector jump therefore should not be read as equivalent overheating in household demand. [S31] Transmission question Why the answer matters Is growth labour- or capital-intensive? Employment demand and wage bargaining may respond differently. Does productivity rise alongside wages? Higher output per worker can limit unit labour cost pressure. Are gains broad across industries? Concentrated expansion can coexist with layoffs elsewhere. Does currency appreciation constrain exporters? A disinflation tool can also affect competitiveness and profits. Keep historical revisions out of causal claims. April's Singapore statement described Q1 using an advance estimate that was later revised. To understand why policy was set then, use the then-available data. To describe the economy now, use a consistent latest vintage. The two questions require separate tables. Use a consistent adjustment basis. The Swiss discussion uses official quarter-on-quarter, seasonally and sports-event-adjusted GDP. Annual growth, annualised quarterly growth and ordinary quarterly growth are different measures and should not be combined into a single unlabelled series. Back to overview ↑ 15 / CHF/SGD quotation and evidence The quote convention determines the financial effect CHF/SGD means Singapore dollars per Swiss franc. A fall in this rate lowers the SGD value of a fixed CHF asset and the SGD cost of repaying fixed CHF principal. A rise reverses those effects. Identity Interpretation CHF/SGD = (SGD per USD) ÷ (CHF per USD) Both USD legs must refer to the same time and compatible quote basis. SGD value = CHF amount × CHF/SGD A fixed foreign-currency amount changes value in the spending currency when the exchange rate changes. Percentage change = (end rate / start rate − 1) × 100 Returns require known dates and reliable observations at both endpoints. Market-data boundary. This report contains no verified live CHF/SGD quote or synchronised bilateral history. It therefore makes no numerical claim about the cross's recent return or current trading range. No missing market observation has been estimated. Horizon matters. A four-week return, calendar-year return and rolling twelve-month return measure different windows. Opposite signs can all be correct. Economic mechanisms alone cannot establish which pattern the bilateral rate actually followed. Attribution requires more evidence. An exact decomposition would need aligned exchange-rate observations, policy expectations, flow or intervention evidence and an identification method. The next section describes conditional mechanisms, not measured contributions. Source: arithmetic identities and author analysis. No exchange-rate target, probability or market-price observation is implied. Back to overview ↑ 16 / CHF/SGD mechanisms Policy divergence and funding flows can influence CHF/SGD Swipe the chart horizontally for the full view. Several forces can influence the same currency cross Directional mechanisms; no attribution percentages or price targets Singapore side Appreciating S$NEER policy Support for SGD against its basket Potential downward pressure on CHF/SGD Swiss side in the September assessment Low CHF rate wider foreign spreads Greater carry appeal limited haven demand Potential downward pressure on CHF/SGD How to read. The final arrow is conditional: a basket move does not guarantee the bilateral result. Sources: MAS October [S01] ; SNB September discussion [S23] . The SNB itself documented a funding-flow explanation. Its September assessment described roughly 3% trade-weighted CHF depreciation since June. Wider foreign interest differentials and low currency volatility made CHF-funded carry trades more attractive, while safe-haven demand was limited. The October publication date should not extend that June-to-September measurement window. [S23] [S46] MAS supplies a separate channel. An appreciating trade-weighted policy band can restrain imported prices and support SGD, but MAS does not target CHF/SGD . CHF can still strengthen against SGD if Swiss-specific demand is strong enough. This distinction prevents a basket-policy statement becoming an unsupported bilateral forecast. The cross-rate identity is exact. With both USD legs observed at the same time: CHF/SGD = (SGD per USD) ÷ (CHF per USD). Holding the other leg constant, a lower numerator or a higher denominator lowers the cross. If both move, their proportional changes determine the result. A chart of the cross alone cannot determine which leg supplied most of the move. Price-level and capital-flow arguments operate on different horizons. Lower Swiss inflation may matter for long-run purchasing power, yet low nominal rates and changing risk appetite can dominate shorter-term flows. Inflation differences alone do not generate a reliable near-term exchange-rate target. Back to overview ↑ 17 / CHF financing implications Low funding cost leaves currency and collateral risk intact Exposure If CHF/SGD falls If CHF/SGD rises Fixed CHF assets, valued in SGD SGD asset value falls SGD asset value rises Fixed CHF debt, repaid from SGD SGD principal repayment cost falls SGD principal repayment cost rises Foreign assets funded in CHF Funding translation can help Liability translation can hurt Fully matched CHF cash flows Smaller currency mismatch Smaller currency mismatch Directional identities only. Asset-price changes, interest, spreads, fees, hedges and collateral terms remain separate. The SNB rate is not a client loan quotation. A financing contract can include a reference rate, bank spread, tenor adjustments, fees and collateral conditions. Its reset date need not match a central-bank meeting. The 0% policy rate therefore cannot be entered as an all-in borrowing cost. [S29] Track principal translation before adding other effects. For fixed principal, SGD liability = CHF principal × CHF/SGD . If interest increases the CHF amount owed, apply the exchange rate to that contractual amount. Do not subtract the same loan a second time from a portfolio NAV already reported net of financing. Swipe the chart horizontally for the full view. A risk-off episode can pressure both sides of a funded portfolio Risk mechanism; illustrative sequence, not a predicted event Asset prices fall CHF demand rises as positions unwind Collateral headroom can shrink How to read. Adverse asset and currency moves can coincide. The magnitude depends on the actual holdings and loan terms. Safe-haven mechanism: [S30] . Carry is compensation for accepting risks, not a guaranteed spread. An unhedged borrowing strategy depends on the currency path as well as interest savings. Hedging replaces part of that uncertainty with a priced forward or option and may introduce rollover, basis, liquidity or premium costs. Practical action: assess the balance sheet in its spending currency. Record the CHF liability, interest reset date, asset currencies, hedged share and collateral headroom separately. This report supplies a research framework; it does not calculate personalised returns from missing loan or portfolio inputs. Back to overview ↑ 18 / Attributed policy assessment summaries Official assessments show how the policy outlook changed across the year Source date / location Independent attributed summary Plain-English reading MAS 29 Jan, paragraph 9 [S03] MAS judged that underlying inflation was moving back toward its usual pace. Normalisation from unusually low inflation. MAS 14 Apr, paragraph 12 [S04] MAS raised the appreciation slope of its exchange-rate band by a small amount. A pre-emptive response to rising imported costs. MAS 27 Jul, paragraph 12 [S05] MAS made a further slope increase, with a smaller adjustment than in April. Further tightening, but a smaller adjustment. MAS 14 Oct, paragraph 11 [S01] MAS left the appreciation slope of its exchange-rate band unchanged. The appreciating stance continues. SNB 19 Mar, forecast paragraph [S20] SNB attributed a modest downward revision in its medium-term inflation forecast to a stronger franc. Currency strength restrained the forecast. SNB 18 Jun, inflation paragraph [S19] SNB judged that the inflation pickup was concentrated, with most other goods and services contributing little. The observed pickup was concentrated. SNB 24 Sep, paragraph 2 [S18] SNB saw only a modest strengthening of medium-term inflation pressure. Some upward pressure, but no major medium-term shift. SNB summary published 22 Oct, concluding policy section [S23] SNB judged that conditions no longer called for an elevated readiness to intervene in foreign-exchange markets. Heightened readiness was removed; the intervention tool remained. These are independent summaries of the cited sources, not verbatim quotations. The SNB publication in October describes the September decision; it is not a new October rate meeting. Read qualitative assessments alongside the numerical forecasts. Descriptions of small or very small changes signal policy calibration, not disclosed basis-point equivalents for the MAS slope. The SNB assessment can change materially while its headline policy rate remains the same. Monthly releases add evidence between policy meetings. The September-to-October Swiss data showed a higher headline rate with unchanged core; Singapore 's September release showed easing annual inflation but positive monthly price changes. These observations update the outlook; they do not retrospectively change what was known at the preceding decision. Back to overview ↑ 19 / Conditional scenarios The next move depends on which risk becomes persistent Conditional scenario Likely policy consideration CHF/SGD implication to test Energy pressure fades; underlying inflation stays contained MAS can preserve its existing path while monitoring pass-through; SNB has less reason to react to temporary headline pressure. Existing policy divergence may remain relevant; no automatic bilateral exchange-rate outcome. Swiss energy shock spreads to wages and services A broader Swiss inflation forecast would strengthen the case for a firmer SNB stance. CHF support could increase, particularly if the change surprises markets. Global risk aversion and carry unwinding Safe-haven CHF demand can tighten Swiss conditions even with no rate increase; SNB may reassess FX intervention. CHF/SGD could rise rapidly, despite a low Swiss policy rate. AI/export demand weakens sharply in Singapore MAS would assess the output gap, employment and medium-term inflation before considering a less appreciating path. SGD support could weaken; concurrent global haven demand could amplify the cross-rate effect. Author analysis. No probabilities, timing or price targets assigned. Mechanisms draw on [S01] [S18] [S23] [S30] . Policy choices remain conditional on the full outlook. The largest mistake would be treating one scenario as the forecast. A risk table identifies what would change the thesis. It does not claim that policymakers will react to any single data release in the way shown. Surprise matters alongside direction. A currency can weaken after a policy tightening if markets expected a larger one. Conversely, a hold can support a currency when investors expected easing. A credible trading interpretation needs the pre-decision market expectation, which this report does not estimate. Use inversion to protect the decision. Instead of asking only why CHF might remain weak, ask what would make that view fail: a haven shock, broader Swiss inflation, a shift in SNB communication, or a weaker Singapore outlook. Those are the conditions that deserve explicit monitoring. History is a reminder about regime risk. The removal of the SNB 's EUR/CHF minimum exchange rate in January 2015 illustrates that policy arrangements can change. It is not evidence that the same event will recur under today's different framework. [S47] Back to overview ↑ 20 / Monitoring priorities Monitor inflation breadth and currency risk before relying on carry Priority What to monitor Action when the evidence changes 1 / CHF balance-sheet exposure Net CHF amount, repayment dates, hedge maturity and collateral capacity Reassess exposure limits and hedge choices using actual contract terms. 2 / Swiss inflation breadth Core 1, domestic products, services, wages and expectations Distinguish another energy spike from a broader inflation regime. 3 / MAS cost outlook Import costs, tariff resets, food prices, services ULC and S$NEER wording Check whether the expected 2027 disinflation remains supported. 4 / Labour-market quality Resident hiring, retrenchments, re-entry, vacancies and Swiss SA survey data Look for sustained slack or cost pressure across more than one release. 5 / Currency-flow conditions CHF volatility, foreign rate differentials, risk appetite and policy surprises Test whether the funding-flow explanation is reversing. Read each release through a consistent sequence. First verify the observation period and publication date; then check revisions and definitions; finally compare the release with the previous policy assumptions. This prevents a revised GDP number or seasonal unemployment change from becoming a false policy signal. The next evidence gaps are identifiable. At this cutoff, Singapore October CPI, detailed Q3 labour results and Swiss Q3 GDP were not yet available. These are the next pieces needed to extend the matched data comparison. Their absence is shown explicitly rather than filled with model forecasts. For client communication, retain the trade-off. Lower CHF funding cost can help cash flow, while CHF appreciation can increase the repayment burden. A favourable historical exchange-rate move does not remove that second risk. Present each effect separately and use the client's actual balance-sheet currency. The conclusion remains conditional. The evidence establishes different policy settings and plausible currency channels. It does not establish a current CHF/SGD price, measure bilateral performance, or justify permanent franc weakness and risk-free financing. Back to overview ↑ 21 / Source and calculation controls Definitions, dates and adjustment methods control the comparison Potential trap Interpretation used here Swiss unemployed, jobseekers and vacancies Separate SECO administrative categories. October counts are 141,015, 230,001 and 40,462 respectively. Singapore vacancies: 68,600 versus 69,900 June figures are seasonally adjusted and unadjusted respectively. Singapore Q3 employment: 27,700 versus 32,000 The first excludes migrant domestic workers. The second includes them. Both are preliminary. Policy rate versus market rate SNB's policy rate is not an all-in loan cost. Singapore market rates are not MAS's policy target. Swiss quarterly GDP Use the non-annualised, seasonally and sports-event-adjusted SECO growth rates. SNB bulletin quarterly figures are generally annualised. Forecast versus observation Annual-average forecasts, monthly year-on-year CPI and interest-rate assumptions have distinct meanings. Sources: [S28] [S44] [S45] [S07] [S22] [S31] . Definitions and units. Year-on-year inflation equals (current index / same-month prior-year index − 1) × 100. Month-on-month inflation uses the prior month. A change from 1.0% to 1.5% is 0.5 percentage points. It is not a 0.5% increase in the price level. Annual inflation is not reconstructed by averaging rounded monthly rates. Source hierarchy. Official statistical releases supply definitions and revisions. Central-bank statements document the information set and rationale at each decision. Analytical scenarios are the author's interpretations and have no assigned probabilities. Rights and attribution. This independently written report uses limited factual extracts and newly drawn charts rather than reproducing official report pages, logos or supplied graphics. Each fact links to its issuer. It is not endorsed by MAS, SNB, FSO, SECO, METI or MOM. Source publications retain their respective rights. Visual conventions. Colour & Tagging Standard V1.2 Merged, 5 November 2026: MAS teal, Switzerland and SNB rose, Singapore jade and CHF/SGD purple. Labels and line styles preserve meaning in greyscale. Reproducibility boundary. Tables retain exact observations used in the charts. Missing values stay missing. No bilateral CHF/SGD market series, current quote or proprietary vendor data is embedded. Back to overview ↑ 22 / Exact observations Exact data behind the inflation and employment comparisons 2026 month SG headline MAS core Swiss headline Swiss domestic Swiss imported May 1.8 1.4 0.6 0.6 0.7 June 1.9 1.6 0.5 0.5 0.2 July 2.2 2.0 0.4 0.5 0.0 August 2.3 2.2 0.8 0.6 1.5 September 2.2 2.0 1.0 0.7 2.1 October Unpublished Unpublished 1.5 0.8 3.7 All values % YoY; each series retains its own CPI definition. Singapore [S10] - [S13] ; Switzerland [S22] [S25] [S24] . Missing observations are not zeros. SG early-2026 monthly CPI January February March April Headline, % YoY 1.4 1.2 1.8 1.8 MAS core, % YoY 1.0 1.4 1.7 1.4 Source: MAS September release, Table A.2 [S12] . SG quarterly employment change, persons Q1 Q2 Q3 advance Excluding migrant domestic workers 9,400 11,400 27,700 Including migrant domestic workers 13,000 14,700 32,000 Retrenchments (separate measure) 3,830 4,620 4,800 Sources: MOM [S14] - [S16] and employment summary [S45] . Retrenchments are not subtracted again from net employment change. Publication timing. Singapore September CPI was released on 23 October. Swiss September CPI was released on 1 October and October CPI on 3 November. The latest common month is September. Policy-decision dates remain distinct from these later releases. Reading the percentages. National CPI levels have different base years and baskets, so their index numbers are not compared. The charts compare rates of change with clear definitions; they do not compare the countries' absolute cost of living. entries.text: MAS and SNB: policy, inflation and currency risk | Public abridgement My Research Earlier published edition All editions PUBLIC ABRIDGED EDITION · 7 NOVEMBER 2026 MAS and SNB: policy, inflation and currency risk Pending further information review. This article is published for general information while the underlying information is reviewed again. It retains selected official-source facts and independent analysis from the 6 November 2026 research, not a fresh verification of every release. Figures and conclusions may be revised. No live prices, dealing quotations or personalised investment advice are provided. Scope of this edition. This is a separate, shortened public edition of this study. Identity The cross-rate identity is exact. With both USD legs observed at the same time: CHF/SGD = ( SGD per USD ) ÷ ( CHF per USD ). Holding the other leg constant, a lower numerator or a higher denominator lowers the cross. If both move, their proportional changes determine the result. A chart of the cross alone cannot determine which leg supplied most of the move. Analysis Price-level and capital-flow arguments operate on different horizons. Historical capped-return illustrations are not executable zero-premium collar quotes. The original revision PDF is not included in this public package. Research / SPX put-and-call collars Educational research · 6 November 2026 Price history · payoff design · execution SPX put-and-call collars A put can protect an expiry value. Selling a call helps pay for it by giving up upside. The history shows the size of that trade-off; market quotes determine whether a particular collar can be entered at zero net option premium. Research checked 6 November 2026, Singapore time · Main history: 1961–2025 · Price returns in USD terms · No live trade quote US Equities Put and call options Scenario analysis 17 / 65 Years below 0% 26.15% of complete calendar years 38 / 65 Years above 9% 58.46% of complete calendar years 0%–9% Hypothetical annual payoff One-year holding period; annual reset Four takeaways The floor helped in 17 years; the cap constrained 38. Ten years stayed between 0% and 9%, inclusive. These are sample frequencies, not future odds. Removing negative annual outcomes did not maximise compounded wealth. A starting 100 became 11,780.24 for the price index and 3,871.85 under the hypothetical annually reset rule, before dividends and costs. A fixed 0% floor and 9% cap are not automatically zero-premium. The report has no historical option quotes. Its pricing example is a model illustration, explicitly separate from a trade. Starting month matters, and protection has a maturity date. The heatmap shows 97 overlapping one-year windows. It does not measure daily collar values or establish a guarantee on early exit. Independent calculations from published levels; price history and scenario, 1961–2025. Display percentages rounded to two decimals. [1] [5] [6] [7] 01 The collar 02 History 03 Wealth 04 Heatmap 05 Trade-off 06 Pricing 07 Implementation 08 Review Method Audit Sources 01 / How the collar works Three positions create one expiry payoff The protection comes from the put; the funding contribution comes from the call sold. The investor also needs underlying equity exposure. For the clean illustration, use matching notionals, the same one-year expiry, a put strike equal to the starting reference level, and a call strike 9% above it. 1 Hold the underlying exposure Participate in changes in the reference price. In practice this means an equity basket or tracking vehicle; the index itself is a calculation. 2 Buy a protective put At expiry, the put pays when the reference settles below its strike. Buying this protection costs a premium. 3 Sell a call Receive a premium and owe the payoff above the call strike. This gives up part of the underlying’s upside. Mechanics: OIC protective collar; contract details are checked separately below. Selected historical regime Broadly flat endpoints · 1966–1978 Price 103.98 Clipped 167.57 13 complete annual periods. Each pair starts at 100 at the preceding year-end. Compare within a pair; the windows have different lengths. How to read. The solid bar is historical price wealth; the dashed bar is hypothetical clipped wealth. All bars start from zero. Each regime resets its initial wealth to 100, and each uses only complete calendar years. NYU year-end levels; own calculations. Illustrative windows selected to show bear, bull and broadly flat price endpoints. Selection is descriptive, not a comprehensive ranking. [1] Protection benefit 224.12 pp of annual downside removed 17 affected years Average lift: 13.18 percentage points per negative year. The largest single-year lift was 38.49 pp in 2008, when the price return was −38.49% and the hypothetical result was 0%. Sum over all years: Σ max(−R, 0) × 100. This adds annual payoff differences only; it is not a cumulative return or an amount of cash saved. Own calculations; 1961–2025; percentages rounded for display. [1] Opportunity cost 423.41 pp of annual upside surrendered 38 affected years Average reduction: 11.14 percentage points per above-cap year. In 1995, a +34.11% price return became +9.00%, giving up 25.11 pp of that year’s gain. Sum over all years: Σ max(R − 0.09, 0) × 100. It describes the price of the cap in annual payoff space, not a compounded wealth calculation. Own calculations; 1961–2025; percentages rounded for display. [1] The historical conclusion is a trade-off, not a recommendation. The annual rule reduced downside and dispersion by construction, but ended with less wealth over the full sample. A different window can favour the transformed path. Real costs, changing collar terms and the ability to stay invested can alter an actual investor’s outcome; none is established by this clipping exercise. 06 / Can the call pay for the put? Zero net premium is a market-pricing condition Choosing a 0% floor and a 9% cap does not make the premiums equal. At a specified timestamp, a conservative separate-leg screen is put ask minus call bid. A package quote may differ; available strikes, size and liquidity still have to support the actual execution. Net option debit d = P ask (K p , T) − C bid (K c , T). Zero net option premium requires d = 0; it does not eliminate costs or surrendered upside. Indicative theoretical example · not a live or historical quote In this model, the desired 9% cap leaves a debit Illustrative option premiums per 100 initial notional Three horizontal bars start at zero. The long put premium paid is 7.077, the short call premium received is 5.011, and the net option debit is 2.066, all per 100 initial notional. Put and call bars are magenta, distinguished by solid fill versus an outlined hatched fill. The net debit bar is neutral slate. These are theoretical model values, not executable quotes. Illustrative option premiums Model values per 100 initial notional · not executable quotes 0 2 4 6 8 Long put (paid) 7.077 Short call (received) 5.011 Net option debit 2.066 How to read. The put cost is larger than the proceeds from the 109-strike call. The difference, 2.066 per 100 notional, must be paid or funded. The bars are theoretical European option values, not traded prices. Keep the 0% price floor Put strike = 100 Solve equal model premiums Call strike ≈ 103.302907 Resulting model cap ≈ 3.302907%, rather than 9% All inputs are hypothetical: S 0 = 100; put strike 100; initial call strike 109; one year; continuously compounded risk-free rate 3%; continuous dividend yield 1.5%; flat implied volatility 20% at both strikes. European Black–Scholes–Merton valuation; no bid–ask spreads, fees, discrete-strike limits, funding charges or skew. Model outputs: put 7.07706385; call 5.01066477; net debit 2.06639908 per 100 notional. Equal model premiums give a call strike of 103.30290744. Extra digits support reproduction, not quote accuracy. Independent Black–Scholes–Merton calculation, assumptions set for this illustration on 6 Nov 2026. OIC explains why market premiums, not formulas, determine actual prices. [11] [12] [13] Capital accounting The premium changes the return denominator Paying the model debit requires 102.06639908 of initial capital. If the expiry price component is 100, the return on that expenditure is approximately −2.024564% . At an expiry value of 109, it is approximately +6.793226% . Return on capital = V T ÷ (100 + d) − 1 This example excludes dividends and all other costs. Borrowing the debit instead creates a separate financing cash flow. A 0% reference-price floor is not a 0% return on a larger initial expenditure. Independent calculation using the model debit above; indicative illustration only. [11] Feasibility condition Solve for a feasible cap or floor Fix the put strike and solve for the call strike—or fix the cap and solve for the put strike. A real zero-premium collar is the result of that pricing exercise. It is not the result of clipping a chart. Strike ordering matters. Retain K p ≤ K c . In the stated continuous-yield model, an ATM put cannot be financed by a call at or above spot when the interest rate is below the dividend yield; at equal rates, the equal-premium cap is 0%. This is a model feasibility condition from put–call parity, not a universal quote rule. Market skew and execution frictions require actual prices. Independent model algebra; theoretical valuation only. [11] What can change the premium balance? Change, other things equal What it does Implication for the collar Raise the put strike More protection; put value rises More call proceeds or a larger debit is needed Raise the call strike More upside retained; call value falls Less funding for the put Increase downside implied volatility relative to call volatility Put protection becomes relatively dearer The same 0% / 9% pair can cost more Higher rates in the stated model Call value rises; put value falls Can improve funding for the same strikes Higher dividend assumptions in the stated model Call value falls; put value rises Can worsen funding for the same strikes Change tenor or volatility across both legs Both values change Net effect depends on strikes, skew and the joint inputs How to read. Read each row as a conditional comparison. Several inputs usually move together. “More volatility” by itself does not tell you the net cost of every collar. OIC option pricing and April 2026 skew discussion; directions for rates and dividends refer to the stated European continuous-yield model. [11] [12] [13] The historical options backtest remains unsubstantiated. No synchronized historical put-ask / call-bid archive was obtained. The missing evidence includes reset timestamps, contract availability, strike increments, expiry and settlement values, sizes, execution rules, dividends, funding and costs. Daily collar volatility and drawdown additionally require marks for the actual contracts held. Instrument history also limits the backtest. Cboe introduced SPX options in 1983. Earlier index years are necessarily counterfactual for listed-SPX execution; any executable backtest needs its own verified start date, available tenors and contract specifications. [18] 07 / What survives outside the payoff diagram? Execution and cash flows determine the account return A clean expiry diagram is a starting point for implementation. Dividend income, actual holdings, option settlement, costs, funding and the investor’s base currency all affect the account result. Check the exposure and the contract together Issue What matters in practice Dividends SPX price returns exclude dividends. A basket or ETF may distribute cash; reinvestment changes exposure. Treat those flows and taxes separately. Clipping total returns does not create SPX option payoffs. [4] Notional and basis Match the option reference, hedge size and dates to the owned exposure. ETF tracking, expenses, portfolio differences and contract-size rounding can leave residual gains or losses. [14] Exercise and settlement SPX is European-style and cash-settled, with a USD 100 multiplier per index point. Traditional SPX uses AM settlement; SPXW weekly and month-end contracts use PM settlement. [8] AM versus closing values AM settlement uses constituent opening trades in a special opening quotation. It can differ from an ordinary index close or a displayed value at one instant. Calendar-year returns do not establish the return at an option’s actual settlement. [9] Assignment European SPX options do not have early assignment. American-style equity or ETF options can, including around dividends; that is a different implementation. [8] [10] Cash and collateral Cash-settled options do not deliver or remove the shares in the account. Plan for cash obligations. Qualifying ETF coverage may receive margin relief, subject to broker policies and ongoing coverage requirements. [15] How to read. Each row identifies a reason why an account can differ from the simple price payoff. The correct comparison requires a cash-flow ledger and the actual contract specifications. Current Cboe documentation and OCC / OIC education, reviewed 6 Nov 2026. No broker account or product term sheet has been inspected. [4] [8] [9] [10] [14] [15] Timing and costs A maturity floor is not an early-exit guarantee Before expiry, both options still have market values. Changes in implied volatility, skew, remaining time, rates and dividends affect those values. Closing the combined position realises available prices, not the expiry diagram. Liquidity and execution can matter most when protection is needed. Spreads and the ability to close both legs together can change the result; closing one leg leaves a different exposure. Exchange and broker fees, funding, taxes and operational errors also belong in the implementation review. OCC liquidity, combination and margin risks; OIC pricing inputs. No daily historical collar marks were obtained. [12] [14] Currency exposure A USD floor is not an SGD floor Currency conversion is a separate source of return. For an unhedged SGD-based account, let FX be SGD per USD: R SGD = (1 + R USD ) × (FX end ÷ FX start ) − 1 Illustrative example: a 0% USD result with a 5% fall in SGD per USD gives −5% in SGD. This is arithmetic, not an FX forecast. Hedging currency introduces its own pricing and cash flows. Nominal protection also does not preserve purchasing power against inflation. No current FX price is used in this report. The legal wrapper changes the risk. A listed-options position, an OTC contract and an issuer note are different arrangements. If exposure is packaged into an OTC or issuer product, counterparty or issuer credit, collateral, liquidity and early-termination provisions must come from its documentation. No actual product terms are inferred here. 08 / Evidence, uncertainty and next steps Use the history to explain the trade-off; use quotes to price it The supported conclusion is specific: in this 65-year price sample, the annual 0%–9% transformation removed negative annual returns and reduced return dispersion, while sacrificing enough upside to finish with materially lower wealth. Whether a particular collar is attractive or zero-premium today is a separate, unanswered question. Keep the evidence status visible Evidence layer What is supported What it does not establish Historical price performance 65 complete annual returns; counts, compounding and annual-endpoint risk metrics Future return probabilities, an investable account return or a current market forecast Hypothetical payoff transformation The algebra of g(R) and its annual-reset historical consequences Historical option availability, zero premiums, daily protection or actual execution Executable collar Current contract mechanics; the inputs and prices needed for a quote A historical or live 0% floor / 9% cap at zero premium; those quotes were not obtained How to read. Each row answers a different question. The three layers should keep separate labels whenever the material is reused in a presentation or dashboard. Methodology synthesis based on the data and primary options sources in this report. [1] [8] [10] [11] [14] Conditional outlook What could change the assessment? Different observed option quotes: put/call skew, rates and expected dividends change which floor and cap can finance each other. A different objective: a willingness to accept some downside, pay a debit or surrender more upside changes the structure. A different horizon: tenor, expiry conventions and reset dates alter both the price and the exposure. A different implementation: dividends, fees, tax, tracking and FX can materially change account returns. These are qualitative scenarios. No target, probability, analyst call or future price path has been invented. Limitations What remains unresolved? Historical executable quotes: the specific annual 0% / 9% zero-premium claim has not been tested. Daily strategy marks: daily volatility, drawdown and early-exit values are not available from clipped annual returns. Longer heatmap validation: this report verifies only the 109 monthly endpoints shown; the wider stored site history is not promoted to a verified dataset. Source use: historical observations are attributed to their published sources and included for reproducibility of this educational analysis. This report does not grant a licence to resell source data or imply endorsement by index or data providers. Practical review checklist Freeze the data definition. Record source, observation dates, price versus total return, precision and excluded periods. Keep 2011’s negative sign and the 17 / 10 / 38 denominator intact. Specify the trade completely. Identify the actual underlying holdings, option symbol, put and call strikes, expiry, settlement convention, quantity and reset timestamp. Obtain simultaneous executable prices. Record bid/ask, size and package price. Solve the cap or floor from those quotes, subject to available strikes. Build the cash-flow ledger. Include dividends, premium debits/credits, financing, fees, spreads, taxes, collateral and FX. Use total capital spent as the return denominator. Stress the exit and settlement. Examine early liquidation, basis differences, insufficient cash and one-leg execution. Check credit terms for any OTC or issuer wrapper. Review the presentation and intended use. Keep source dates, units, line styles and caveats beside the figures. A commercial data product or investment product requires a separate rights and compliance review. Methodology / Reproduction One fixed dataset, explicit formulas The annual calculation uses source precision before display rounding. NYU’s published year-end levels have up to two decimal places; derived returns are not rounded before classification or compounding. The original annual dataset is preserved consistently: NYU’s 2001 and 2003 levels differ by 0.01 index points from ERP’s annual reference rows. No sources are silently spliced. Four full-series charts are replaced with verified aggregate comparisons; the raw annual appendix, copied source documents and data downloads are not republished while redistribution rights remain unverified. This is a hypothetical payoff study, not IFI performance or an executable historical collar. ← Research Explained · Market Intel · Print / save PDF Two five-slide presentations Editable PowerPoints with speaker notes, using aggregate historical results and original hypothetical payoff examples. Implementation and review checklist 01 / RESEARCH IFI SPX Returns, 0%-9% Payoffs and Zero-Cost Collars Recommendation: present the 0%-9% section as a historical scenario calculator, with a separate options-pricing feasibility panel. IFI is a research-module label here; its product terms and actual performance are not assumed. The floor helped in 17 of 65 years; the cap constrained 38. For complete calendar years 1961-2025, 26.15% of price returns were negative, 15.38% were between 0% and 9% inclusive, and 58.46% exceeded 9%.
