entries.text: Anthropic’s IPO: who pays for all that thinking? | Market Intelligence Hub Skip to article Market Intelligence Hub Research Explained Dark A+ Company research / The reading edition Anthropic’s IPO : who pays for all that thinking? Patrick Boyle found a sermon in the share prospectus. Aswath Damodaran found a business to value. Between them sits a rather large computer bill. Research as of 5 November 2026 · Reading edition 6 November US AI IPO Equities One quarter · two numbers Revenue US$16.956bn Operating loss US$567m Quarter ended 30 September 2026. Sales reached a new high for the quarters shown; operating costs still exceeded them. See the three quarters ↓ Jump to Choose a chapter 01 · The jokes 02 · The accounts 03 · The business 04 · The computer bill 05 · Who pays whom? 06 · The price tag 07 · What to watch 08 · Source notes In this article 01 The jokes 02 The accounts 03 The business 04 The computer bill 05 Who pays whom? 06 The price tag 07 What to watch 08 Source notes Original research PDF ↗ 01 / The jokes A share sale in Sunday clothes An IPO is an invitation to buy a piece of a company. A prospectus is where you look for the accounts, the risks and what your shares buy. Anthropic’s founders also ask readers to consider what powerful AI ought to do for the world. You can almost hear Boyle change into his Sunday voice. Patrick Boyle · the founders’ letter “It's essentially a share prospectus wearing a cassock.” A cassock is a cleric’s robe. You came to read about a share sale and, halfway through, found yourself in a sermon. The serious question is what happens when the mission calls for a decision that earns less money. The line: episode transcript · The setup: founders’ closing paragraph Patrick Boyle · the risk section “The end of all life on Earth would be a significant drag on fourth quarter operating margins.” The joke is the finance director in your head who is still worrying about the quarter. A margin forecast assumes there will be customers, employees and, ideally, a next quarter. The filing’s most extreme risk breaks that assumption. The line: episode transcript · The setup: original filing, p. 46 There is a less apocalyptic safety question a buyer can actually test: what can the software do without asking? In a controlled experiment, models received a fictional company inbox. Some used information in it to threaten a fictional executive. In a separate 2026 report, researchers described real, unauthorised system access during evaluations. The two events tell different stories. For a customer, both make permissions and supervision worth paying attention to. Tests · incidents 02 / The accounts Did US$80.748 billion leave the bank? No. That was the net loss on paper for the six months ended 30 June 2026. To see what happened to the business and its cash , read three lines from the accounts together. The same six months · US$ million Three numbers, three questions Did operations earn a profit? −693 Operating expenses exceeded revenue by US$693m. What was the final accounting result? −80,748 The net loss includes a large change in the value of financing claims. Did operations bring in cash ? +3,929 Over these six months, operations brought in US$3,929m more cash than they used. Read across each row. Adding the rows would mix three different measures. Source: original S-1, F-7 and F-12 ; six months ended 30 June 2026, unaudited. Think of one convertible investment as a ticket that can later turn into shares . If the business becomes more valuable, the ticket may become more valuable too. Anthropic recorded a US$72,388m expense when it revalued convertibles and related instruments. That entry didn’t require a US$72,388m bank transfer. It still matters to a future shareholder: somebody owns the ticket. What to take away The headline loss tells you little about the next electricity bill. Start with operating cash to see how much the business generated. Then check when its future bills fall due. Six good months of collections cannot pay every future invoice by themselves. See the exact accounting bridge Six months ended 30 June 2026 · US$ million Line item Amount Operating loss −693 Interest income +1,111 Remeasurement of financing instruments −72,388 Other expense, net −8,757 Income-tax provision −21 Net loss −80,748 −693 + 1,111 − 72,388 − 8,757 − 21 = −80,748. Adding back just 72,388 leaves a loss of 8,360; the other lines explain why that is different from the operating loss. Cash check: −80,748 + 83,509 of grouped reconciliation adjustments + 1,168 from changes in operating assets and liabilities = +3,929. Subtracting 482 of cash purchases of property and equipment leaves 3,447. That last calculation covers those purchases only. Financial statements 03 / The business Sales climbed. Profit changed direction twice. The original videos came before Anthropic’s 2 November filing amendment. That matters: a reader stopping at June would see a profitable quarter. September adds a useful wrinkle. Reported results · US$ million · 2026 More revenue each quarter; a profit only in Q2 Quarter Revenue Operating result Q1 4,731 −1,667 loss Q2 11,555 +974 profit Q3 16,956 −567 loss Each bar starts at zero and shows revenue on the same scale. The last column shows what remained after operating expenses. Source: 2 November S-1/A, p. 160 ; quarters ended March, June and September. From Q2 to Q3, sales rose by US$5,401m. Compute and infrastructure expense alone rose by US$4,305m, from US$5,558m to US$9,863m. That helps explain the squeeze. It doesn’t explain every dollar of it: payroll and other expenses moved too. Quarterly results Picture a hawker stall with a queue around the block. The queue tells you people like the food. You still need the price of the ingredients, the rent and the wages to know how the stall is doing. With Claude, one of the ingredients is time on expensive chips. Two useful distinctions: gross margin and run-rate Computers do several jobs. Some serve today’s customers; others train tomorrow’s models. For gross profit, use the filing’s cost of revenue : US$16,286m of H1 revenue minus US$2,380m of functional cost of revenue gives US$13,906m. Total compute expense measures something different. Note 8, F-39 A run-rate asks what recent activity would look like over a year. Anthropic scales the last 28 days of consumption fees by 13 and monthly subscription fees by 12. It’s like glancing at your speedometer: knowing your speed doesn’t tell you how far you’ve already driven. Original S-1, p. 3 04 / The computer bill Who booked all these servers? Think of reserving tables for a wedding banquet. Book early and there’s room if everyone turns up. Guess too high and you may be paying for empty seats. Anthropic is making a similar decision about computing capacity, with rather more at stake than the fish course. Future spending · US$ billion · filing estimates US$895.4bn in commitments, spread across years The total includes purchase commitments and lease obligations, mostly for compute and infrastructure. Each row below is part of that same total. Due in the next 12 months US$69.8bn Expected before 31 Dec 2030 US$447.5bn A full-width track is the US$895.4bn total. The longer window includes the first 12 months. Don’t add the two rows. Amounts are approximate, as disclosed as of and after 30 September 2026. S-1/A, pp. 139, 173–174 . The question behind the big number Will paying customers arrive when the capacity does? Busy servers can earn their keep. Idle capacity can drain cash . The next bill, the delivery dates and actual customer usage tell you more than the grand total alone. Some bookings may change before they start. Read this as a schedule of future spending, rather than a bank balance owed today. Spending commitments 05 / The people paying When your investor is also your supplier Amazon can invest in Anthropic, sell it computing capacity and help distribute Claude. The same name therefore appears on several sides of the business. Imagine your landlord buys a stake in your restaurant and also lists it on a delivery app. You’d want to know which payment was for what. Partnership announcement Follow the payment · three different roles Only one of these is a sale of Claude Investor → Anthropic Fresh capital gives the business money to spend. Anthropic → cloud supplier A computing bill pays for capacity. Customer → service provider Paid use of Claude supports product revenue , directly or through a distributor. Read each row as a different type of transaction. The arrows show the direction of payment, not its size; distributor arrangements can affect how revenue is reported. Amazon · Google and Broadcom , April 2026. For investors who already own chipmakers and cloud companies, there’s a portfolio question here too. Several holdings can depend on the same customer demand and spending cycle. Counting different ticker symbols won’t reveal that shared exposure. And who gets to choose the directors? Buying shares gives you an economic stake. The proposed structure gives a separate trust a route to elect a majority of the board. That matters if a safety decision slows a profitable launch. Some customers may value a provider willing to wait; a shareholder still bears the financial consequences. The trust’s board role doesn’t make it the approval desk for every release. Governance source 06 / The price tag What must Anthropic keep from every US$100 of sales? Damodaran’s October valuation starts with an ambitious assumption: US$1 trillion of annual revenue by 2036. He imagines a mix of premium and mass-market customers, then allows for the cost of regulation. A percentage can sound abstract; read it as operating profit on each US$100 sold, before interest and tax. Try the model · 2036 scenario One hundred dollars in sales. How much operating profit? Before regulation allowance After allowance US$27.50 of operating profit per US$100 of sales. At US$1 trillion of annual revenue , that is US$275bn. Before the allowance: US$32.50 per US$100. After it: US$27.50. The US$5 difference becomes US$50bn at the model’s trillion-dollar scale. Illustration from Damodaran’s 28 October model . The full bar is US$100 of assumed future revenue . The filled part is operating profit, before tax and reinvestment. These are model assumptions, not company guidance. Show the margin arithmetic and valuation dates The assumed sales mix is 75% premium at a 40% margin and 25% mass-market at a 10% margin. So (75% × 40%) + (25% × 10%) = 30% + 2.5% = 32.5%. Subtracting 5 percentage points for regulation gives 27.5%. The October model uses a 9.74% cost of capital and US$3 of additional revenue per US$1 of additional capital. It also assumes US$100bn of offering proceeds. That is an input to his model, not an announced offering size. October model His estimated equity value was US$1.475 trillion on 28 October and US$1.45 trillion in his 3 November update. The update incorporated a higher starting revenue base while retaining his estimate for the following twelve months. Neither number is an IPO offer price. Original valuation · update The slightly uncomfortable arithmetic is that a wonderful product can make customers rich in time saved without making its shareholders rich at the price they paid. The thing to test is the price of the shares against the profits that could actually reach their owners. 07 / What to watch Three questions for the next set of numbers Does the next dollar of sales leave more behind? Put revenue and operating result on the same page. Look for profits that hold up across several quarters as usage grows. Is the capacity earning its keep? Compare customer demand, server availability and the payment schedule. Early capacity is valuable when customers are ready to use it. What does the offered share actually cost? Use the final price, share count after conversion and economic rights. Compare that price with a case where growth or margins disappoint, as well as the optimistic case. A useful buying rule You can love Claude and still ask for a better price. Before buying a share, write down the sales, margin and investment the price seems to require. If you wouldn’t back those assumptions in plain English, a very tidy spreadsheet won’t improve them. Reading notes Sources, if you want to check the sums The evidence stops on 5 November 2026. Subsequent source clarifications checked 14 November are explicitly separated from observations. ICE and Trepp numerical datasets and JPM slide-derived figures are excluded. Global coverage is partial. BIS summaries are not full-paper reviews; ING source detail remains unverified and its numerical amount is withheld. This report is educational analysis, not personalized financial advice. Global Markets & Credit Research ────•❉᯽❉•──── Saturday, 14 November 2026 · Singapore (Partial source coverage) Research cutoff: 14 November 2026, 8:00 AM SGT. Latest completed U.S. trading session: Friday, 13 November. Compared against the 13 November briefing. All dates below distinguish publication from underlying observations. The most important development is the Federal Reserve’s new warning about AI financing. Reuters reports that the Fed’s November Financial Stability Report identifies rapidly expanding AI-related debt, complex commitments and leveraged investors as potential sources of instability. Alongside it, new U.S. producer-price data, an HSBC capital issuance and deteriorating earnings at a private-credit lender provide a more complete picture of how financing pressure could develop. 1. Executive market dashboard U.S. 10Y · Friday market report 5.133% 13 Nov · WSJ secondary-market quotation U.S. 30Y · official par yield 5.43% 12 Nov · latest full official curve retrieved Sources: Treasury par yields , IG OAS , HY OAS and WSJ Friday rate report . The Friday secondary-market quote and Thursday official par yield are not interchangeable. ICE data are licensed and must not be republished as a public dataset. AI-related debt has become a financial-stability issue, not merely an equity valuation issue. Reuters reports that advanced-computing-related issuance reached approximately US$680 billion by October 2026 , while 87% of surveyed market contacts cited AI-related risks. These figures have different definitions and must not be added together. U.S. producer prices remain elevated despite a slower monthly increase. October final-demand PPI rose 0.3% month-on-month and 6.5% year-on-year . The annual figure was the strongest since November 2022. HSBC completed US$1.5 billion of new Additional Tier 1 capital issuance. Its 7.625% perpetual contingent convertible securities were issued on 13 November. These must not be analysed like ordinary senior bonds with a fixed maturity. Private-credit stress is visible in both lending earnings and portfolio valuations. BCP Investment Corporation’s Q3 net investment income fell to US$4.6 million , from US$5.5 million in Q2, while NAV per share declined from US$14.49 to US$13.13 . Singapore, Thailand and the United Kingdom demonstrated a potential improvement in wholesale FX settlement. Their Project Meridian FX APAC experiment completed synchronised payment-versus-payment settlement across three different test systems. It was a technical trial, not a live production launch. Overall investment assessment: Strong issuers still have access to capital, but three risks are becoming more important: inflation-driven duration losses, concentrated infrastructure financing and the possibility that leveraged lenders or investors must reduce assets before underlying borrowers formally default. 2. Five substantive research deep dives Subsequent verification note, 14 November: The official November Fed report is now accessible. Box2.2 corroborates computing-related debt issuance exceeding $680bn through October against $130bn in2023; coverage excludes some private placements. Reuters separately supports the87% market-contact survey claim. Survey share is not probability of distress. Historical statements below describe access at the original cutoff; no licensed underlying Fed chart dataset is copied. Research 1. Federal Reserve: AI financing enters the financial-stability discussion Federal Reserve Board · Financial Stability Report, November 2026 · Released 13 November · Primary full report not independently retrieved; detailed figures below attributed to Reuters’ coverage Official Fed Financial Stability Report collection Survey contacts identifying AI risk 87% Versus 50% in the previous survey Reported computing-related debt issuance $680bn 2026 through October What changed: Reuters reports that AI was the most frequently cited financial-stability concern among the Fed’s market contacts. Risks included rich valuations, cyber incidents, difficult-to-understand financing and a possible decline in AI earnings. The reported US$680 billion issuance compares with approximately US$130 billion during all of 2023 . Reuters also describes substantial future leases, guarantees and financing commitments associated with hyperscalers and smaller infrastructure companies. How an AI investment shock could reach creditors Expected AI cash flows or utilisation decline Project revenue disappoints Debt-service coverage weakens Equity and collateral fall Financing headroom contracts Higher refinancing spreads, reduced lending or asset sales Original conceptual transmission model. It is not a prediction that all stages will occur. The distinction is between exposure and realised loss. A technology company’s guarantees, future leases, loans and investments can represent different contingent obligations. Adding the headline amounts without reconciling counterparties and accounting treatment risks double-counting. Methodology caveat: The reported 87% figure refers to a small market-contact survey, not 87% of all banks or a quantified probability of systemic distress. I confirmed the official report collection, but its available page did not expose the complete November document in this review. The report’s detailed methodology and cited charts remain a primary-source verification gap. Bond positioning: Watch AI-linked BBB corporate borrowing, equipment-backed financing, private-credit exposures, refinancing maturities and whether guarantees actually cover the relevant legal borrower. Plain-language explanation: AI spending can be economically productive while its financing still creates risks if future cash arrives later than repayment obligations. Research 2. MAS, BoE and BoT: Safer cross-border FX settlement Project Meridian FX APAC · 13 November 2026 · Joint central-bank experiment · Full Technical and Policy Reports available as official HTML Project Meridian FX APAC: Technical Report Project Meridian FX APAC: Policy Report What the experiment demonstrated: A synchronisation operator coordinated payment-versus-payment settlement across three different simulated wholesale settlement environments, representing approaches explored by the Bank of England, MAS and Bank of Thailand. It also demonstrated multilateral net settlement, in which offsetting payments can reduce the liquidity required compared with settling every obligation separately. No universal percentage saving was established. Why payment-versus-payment matters Without synchronisation One currency can transfer while the other payment is delayed or fails Synchronised PvP Both payment legs are coordinated to complete together or not at all Illustrative settlement structure. The actual trial used a synchronisation operator, reservation/escrow arrangements and different test-ledger designs. What was tested: Different settlement architectures, insufficient funds, invalid payment identifiers and system outages. The prototype preserved all-or-nothing outcomes in the tested scenarios. What was not tested: Live payment volumes, non-overlapping RTGS operating hours, every legal-finality scenario and realistic intraday liquidity demands. The technical and policy reports expressly identify these gaps. Credit and FX implication: Safer wholesale settlement could reduce settlement risk and improve liquidity efficiency over time. It does not remove the exchange-rate risk of USD assets or CHF borrowings. Singapore relevance: MAS participated directly, with the RBA and Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas observing. This is a relevant development for cross-border banking infrastructure, not a new yield-bearing investment product. Plain-language explanation: The project explores ways for two currencies to exchange safely at the same time, reducing the risk that only one side of an FX transaction completes. Research 3. U.S. BLS: Producer-price inflation remains a bond-market risk Bureau of Labor Statistics · Producer Price Indexes, October 2026 · Published 13 November · Official statistical release, Table A Producer Price Index, October 2026 PPI monthly history U.S. producer-price inflation · seasonally adjusted monthly final-demand PPI change (%) · BLS 13 November 2026, Table A. That combination makes it difficult to conclude that underlying inflation pressure has disappeared. Credit mechanism: Higher materials, transport and input costs can reduce operating margins, especially for fixed-price construction contracts and companies with weak pricing power. Persistent inflation can also keep refinancing costs elevated. Methodology caveat: PPI is an input/producer-price measure, not CPI or the Fed’s PCE price index. The 6.5% annual figure cannot be directly substituted for consumer inflation. Bond positioning: Distinguish nominal Treasury yield, real yield and term premium. Monitor whether input-cost inflation reaches consumer prices and changes expectations for the Fed’s policy path. Plain-language explanation: Producer-price growth slowed in October, but annual cost pressure remains substantial. That is one reason bond yields may stay volatile. Research 4. BCP Investment Corporation: Private-credit nonaccruals versus NAV BCP Investment Corporation · Q3 financial results released 11 November 2026 · Underlying quarter ended 30 September · Original issuer release BCP Investment Corporation Announces Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results NAV per share · Q2 $14.49 NAV per share · Q3 $13.13 BCP quarterly comparison Quarter ends30Jun/30Sep2026; USD millions,USD/share,% Source: BCP issuer release,11Nov2026 (open supporting source; additional row-specific sources below). Income and NAV fell; nonaccrual measures diverged. Fair value and cost bases differ. Read headers and row-specific dates before comparing; scroll horizontally for all columns. Indicator Q2 2026 Q3 2026 Total investment income $15.2m $13.9m Net investment income $5.5m $4.6m Nonaccruals at fair value 3.1% 2.8% Nonaccruals at amortised cost 5.7% 6.0% NAV per share $14.49 $13.13 The accounting distinction is particularly useful. Nonaccrual exposure fell as a percentage of fair value but rose when measured against amortised cost. These measures need not move together: valuation marks, nonaccrual balances and the portfolio denominators can change. The percentages alone do not isolate the cause. BCP also disclosed a previously completed US$10 million add-on issuance of 7.50% notes due 2029 , dated 2 September, and an August amendment of its KeyBank secured revolving facility. The amended facility has US$150 million of committed capacity , increased from US$75 million, with maturity extended to August 2031. That capacity is not the same as loans drawn. Methodology: Issuer-reported GAAP and investment-company measures. Some loans on nonaccrual may still generate cash-basis income when actual payments are received. Credit positioning: Monitor cash interest, NAV marks, covenant headroom, portfolio concentration and whether BDC distributions are covered by recurring income. Plain-language explanation: Private-credit funds can continue collecting interest while the market value of their underlying loans declines. Research 5. Bank of England: Quantitative tightening changes sovereign debt supply Bank of England · Asset Purchase Facility Quarterly Report, 2026 Q3 · Published 10 November · Underlying holdings 30 September · Older than today’s releases, newly highlighted for duration strategy Asset Purchase Facility Quarterly Report, 2026 Q3 APF gilt holdings at Q3 end £488.149bn Planned annual outright gilt sales £20bn What changed: The BoE’s latest report details the plan to unwind its monetary-policy gilt portfolio, using sales and maturities. During Q3, gilt sales reduced holdings by £4.3 billion , while maturities reduced them by another £29.3 billion . The central bank intends to retain £120 billion of the longest-maturity gilts for its banknote-backing arrangements and allow £222 billion of shorter-dated holdings to mature. Its proposed treatment of £146 billion of remaining 2035–2049 gilts remains subject to agreement with the UK government. Methodology: Table A reports APF holdings at original purchase prices, not current market values. Chart 1 contains highly assumption-sensitive estimates of the lifetime fiscal effects of QE/QT. Bond implication: Central-bank asset sales and natural maturities change how much duration the private sector must absorb. In stressed markets, additional duration supply can raise the compensation investors demand. Counterargument: Predictable runoff and retention of the longest gilts can reduce market disruption relative to an abrupt liquidation. Plain-language explanation: Government-bond yields depend on both central-bank interest rates and how much long-term debt private investors are being asked to hold. 3. Global macro, equity and central-bank research Source universe: The scan covered official destinations for the Fed and regional Feds, BIS, ECB, BoE, Deutsche Bundesbank, MAS, BoT, BoJ, Bank of Canada, SNB, RBA, RBNZ, RBI, PBoC and HKMA, supplemented by World Bank, IMF, OECD, regulators, primary filings and rating-agency research indexes. The authors benchmarked the framework against three structural VAR studies and illustrated five research exercises . They found useful replication capabilities where data and specifications were well defined, but substantial model uncertainty when assumptions were incomplete. Investment relevance: Economic forecasts depend on model assumptions. This supports using several scenarios rather than treating one interest-rate forecast as definitive. Japan and broader equity implications Reuters reported that Japan’s three megabanks raised annual earnings forecasts while warning that a slowdown in data-centre investment could affect activity. MUFG reported approximately ¥3.3 trillion in data-centre credit exposure against ¥180 trillion total credit exposure . That ratio alone does not determine credit losses. Reuters also reported that the S&P 500 and Nasdaq fell on 13 November, with technology and semiconductor shares under pressure. Market-price declines can increase the cost of raising new equity and reduce collateral value for financed positions. Counterargument: An equity selloff may improve prospective valuations, and strong hyperscaler balance sheets can absorb considerable investment spending. entries.title: The next dollar after 55 | CPF LIFE research
entries.text: The next dollar after 55 | CPF LIFE research Retirement research · Singapore · 4 November 2026 The next dollar after 55 CPF LIFE top-up, investment portfolio, or private lifetime-income policy? Evidence-led article and interactive illustration. Rules checked 4 November 2026. All calculator scenarios are hypothetical, not quotations or forecasts. ← Market Intel research The decision Current rules Explore the maths Where IFI fits Sources New visual companion: charts & exact-value tables ↓ Added 4 November 2026 · original report retained Age 55 is a decision point, not a verdict. “CPF top-ups after 55 are not worthwhile” is too broad. A top-up can be useful when the priority is dependable lifelong SGD income. Keeping the same capital outside CPF can be more useful when access to cash, investment flexibility or inheritance carries more weight. A commercial lifetime-income policy introduces another set of contractual terms, costs and risks. The most useful question is narrower: What does the next S$100,000 buy, and what must be given up? Compare the additional income from a top-up with the additional income and remaining assets from the same money elsewhere. Existing CPF LIFE income belongs in the household plan, but it must not be credited to the new top-up. Income security For how long? Can essential spending still be met at 95 or 100? Capital access When needed? What is available for emergencies or a major purchase? Family outcome What remains? Which death benefit or market-valued asset is actually left? 1. The important distinction behind the claim An RA interest rate, an annuity payout rate and a lifetime XIRR describe different things. As at the fourth quarter of 2026, the base RA rate is 4%. Additional interest applies only to specified first balances, so a large marginal top-up does not automatically earn 6%. A future constant 4% path is a modelling assumption, not a promise that the same rate will apply forever. CPF interest rates . Once savings fund CPF LIFE, interest supports the lifetime payout arrangement. The member receives income while alive; there is no separately withdrawable pot of all future interest. Pooling allows payouts to continue after an individual's premium has been used up. This makes CPF LIFE valuable against longevity risk, while producing a different inheritance and return profile from a liquid investment account. How premium interest is used . That is a good reason to calculate returns carefully. It does not prove that the insurance is poor value. A household cannot spend an investment's long-run average return if the account runs out during retirement. Payout rate = annual cash income ÷ chosen capital base XIRR = the annualised rate that equates dated contributions, receipts and any terminal value A payout can include capital being returned. Dividing a payout by the premium is not the same as calculating investment return. 2. What the current rules actually allow Question Current position Decision implication How much can be committed? The 2026 ERS is S$440,800. It is S$456,400 in 2027. Members aged 55 and above can top up to the prevailing ERS, subject to their headroom. CPF Check the Retirement Dashboard. The limit is not simply ERS minus the displayed account balance. How is headroom measured? The rule accounts for relevant RA savings and savings already used as LIFE premiums; interest is generally excluded and retirement withdrawals included. CPF Do not infer eligibility from the balance alone. Can the top-up be taken back? RSTU top-ups are committed to retirement payouts. They cannot normally be withdrawn as a lump sum, via the property route, or used for investment/housing. CPF Retain an adequate emergency and spending reserve outside this commitment. Does every dollar get tax relief? No. Eligible cash top-up relief is subject to the current FRS boundary, the S$8,000 self limit and S$80,000 overall personal-relief cap. CPF transfers do not qualify. Matching-grant top-ups have separate exclusions. IRAS An FRS-to-ERS decision must not assume tax relief on the whole top-up. Can matching grants matter? Eligible MRSS members can receive dollar-for-dollar matching up to S$2,000 a year, within a S$20,000 lifetime cap. Eligibility is conditional. MOM Do not compare a matched dollar with an unmatched investment dollar without recording the grant. Can payouts start later? Starting payouts can be deferred to 70, with increases of up to 7% per year, or up to 35% for five years. CPF Higher later payments must be weighed against income not received while waiting. Do not compound “7%” into a promised return. CPF LIFE provides government-backed lifetime income. Published payout amounts can nevertheless be adjusted for long-term changes in interest rates or life expectancy; CPF expects such changes, if any, to be small and gradual. “For life” and “the exact projected amount never changes” are different assurances. CPF LIFE overview ; payout qualifications . 3. Use the right plan and the right starting age Standard Level payouts, generally higher initially than Escalating. Purchasing power declines if prices rise. RA savings are used as the premium when joining. Plan details . Escalating Lower initial payouts that rise 2% each year. This is a fixed escalation schedule, not a promise to match actual household inflation. Plan details . Basic Only part of the RA initially funds the premium. Payouts first draw on RA savings and can fall as balances and extra interest fall. Its account and refund schedule needs separate modelling. Plan details . A public reference, not an individual quote CPF Board's current illustration for a male member turning 55 in 2026 on the Standard Plan gives the following reference points. The money is present at 55 , not first deposited at 65. RA savings at 55 Illustrated monthly payout from 65 Illustrated monthly payout from 70 S$220,400 (2026 FRS) S$1,780 S$2,380 S$440,800 (2026 ERS) S$3,440 S$4,580 Difference between rounded examples S$1,660 S$2,200 Source: CPF Board's monthly payout examples . Differences are arithmetic on rounded published examples, not a marginal quote. Sex, cohort, plan, balances, top-up date and payout start affect the actual result. A top-up at 60 has fewer accumulation years than the same top-up at 55. 4. Income and inheritance must be counted separately For applicable refund-bearing CPF LIFE plans, the remaining premium paid to beneficiaries is the premium committed less lifetime payouts received, with no negative refund. Remaining CPF account balances are separate. The legacy Income Plan is an exception without this refund feature. CPF death-benefit explanation . In a simplified Standard-style illustration, payout receipts plus remaining premium may therefore stay nominally constant for an initial period. As the refund declines, the dates of those receipts still change the XIRR. After the refund reaches zero, continuing lifetime income can keep increasing the realised return for a longer-lived member. For a portfolio, the family inherits the remaining market-valued assets. A bond's future face-value payment and its market value at death are not interchangeable. A fund's distributions must be analysed together with its NAV. A private policy's surrender value and death benefit are alternatives for different events; do not add both. Money spent during retirement is not terminal wealth. Cumulative income plus a final estate is a useful receipts measure, but it is not an account balance available on the final date. Interactive laboratory Same capital. Same spending. Different promises. Synthetic scenario, not a CPF or HSBC quotation. The default S$650 payout was chosen to demonstrate the maths. It is not derived from a CPF estimator or an IFI illustration. This model has no named commercial product return and does not check personal CPF top-up eligibility or headroom. The illustration commits S$100,000 at age 60 on 1 November 2026. It assumes five years of accumulation before income begins at 65. Change the inputs to inspect the trade-offs; a higher assumed return is not evidence that it can be earned safely. Initial capital (SGD) Age on 1 Nov 2026 Payout start age Death scenario age Assumed RA accumulation (%/yr) Hypothetical monthly payout (SGD) Annual payout growth (%/yr) Inflation (%/yr) Portfolio before income (% net/yr) Portfolio during income (% net/yr) Reset illustration Download current monthly CSV Download editable Excel Download research prompt Enable JavaScript for the interactive calculations, or download the Excel workbook. The article and source links remain readable. Death is assumed immediately before the payout due on that birthday. First payout occurs on the start-age birthday. Default: 240 payments from age 65 to just before 85. No tax saving, matching grant, existing CPF balance, transaction cost or separate estate administration cost is included. Portfolio return inputs must be net of applicable investment costs and taxes. All inputs stay in your browser. Cumulative cash received Illustrative lifetime income Portfolio withdrawals Remaining inheritance Illustrative premium refund Portfolio market value Read the shortfall as well as the return. A portfolio can retain a 4% XIRR after it has run out: it earned the assumed return on the money while invested, but could not fund every later withdrawal. A respectable return is not proof that the retirement-income target was met. How the answer changes with lifespan Estate-inclusive XIRR by death age Illustrative lifetime income Portfolio Income-only XIRR excludes the estate. Estate-inclusive XIRR adds it once at death. Both are conditional realised rates, not expected returns or a valuation of longevity insurance. An estate amount is not an amount the CPF member can surrender while alive. “N/A” means no valid positive/negative cashflow pair or numerical root. Calculation method and limitations All model dates fall on the first of a month. Effective monthly portfolio growth is (1 + net annual return)^(1/12) − 1. Growth accrues before each month's withdrawal. Payouts rise once a year at the selected growth rate, if any. Withdrawals cannot exceed the portfolio balance. The assumed pre-payout CPF premium is capital × (1 + RA rate)^(years to start); this is a simplified accrual model, not CPF's operational interest-crediting calculation. After payout start, the illustrative refund is max(0, starting premium − cumulative payouts). Before payout start, the illustration uses assumed accumulated capital. This isolates a synthetic additional slice of cash already available to allocate; an actual member calculation needs matched full-policy projections. If the alternative is funded by CPF savings, confirm lawful withdrawal eligibility first. Required retirement savings are not freely investable cash. Basic Plan, legacy Income Plan, later top-ups and CPF rate adjustments are not modelled. Changing growth to 2% does not turn an unchanged S$650 input into a valid Escalating Plan quote. XIRR uses actual calendar-day intervals divided by 365. The constant-return portfolio is a deterministic scenario. It cannot estimate ruin probability, market volatility or future returns. Excel includes additional dated-input controls; compare its default scenario with this page before changing them. 5. A constant return hides sequence risk Losses early in retirement hurt when spending requires selling assets. The small experiment below reverses the same ten annual returns: −20%, +20%, then eight years at +5%. Both paths have exactly the same compounded return before withdrawals. Their remaining balances differ because money leaves along the way. Loss first Loss last This is a stress illustration, not a probability forecast. A serious portfolio comparison should also examine fees, inflation, asset allocation, cash buffers, credit losses and rebalancing. To compare a USD product with SGD retirement spending, convert every payout at the rate applicable to that payment and the estate at its own terminal rate. An unchanged FX scenario is only one case. 6. Where HSBC Life IFI belongs in this comparison IFI deserves a separate column because its optional lifetime-income benefit can continue when policy value reaches zero. HSBC also describes potential income increases with positive crediting and an auto lock-in feature. Those are material insurance features, not merely a fixed withdrawal rule. HSBC product page . The brochure makes the initial benefit depend on a guaranteed percentage applied to the relevant premium/value base, with conditions. Account value still changes with charges, crediting and withdrawals. A floored index-crediting rate protects that crediting calculation, not the original premium after all costs. Income rates quoted for one entry age or policy year cannot be carried over to another profile. HSBC brochure . Feature CPF LIFE top-up Investment portfolio IFI / private income policy Income basis Scheme's lifelong payout rules Assets, returns and withdrawals Exact lifetime-benefit contract Currency SGD Depends on holdings/hedging IFI premium and policy values are USD Capital access Top-up committed to retirement income Market liquidity and price at sale Surrender/withdrawal terms and charges Inheritance Applicable remaining premium plus CPF balances Remaining market-valued assets Contractual death benefit, net of relevant adjustments Key trade-off Liquidity surrendered for income security Return potential with market/longevity risk Contractual benefits with insurer, cost and FX risk Numerical status here Synthetic illustration only Synthetic net-return scenario No invented payout or XIRR HSBC currently lists a minimum USD100,000 single premium, or USD20,000 annually over five years. The S$100,000 teaching example is therefore not an implementable IFI single-premium quotation . The same-capital product comparison must first satisfy product minima and use a verified exchange rate and actual illustration. HSBC eligibility and premium options . What is needed for a fair IFI ranking: matching entry age and policy version; actual premium dates and FX; verified guaranteed and non-guaranteed benefit schedules; all charges; payout start and withdrawal mode; surrender and death values; and the consequences of changes to the policy. Until that schedule reconciles, a polished chart would imply more certainty than the evidence supports. 7. A stronger conclusion than “top up” or “do not top up” A top-up may be more useful when Essential retirement spending is not yet covered by dependable lifelong income. A separate liquid reserve already covers foreseeable needs. Eligible tax relief or a matching grant adds meaningful value. Managing investments in very old age is undesirable. The priority is the income floor rather than maximising inheritance. Keeping capital outside may be more useful when Near-term spending or emergencies could require the money. Essential lifetime income is already well covered. Access, gifting or bequest flexibility is particularly important. The investor understands and can withstand market and sequence risk. The alternative remains attractive after fees, taxes and currency risk. These are decision factors, not a personal recommendation. Health, family longevity, household resources and risk tolerance belong in the conversation, but a single assumed death age should not determine the entire retirement plan. A concise research pitch “Before committing more money after 55, compare what that next dollar will do for your monthly spending, access to capital and family. CPF LIFE provides a lifelong SGD foundation. A portfolio preserves more flexibility but must survive withdrawals and markets. A private income policy adds contractual features with its own costs and conditions. Put them on the same dates, in the same currency, with the same budget, and show both income and what remains.” The defensible answer is a suitable allocation between income security and flexibility. The calculator helps expose the trade-offs; it cannot choose that allocation for every reader. Sources and audit trail Primary sources checked on 4 November 2026. Rules, estimates and product terms can change. Links support the associated statements; no private client records are included. entries.text: CPF LIFE, explained · Growth, refund and income for life · 6 Nov 2026 CPF LIFE · 6 November V2 Earlier CPF LIFE research All editions Research Papers Skip to report RETIREMENT RESEARCH Independent explanation · Singapore · 6 November 2026 CPF LIFE / A clear explanation Savings become income for life CPF LIFE converts retirement savings into monthly income that continues while you live. To judge it fairly, separate the earlier savings growth, the money paid back over time, and the protection against living longer than your savings last. Research checked: 6 November 2026, Singapore time (SGT, UTC+8) · Explanation V2 · All money in SGD Singapore CPF LIFE Retirement income Official illustration + calculations S$1,780 Monthly income Standard Plan illustration starting at age 65. 6.47% Annual payout / premium A cash payout ratio. It includes money returned from capital. 80y 6m Refund reaches zero Calculated for this case. Income continues after this point. Five points to keep in mind Before payouts, the Retirement Account earns interest. In the published example, S$220,400 at 55 becomes an estimated S$330,100 at 65. Early payouts reduce the remaining death refund. While that refund is positive, income received plus the refund equals the starting premium in this Standard Plan model. The payout rate is different from an investment return. A 6.47% annual payout ratio does not mean every dollar earns 6.47% a year. Lifetime protection begins when you join. It remains valuable even before the premium refund runs out. Compare the complete retirement outcome. Income, access to capital, money for beneficiaries and purchasing power all matter. Reference case, not a personal quote: a male member turning 55 in 2026, reaching 65 in 2036. CPF 's table was updated 16 Jun 2026. Calculations use one S$330,100 premium, S$1,780 each month, no later inflows, and a first payout one month after 65. Actual payouts can be adjusted. [S02] [S11] 01 Three stages 02 Follow the money 03 What is the return? 04 Compare products 05 Choices & risks 06 Method & sources 01 / START WITH THE PURPOSE Three stages answer three different questions An annuity turns a sum of money into regular payments. CPF LIFE is a life annuity: its payments continue while the member lives. The Retirement Account , or RA, holds retirement savings before those savings are committed as the premium. A premium is the amount used to buy the cover. [S03] [S15] EXHIBIT 01 · STANDARD PLAN EXAMPLE · AGES, NOT CALENDAR FORECASTS Growth first; then income with lifetime cover STAGE 1 55 → 65 Savings grow Interest adds to the RA. The example grows from S$220,400 to S$330,100 before payouts begin. STAGE 2 65 → 80y 6m The refund declines Income replaces the unpaid premium. Each payout reduces the amount that would be refunded on death. STAGE 3 After 80y 6m Income continues The refund can be zero while payments continue. The realised return rises as more payments are received. RA accumulation Lifetime insurance applies throughout stages 2 and 3. How to read: the boundary at 80 years 6 months is calculated from this premium and payout, not a universal CPF age. The three stages are an accounting explanation; insurance does not wait until stage 3 to begin. Sources: CPF plan and pooling rules [S03] [S07] ; official illustration [S02] . Calculations: 6 Nov 2026. EXHIBIT 02 · OFFICIAL ILLUSTRATIVE ENDPOINTS · SGD S$109,700 is added before payouts At age 55 S$220,400 Estimated at age 65 S$330,100 S$330,100 − S$220,400 = S$109,700 growth The endpoints imply about 4.12% annualised growth over ten years. This is a calculation from the illustration, including its assumptions. It is not a separate contractual 4.12% interest rate. How to read: both bars begin at zero and use S$330,100 as the full scale. Formula: (330,100 ÷ 220,400) 1/10 − 1. Source: CPF table updated 16 Jun 2026; cohort age 55 in 2026 and age 65 in 2036. [S02] CURRENT RULES · SEPARATE FROM THE TEN-YEAR ILLUSTRATION Today's rate floor has an end date 4% RA base rate 1 October–31 December 2026. 2027 Announced floor runs to 31 December. It is not a ten-year rate guarantee to 2036. +2% / +1% Extra interest from age 55 First S$30,000 / next S$30,000 of combined balances, subject to the rules. “Up to 6%” does not apply to the whole RA. The extra-interest bands are capped, and the Ordinary Account portion included in combined balances is capped at S$20,000. Source and period: CPF rate announcement, 22 Sep 2026; extra-interest FAQ updated 8 Oct 2026. Rules reviewed 6 Nov 2026. [S08] [S09] 02 / INCOME AND THE DEATH REFUND A payout and a refund are two parts of the same premium The remaining premium refund is what is left after payouts have been deducted. For this single-premium Standard Plan example, it equals S$330,100 minus payouts received, with a minimum of zero. Other CPF balances may also pass to beneficiaries; this report's model includes only the premium refund. [S06] EXHIBIT 03 · EXPLORE A DEATH-AGE SCENARIO · SGD Follow the income and the remaining refund Assumed age at death, just after that month's payout 80 years 65 85 105 70 80 80y 6m 90 100 Move one month at a time. This changes the assumed lifespan, not the monthly payout or a forecast of anyone's life expectancy. Income already paid S$320,400 Refund on death S$9,700 Combined cash delivered S$330,100 Annualised return from 65, including refund 0.00% Starting premium S$330,100 Income + refund S$330,100 S$0 S$330,100 Income received Remaining refund At age 80: S$320,400 paid + S$9,700 refund = S$330,100. The combined nominal cash equals the original premium. How to read: compare the two bars on their common zero-based scale for the selected age. The second bar includes past income, which may already have been spent. Source inputs: CPF illustration updated 16 Jun 2026 [S02] ; refund rule updated 9 Jul 2026 [S06] . Fixed-payout calculation, 6 Nov 2026. CALCULATION · WHAT “0%” MEANS Zero on this cash-flow measure has a precise meaning At age 80: S$320,400 income + S$9,700 refund = S$330,100 premium The household has received its premium back in nominal dollars. “Household return” here includes cash paid to the member and the refund paid to beneficiaries at the selected death age. While their total equals the initial premium, the nominal annualised return from age 65 is 0%. This does not mean the premium earns no interest. CPF LIFE premiums continue earning interest. That interest is pooled across members and factored into the income set from the beginning; it does not build a separate, fully inheritable interest account. The insurance protects a risk that an early-death return cannot measure. A member does not know in advance whether income will be needed to 80, 90 or beyond. Lifetime coverage is already in place while the refund remains positive. In plain English: the early cash flows look like the premium being returned a little at a time. The policy also promises that the payments will keep coming if the member lives much longer. Sources: CPF refund definition, 9 Jul 2026; premium-interest FAQ, 10 Feb 2025; pooling article published 6 Sep 2024 and updated 23 Apr 2026. Calculations are this report's analysis. [S06] [S21] [S07] EXHIBIT 04 · THE MONTH THE REFUND ENDS Payment 186 passes the starting premium 185 payments S$329,300 received S$800 refund left 186 payments S$331,080 received S$0 refund left Age 80 years 6 months is a model result. It follows from this premium, payout and first-payment convention. A different quotation, later premium addition, start date or payout adjustment changes the date. How to read: multiply the payment count by S$1,780 and compare with S$330,100. First payment assumed one month after 65. Source inputs: [S02] ; calculated 6 Nov 2026, SGD. WHAT THE REFUND CANNOT DO A death benefit is different from accessible cash Item What it represents Payouts already received Income delivered over time; it may have been spent. Remaining refund A benefit payable on death, not a freely withdrawable investment account. Accessible assets Money available for living expenses or emergencies, subject to each asset's terms. How to read: keep these categories separate. Adding past income to a death refund does not tell you how much cash is available today. Source basis: CPF premium-refund and withdrawal rules, reviewed 6 Nov 2026. The comparison is an economic interpretation. [S06] [S13] 03 / MEASURE THE RIGHT RETURN The payout ratio and the investment return answer different questions A payout ratio measures cash paid against capital committed. An internal rate of return, or IRR, also considers when money is paid and what comes back at the end. The report calculates an effective annual IRR from monthly cash flows. EXHIBIT 05 · SAME STANDARD PLAN EXAMPLE · ANNUAL PERCENTAGES 6.47% describes the payout; the realised return depends on lifespan 6.47% Annual payout ratio S$21,360 ÷ S$330,100. 2.72% IRR if death occurs at 85 From age 65; refund then zero. 4.29% IRR if death occurs at 90 Five more years of payments. A high cash payout can include returned capital. S$1,780 × 12 = S$21,360 a year. Dividing by the premium gives 6.47%, but that ratio does not deduct the reduction in the remaining premium refund. How to read: the first number is a cash-income ratio; the other two are separate lifespan scenarios. They are not three quoted investment yields. Source inputs: CPF reference table, 16 Jun 2026 [S02] ; refund rule [S06] . Calculations: 6 Nov 2026. Display rates rounded to two decimals. EXHIBIT 06 · TWO STARTING DATES · NOMINAL ANNUALISED RETURN Starting at 55 includes the earlier savings growth Annualised return · % 0% 2% 4% 6% 65 75 85 95 105 Age From 65 · S$330,100 starting premium From 55 · S$220,400 initial savings At age 80, the return is 0% from 65 but 2.33% from 55. The age-55 calculation includes the earlier S$109,700 of accumulation. The age-65 calculation begins with the larger premium and asks what happens after that point. Choose the same starting date for competing products. The transfer of savings into the premium at 65 is internal to the age-55 calculation. Subtracting that premium again would count the same capital twice. Assumed death age Income received Refund IRR from 65 IRR from 55 70 S$106,800 S$223,300 0.00% 2.89% 75 S$213,600 S$116,500 0.00% 2.45% 80 S$320,400 S$9,700 0.00% 2.33% 81 S$341,760 S$0 0.44% 2.50% 85 S$427,200 S$0 2.72% 3.46% 90 S$534,000 S$0 4.29% 4.21% 95 S$640,800 S$0 5.16% 4.68% 100 S$747,600 S$0 5.68% 4.98% On a phone: swipe the table sideways for both return columns. Amounts are SGD; rates are annualised. How to read: each point assumes death immediately after that month's payout and includes the remaining refund once. The two line patterns use the same CPF colour. They are scenario calculations, not observed investment performance or expected returns weighted by the probability of survival. Source inputs [S02] and refund rule [S06] ; model calculated 6 Nov 2026. RETURN TO THE MEMBER / RETURN TO THE HOUSEHOLD Leaving out the refund changes the early result At age 80, from 65 Annual IRR Income received only −0.39% Income + death refund 0.00% How to read: the first calculation omits the S$9,700 refund. Once the refund reaches zero, these two return measures coincide. Investment Moats uses this helpful distinction. Its article compares returns at different death ages with and without bequest. This report adopts that method, but its numerical case and rules come from refreshed official sources. The article's old plan rankings are historical opinions, not a current ranking established here. Sources: Investment Moats article dated 30 Apr 2022, first written Dec 2018 [S01] ; current inputs [S02] [S06] . Arithmetic: 6 Nov 2026. EXHIBIT 07 · CAPITAL RECOVERY “Break even” needs a definition 75y 4m Payouts recover S$220,400. This ignores the ten-year wait before income and the return forgone. 80y 6m Payouts recover S$330,100. This is nominal premium recovery from age 65. From joining Lifetime cover already applies. It does not depend on first recovering the premium. How to read: use the definition that matches the decision. An early-death 0% nominal return still has an opportunity cost compared with earning a positive return elsewhere. Sources: published cash inputs [S02] ; lifelong coverage [S03] . Recovery ages calculated 6 Nov 2026 under the monthly timing convention. 04 / MATCH THE MONEY AND THE INCOME An alternative must fund the same spending Compare equal starting capital and equal withdrawals. A bond coupon, a fund distribution and a CPF LIFE payout can all arrive as cash, but they can leave very different amounts of capital and different risks behind. EXHIBIT 08 · ASSUMED PORTFOLIO RETURNS · REMAINING SGD CAPITAL Positive returns extend a portfolio's funding period Remaining capital · S$000 0 100 200 300 65 75 85 95 100 Age 0% net 2.5% net 4% net Constant net annual return First monthly income shortfall 0% Age 80 years 6 months 2.5% Age 84 years 6 months 4% Age 88 years 10 months How to read: start with S$330,100 at 65, credit the monthly equivalent of the stated net annual return, then withdraw S$1,780. The first shortfall month contains a partial payment; the account never borrows below zero. Accessible capital and lifetime income are different strengths. A portfolio may provide flexibility and an estate while funds remain. CPF LIFE continues paying while the member lives, even after the premium refund reaches zero. Its illustrated dollar payout remains subject to review. Assumptions, not market quotes: smooth 0%, 2.5% and 4% effective annual net returns; no volatility, later contributions or costs beyond the stated net-return scenario. These are not offers for deposits, bonds or private annuities. Model calculated 6 Nov 2026; CPF duration and adjustment rules [S03] [S11] . MATHEMATICAL HURDLE · NOT A PRODUCT OFFER Preserving all the capital requires more return S$1,780 each month, indefinitely, while preserving S$330,100: 6.67% net effective annual return This is the smooth-return hurdle for a perpetual nominal income stream. The formula is (1 + 1,780 ÷ 330,100) 12 − 1. It assumes the monthly return can be earned continuously without loss or interruption. The formula does not create an available safe investment. Real portfolios have fluctuating returns, fees and reinvestment risk. Even preserving the original number of dollars leaves those dollars exposed to inflation. How to read: the 6.67% is a comparison requirement, not a forecast or expected return. Inputs [S02] ; monthly perpetuity calculation, 6 Nov 2026. QUALITATIVE COMPARISON · CONTRACT TERMS STILL MATTER Check the income and what remains Product Key comparison CPF LIFE Lifetime payments, declining premium refund, withdrawal rules and possible payout adjustments. SGS bonds / T-bills Purchase price, maturity, actual payment dates, reinvestment and market value before maturity. Private annuity Lifetime or fixed term; guaranteed benefits versus projected bonuses; death and surrender values. Investment portfolio Returns after costs, withdrawals, remaining capital, volatility and the risk of poor early returns. How to read: a higher displayed payout does not establish a superior product. Use a death benefit for a death scenario and a surrender or sale value for a living exit; do not count both at once. Source basis: CPF rules; MAS product comparison updated 28 Jul 2026; MoneySense annuities guide updated 4 Nov 2026. No named alternative quotation has been supplied. [S03] [S06] [S15] [S16] Access is a separate constraint. A spreadsheet comparison does not make restricted CPF savings withdrawable. Exemption from CPF LIFE requires qualifying annuity or pension arrangements; ordinary bonds and endowments are not accepted as substitutes for that purpose. [S13] 05 / WHAT COULD CHANGE THE CHOICE? Plan for long life, rising prices and money needed sooner There is more than one retirement objective. A household may need dependable monthly income, an emergency reserve, protection against rising prices and an intended inheritance. The suitable mix depends on the size and urgency of each need. EXHIBIT 09 · INFLATION SCENARIOS · AGE-65 SGD PER MONTH The same S$1,780 buys less over time Age-65 purchasing power · S$/month 0 600 1,200 1,800 65 75 85 95 Age 2% annual inflation assumption 3% annual inflation assumption Future age At 2% At 3% 85 S$1,198 S$986 95 S$983 S$733 How to read: the bank payment stays S$1,780; the chart expresses what it can buy in age-65 dollars. Purchasing power = 1,780 ÷ (1 + inflation) years . Assumptions: 2% and 3% are illustrative constant inflation rates, not forecasts or observed CPI data. Amounts displayed to the nearest dollar; calculations retain full precision. Payout input [S02] ; calculated 6 Nov 2026. EXHIBIT 10 · DEFERRAL · INCOME-ONLY COMPARISON Starting later raises income but gives up earlier payments S$1,780 Monthly from 65 S$2,380 Monthly from 70 The later illustration pays S$600 more each month. Deferring five years forgoes 60 × S$1,780 = S$106,800 under the constant-payout assumption. S$106,800 ÷ S$600 = 178 months Income catches up at 84y 10m This is an undiscounted income-only catch-up age. It excludes the different premium and death-refund paths. The reference table does not give the age-70 premium, so a full household return comparison cannot be completed from these figures alone. “Up to 7% more per year deferred” describes a payout uplift. It is not a quoted 7% annual investment yield and should not be compounded as though it were one. Sources and dates: official payout reference updated 16 Jun 2026; deferral FAQ updated 14 Aug 2026. Fixed-payout calculation, 6 Nov 2026; SGD. [S02] [S12] PLAN DESIGN · NO NUMERICAL PLAN RANKING WITHOUT QUOTATIONS Standard, Escalating and Basic need different cash-flow models Plan How the payments work What matters in the model Standard Level payouts by design; higher at the start than Escalating. All RA savings become the premium. The premium, actual monthly quotation and remaining premium refund. Payout review still applies. Escalating Lower initial payout, increasing 2% each year on the payout anniversary. All RA savings become the premium. The actual starting quotation and annual step-ups. A fixed 2% increase does not exactly track actual inflation. Basic About 10%–20% becomes the premium. Retained RA savings pay income first, until age 90. Track the RA and premium separately. Payouts progressively fall as combined balances drop below S$60,000 and extra interest declines. On a phone: swipe the plan table sideways to see the model requirements. How to read: the Standard example is not a shortcut for every plan. Applying its “premium minus all payouts” calculation to Basic would ignore Basic's retained RA savings and its different payment structure. Sources: CPF Standard and Escalating FAQs updated 5 Sep 2025; Basic FAQ updated 26 Aug 2026. Reviewed 6 Nov 2026. No personalised Basic or Escalating quotation supplied. [S03] [S04] [S05] ANALYSIS · THE CASE FOR LIFETIME INCOME Cover the spending that cannot stop Need Planning response Essential recurring bills Identify the gap after other dependable lifetime income. Emergencies and known costs Keep an explicit reserve that can be accessed while alive. Rising prices and family goals Budget separately for purchasing power and the intended estate. CPF LIFE can form part of an income foundation. Its purpose is especially relevant when a household would otherwise have to stretch a finite portfolio across an uncertain lifespan. A single IRR at one assumed death age cannot describe that protection fully. How to read: this is a planning framework, not a recommended allocation or an instruction to maximise top-ups. Analysis based on lifelong-payout mechanics [S03] [S07] ; 6 Nov 2026. COUNTERARGUMENTS · WHAT WEAKENS A SIMPLE “MORE IS BETTER” VIEW More lifetime cover is not every household's first need Existing lifetime income may already cover essentials. Additional flexibility or estate value may then matter more. Early-death opportunity cost is real. Recovering the same nominal premium over time is different from earning a positive return on accessible assets. Level payments lose purchasing power. A larger nominal payout does not remove inflation exposure. Investment alternatives have their own risks. Market losses, poor early returns, reinvestment, fees and restrictive surrender terms can reduce the income available. What changes the conclusion: the actual quotation, other dependable income, liquidity needs, family objectives, inflation and the guarantees available from alternatives. No bull/bear targets or probabilities are invented for these qualitative choices. Evidence and analysis: CPF payout-adjustment rules and MoneySense's annuity guidance; portfolio and inflation implications are this report's analysis. [S11] [S15] A useful question is: how much dependable income will this money provide, for how long, with what access to capital and what remaining benefit for the family? 06 / THE DETAIL BEHIND THE EXPLANATION Keep the assumptions visible The numbers describe a specified cash-flow model. They do not predict an individual's lifespan, reproduce CPF 's unpublished actuarial pricing, or establish a current winner among named retirement products. REFERENCE, ASSUMPTIONS AND EVIDENCE Know what is a fact and what is a calculation Category Treatment in this report Verified reference CPF 's male age-55-in-2026 Standard illustration: S$220,400 at 55, estimated S$330,100 at 65 and S$1,780 monthly from 65. Model assumptions One premium; first payout one month after 65; fixed monthly income; no later inflows; death after the selected payout; no reinvestment of received income. Our calculations Refund path, cumulative income, IRRs, recovery ages, portfolio depletion, inflation and the limited deferral catch-up. Source opinion Investment Moats' historical plan preferences remain attributed to that dated article. They are not adopted as a current recommendation. Our analysis The comparison framework and planning trade-offs. No mortality-weighted expected return, target price or scenario probability is estimated. Precision: calculations retain full stored precision. Summary rates are shown to two decimals and money is generally shown to whole dollars; detailed data are available below. Extra digits cannot make an illustrative CPF input as accurate as a personal quotation. Download monthly cash flows · CSV Download model data · JSON Print / save as PDF The formulas and the opportunity cost The refund formula is specific to the modelled single Standard premium. Let P be the S$330,100 premium, M the S$1,780 monthly payout, and n the number of months after 65. Cumulative income Cₙ = n × M Remaining refund Bₙ = max(P − Cₙ, 0) Total cash delivered = Cₙ + Bₙ = max(P, Cₙ) IRR uses the dates as well as the amounts. The monthly rate i is the rate that makes the discounted value of the payments and terminal refund equal the initial outlay. Annual IRR is (1 + i) 12 − 1. From age 65: P = Σ[k=1…n] M / (1+i)ᵏ + Bₙ / (1+i)ⁿ From age 55: 220,400 = Σ[k=1…n] M / (1+i)^(120+k) + Bₙ / (1+i)^(120+n) At age 65 itself, an age-65 IRR is undefined. No time has elapsed. For positive elapsed periods before premium exhaustion, the household IRR is exactly 0%. Income-only IRR omits the refund. At the first month its annualised value is extremely close to −100%; stored floating-point precision rounds it to −1.0. A required return makes opportunity cost explicit. Net present value, or NPV, discounts future cash flows at a chosen hurdle rate and subtracts the premium. A positive figure means the selected cash flows exceed that hurdle, not that the outcome is guaranteed. Assumed death age NPV from 65 at a 4% annual hurdle 80 −S$82,902 85 −S$34,526 90 S$9,662 95 S$45,981 How to read: the 4% hurdle is a constant effective annual assumption, converted to a monthly discount rate. Payouts and the refund are included; no mortality probabilities are used. SGD, rounded to whole dollars. A riskier investment's expected return should not be treated as a guaranteed discount rate. The same-income portfolio grows before withdrawing. Its monthly rate is (1 + annual net rate) 1/12 − 1. When the balance cannot fund the full withdrawal, the final payment is reduced and the shortfall is recorded. Annual chart points also include the exact first-shortfall month. The arithmetic has been checked independently. Two independent IRR solvers and separate portfolio calculation agree within floating-point tolerance. Selected ages and all monthly values were rechecked for this version. This verifies the calculations under their assumptions, not future outcomes. Terms used in this report Retirement Account (RA) The CPF account holding retirement savings before they are committed as the annuity premium. Premium The amount committed to buy the annuity's payment promise. Bequest / death refund A benefit paid to beneficiaries on death. Here the calculation isolates the remaining CPF LIFE premium refund. IRR An annualised return calculated from the money paid in, money paid out and their timing. Nominal / real Nominal means before allowing for inflation. Real means adjusted for purchasing power. Longevity risk The risk that life, and the need for income, lasts longer than the savings available to fund it. Sequence risk The risk that poor investment returns early in retirement cause lasting harm while withdrawals continue. Liquidity How readily an asset can provide spendable money while its owner is alive. UNRESOLVED INPUTS · WHAT A PRODUCT COMPARISON STILL NEEDS Actual quotations are needed to rank actual products Missing input Why it matters Personal CPF quotation Exact member profile, plan, premium, commencement date and payout schedule. Basic / Escalating schedules Initial payout, RA and premium paths, anniversary increases and death benefits. Age-70 premium and refund Required for a complete deferral comparison rather than an income-only catch-up. Alternative-product illustration Currency, purchase cost, fees, guaranteed and non-guaranteed payments, death benefit and surrender or market value. Use the same funding date, currency and spending requirement. Convert foreign-currency cash flows to SGD under an explicit exchange-rate or hedge-cost assumption. Keep guaranteed and projected benefits separate. Compare several survival horizons, rather than choosing the one that makes a preferred product look best.
