entries.text: CPF LIFE yields | Research report Market Intelligence Hub · Research Explained · CPF LIFE calculator research CPF LIFE YIELD RESEARCH 5 November 2026 · SGD · Sources linked throughout Contents CPF LIFE yields: growth, capital recovery and income for life 1. What “yield” means in this analysis 2. Ages 55 to 65: RA interest is genuine accumulation 3. Payouts reduce the premium refund 4. After premium recovery: survival drives the return 5. Two starting dates produce two valid IRRs 6. “Break-even” needs a definition 7. Discounted cash flows show the opportunity cost 8. A separate portfolio must fund the same income 9. Inflation and longevity change the planning question 10. Standard, Escalating and Basic need different models 11. Deferral and top-ups require incremental comparisons 12. Comparing CPF LIFE with other products 13. Requirements for a reliable CPF LIFE builder 14. Strategy, counterarguments and next actions 15. Method, limitations and audit notes Sources and reference register CPF LIFE yields: growth, capital recovery and income for life Research report and product-comparison framework | 5 November 2026 | All money in Singapore dollars The payout rate, the interest credited to retirement savings, and the return earned across a lifetime answer different questions. A useful comparison must show all three. This report develops the investment-return approach in the supplied Investment Moats article, checks the current CPF rules, and builds a transparent monthly cash-flow model. The central numerical case uses CPF Board 's published example for a male member turning 55 in 2026 on the Standard Plan. It is an illustration, not a personalised payout quotation. Actual pricing depends on the balance, start age, mortality and interest assumptions. [S01] [S02] [S19] Reference input Published amount RA savings at age 55 S$220,400 Estimated RA savings at age 65 S$330,100 Standard Plan monthly payout from age 65 S$1,780 Five findings Before payouts begin, RA savings earn interest. The published endpoints imply 4.12% a year across ten years, including the effect of extra interest and the illustration's assumptions. This is not a separate contractual 4.12% rate. From 65, cumulative Standard Plan payouts plus the remaining premium refund equal the starting premium while that refund is positive. The model therefore gives a 0% nominal household IRR over those horizons. The premium refund reaches zero at the 186th payment, age 80 years 6 months under the stated timing convention. There is no universal age-81 threshold. The annual payout rate is 6.47%. The annualised IRR from age 65 is 2.72% at age 85, 4.29% at 90 and 5.16% at 95. These are conditional outcomes, not promised annual investment yields. CPF LIFE supplies lifetime income. A fair alternative must also show its remaining capital, withdrawal shortfalls, inflation exposure and access to money. Evidence labels used throughout: Fact means a current source statement. Calculation means arithmetic derived from specified inputs. Assumption means a modelling choice. Judgment means a planning interpretation. Full precision is retained in the calculation files; display figures use sensible rounding. Report and presentations Read the complete research on this page. Download the presentations, speaker notes and calculation audit below. Financial briefing PowerPoint · 5 slides with speaker notes. Clear visual story PowerPoint · 5 slides with speaker notes. Download the 10-page speaker-notes PDF · Download calculation model and full-precision data Public research edition dated 5 November 2026. Figures use the published CPF reference case and stated modelling assumptions, not a personalised quotation. 1. What “yield” means in this analysis A cash payout can contain a return of capital Measure What it answers RA credited interest How fast eligible CPF savings earn interest before the premium is committed. Annual payout rate Annual cash paid divided by the stated starting capital. It does not deduct capital returned through payouts. Income-only IRR The annualised return using the initial outlay and payouts received while alive. Household IRR The annualised return including both payouts and the premium refund on death. Net present value (NPV) Whether discounted payouts and the refund exceed the initial outlay at a stated opportunity-cost rate. Real return The return after adjusting for the assumed inflation path. Insurance value The value of continuing income when the member survives longer than planned. A single death-age IRR does not measure it fully. Calculation. S$1,780 × 12 = S$21,360 a year. S$21,360 / S$330,100 = 6.470766% as an annual payout rate. Dividing by the original S$220,400 instead gives 9.691470%, but that mixes income beginning after a ten-year wait with capital committed at 55. Neither ratio is the IRR of the complete cash flows. What the Investment Moats article contributes The article first appeared in December 2018 and carries an April 2022 date. Its useful method is to calculate returns at different ages of death, separately including and excluding bequest. It also recognises retirement-income durability as a distinct objective. The historical plan rankings and “break-even” ages depend on an older example and estimator. The author notes that the earlier bequest output is no longer easily reproducible. This report adopts that comparison method, refreshes the rules and inputs, and avoids presenting the old ranking as a current product recommendation. [S01] Judgment. The right comparison is a dated cash-flow comparison with explicit guarantees. A high distribution rate alone cannot establish that a product creates more wealth, and a low early-life IRR alone cannot establish that longevity protection lacks value. 2. Ages 55 to 65: RA interest is genuine accumulation The accumulation stage has a different accounting basis from CPF LIFE payouts Fact. The RA base rate is 4% a year for October to December 2026. The Government has extended the 4% floor through 31 December 2027. For members aged 55 and above, extra interest applies to the first S$60,000 of combined CPF balances: 2% on the first S$30,000 and 1% on the next S$30,000, subject to the account rules and OA cap. “Up to 6%” therefore does not mean 6% on the entire RA. [S08] [S09] Fact. CPF computes interest monthly and credits it for annual compounding. Contributions received during a month start earning interest the next month, while withdrawals or deductions stop earning interest from that month. Account flows and dates matter. [S10] The published RA illustration adds S$109,700 before payouts ... ... 0 100 200 300 S$220,400 Age 55 S$330,100 Age 65 estimate S$000 Source: CPF Board , 16 Jun 2026, male member turning 55 in 2026. Published reference amounts, SGD. [S02] Calculation. S$330,100 − S$220,400 = S$109,700. The growth rate that connects the two published endpoints is (330,100 / 220,400)^(1/10) − 1 = 4.122214% a year. This is an implied growth rate, not the quoted base interest rate. It also does not prove that a simple annual formula exactly reproduces CPF 's underlying illustration. Assumption. For the return model, S$220,400 is committed exactly at age 55, there are no later contributions or withdrawals, and all S$330,100 becomes the Standard Plan premium exactly ten years later. Actual CPF projections may incorporate transaction dates and profile details not exposed in the reference table. The current rate floor stops at a stated date. It must not be described as a guaranteed 4% rate for every year from 2026 to 2036. Comparison implication. A product bought at age 55 must be assessed from that same date and with the same contribution schedule. For a comparison starting at 65, both sides should begin with the same accessible capital, or the capital difference must be explicitly funded. 3. Payouts reduce the premium refund The “bequest is the balance” observation has a precise scope Fact. Standard Plan members use all their RA savings as the premium when joining. On death, beneficiaries receive any remaining CPF LIFE premium balance, together with other remaining CPF account balances. The premium balance is the premium paid less CPF LIFE payouts already received. This report models the premium refund only. Other CPF balances and assets are outside the calculation. [S03] [S06] For one premium P and cumulative payouts Cₙ: Bₙ = max(P − Cₙ, 0). Therefore Cₙ + Bₙ = max(P, Cₙ). While Bₙ remains positive, total nominal cash delivered to the member and beneficiaries equals P. Age Payouts received Premium refund Combined 70 S$106,800 S$223,300 S$330,100 75 S$213,600 S$116,500 S$330,100 80 S$320,400 S$9,700 S$330,100 81 S$341,760 S$0 S$341,760 85 S$427,200 S$0 S$427,200 Calculation. At age 80, 180 payments total S$320,400. The remaining refund is S$330,100 − S$320,400 = S$9,700. Adding the two gives S$330,100. Discounting these positive cash flows against the initial S$330,100 gives exactly 0% nominal household IRR. The member's income-only IRR is −0.39% at that age because it excludes the remaining S$9,700 refund. Fact and interpretation. CPF LIFE premiums continue to earn interest. CPF pools that interest and uses it in setting payouts from the start. Interest that has not been paid out does not become a separate inheritable account balance. The refund identity supports the capital-recovery interpretation without proving that the premium earns no interest. [S07] [S18] Limits. A death benefit is not cash available to withdraw while alive. Cumulative payouts are past income and may already have been spent. Adding them to a refund measures total cash delivered over time; it does not measure the member's remaining wealth or liquid account balance. 4. After premium recovery: survival drives the return Lifelong protection applies from joining, even though its realised cash benefit becomes clearer later Calculation. After 185 payments, payouts total S$329,300 and the refund is S$800. Payment 186 raises cumulative payouts to S$331,080, exhausting the refund and exceeding the premium by S$980. With the first payment one month after 65, this occurs at age 80 years 6 months. Payout timing and the actual quotation can move the date. The combined cash total rises once the refund reaches zero ... ... 0 200 400 600 70 75 80 85 90 330.1 330.1 330.1 427.2 534.0 Payouts received Premium refund S$000 Model: Standard Plan, S$330,100 premium and S$1,780 monthly, unchanged payouts, no later inflows. Values are cumulative SGD. CPF reference [S02] ; refund rule [S06] . Age at death Paid in total Refund IRR from 65 IRR from 55 80 S$320,400 S$9,700 0.00% 2.33% 81 S$341,760 S$0 0.44% 2.50% 85 S$427,200 S$0 2.72% 3.46% 90 S$534,000 S$0 4.29% 4.21% 95 S$640,800 S$0 5.16% 4.68% 100 S$747,600 S$0 5.68% 4.98% Household IRR includes the premium refund at the selected death month. Once that refund is zero, household and income-only IRR coincide. At age 90, S$534,000 of payouts exceeds the age-65 premium by S$203,900, and the age-65 IRR is 4.29%. The arithmetic does not imply that 4.29% was credited every year. Fact. CPF reviews payouts for changes in mortality experience and interest rates. Any adjustment takes effect in July and CPF expects changes to be small and gradual. Lifetime duration and an unchanging illustrated dollar amount are different promises. [S11] 5. Two starting dates produce two valid IRRs The return from age 55 includes the earlier RA accumulation The starting date changes the result, even with identical payouts ... ... 0% 2% 4% 6% 65 70 75 80 85 90 95 100 From age 65 From age 55 Annualised nominal return Annualised nominal household IRR, %. Age 55 starts with S$220,400. Age 65 starts with S$330,100. Each horizon assumes death after that month’s payment. Calculations from [S02] and [S06] . At age 80, household IRR is 0% from age 65 but 2.33% from age 55. The age-55 calculation includes S$109,700 of accumulation before payouts begin. The age-65 calculation deliberately treats S$330,100 as the new starting capital. Both calculations are correct for the questions they answer. The age-55 curve initially falls as the same nominal premium is returned over a longer period, then rises as lifetime payouts move further beyond that premium. At sufficiently long horizons, the age-65 IRR can exceed the age-55 IRR because it excludes the ten-year waiting period. This is a timing effect, not a contradiction. Age Income-only IRR from 65 Household IRR from 65 Household IRR from 55 70 -31.96% 0.00% 2.89% 75 -7.78% 0.00% 2.45% 80 -0.39% 0.00% 2.33% Method. The monthly rate i solves the present-value equation, including the refund in the terminal month when applicable. Annual IRR is (1+i)^12 − 1. For the age-55 calculation, payments occur at months 121 onward and the premium transfer at month 120 is internal to the model, not a second external investment. Do not subtract the age-65 premium again in the age-55 cash-flow series. That would count the same committed capital twice. IRR describes the timing of specified cash flows. It does not, by itself, state the wealth obtained by reinvesting payouts. A comparison of terminal wealth needs a separate, consistent reinvestment assumption for every product. 6. “Break-even” needs a definition Nominal capital recovery, discounted value and insurance utility are different tests Test Reference result Meaning Recover age-55 contribution from payouts Payment 124; age 75 years 4 months Payouts reach S$220,720, exceeding S$220,400. This ignores the opportunity cost of the entire waiting period. Recover age-65 premium from payouts Payment 186; age 80 years 6 months Payouts reach S$331,080, exceeding S$330,100. Recover the premium including refund Every positive-duration horizon before exhaustion Combined nominal payments equal the premium. The timing of those payments still matters. Achieve a 4% discounted return from 65 Positive NPV first occurs at payment 286 in this model This requires the discounted payout value to exceed S$330,100. Receive useful longevity protection Applies when CPF LIFE begins Value depends on the member’s need for income assurance, not just a realised death-age return. A nominal 0% household IRR does not preserve purchasing power. If inflation were a constant 2%, the corresponding real annual return would be 1/1.02 − 1 = −1.96%. Inflation is a scenario here, not a forecast. The same distinction matters for a bond that returns principal only at maturity. An early death creates an opportunity cost relative to a positive-return liquid portfolio, even when the original premium is fully returned through payouts and refund. Conversely, a member who survives well beyond the modelled portfolio's funding horizon benefits from continued CPF LIFE income. Both observations belong in a balanced comparison. Judgment. The investment lens helps detect misleading yield claims. The insurance lens asks how the household will pay essential bills if it lives longer than its assets last. A defensible recommendation uses both lenses and identifies which risk the household is trying to reduce. 7. Discounted cash flows show the opportunity cost Scenario rates are comparison assumptions, not current product offers For a selected death month n and annual discount rate d, NPV equals −P + the sum of each monthly payout discounted to age 65 + the terminal refund discounted to age 65. The refund is included once. A positive NPV means that this particular sequence of benefits exceeds the hurdle rate. It is not an expected return across all possible lifespans. Death age NPV at 0% NPV at 2.5% NPV at 4% 70 S$0 -S$32,368 -S$49,742 75 S$0 -S$50,014 -S$74,994 80 S$0 -S$55,919 -S$82,902 81 S$11,660 -S$48,064 -S$76,676 85 S$97,100 S$6,683 -S$34,526 90 S$203,900 S$67,934 S$9,662 95 S$310,700 S$122,071 S$45,981 100 S$417,500 S$169,920 S$75,833 Assumption. The 0%, 2.5% and 4% rates are constant annual effective nominal hurdle rates. They are not quotes for deposits, bonds or an insurer. Although 2.5% and 4% are familiar CPF reference rates today, they do not mean a member can keep the CPF LIFE premium in a liquid account paying those rates for decades. [S08] At age 85, the 4% NPV is -S$34,526. At age 90 it is S$9,662. The sign changes because the member receives another five years of income. Selecting only the later positive figure would hide the trade-off faced at the time of purchase. For guaranteed benefits in the same currency, a dated term structure can be a more informative discount benchmark than one flat rate. Risky investment returns should not be used as though they were guaranteed discount rates. This report retains flat rates to make the sensitivity transparent rather than inventing a current executable market comparison. A household-specific decision needs the actual alternative available on the same date, with the same currency, fees, guarantee basis and accessible capital. 8. A separate portfolio must fund the same income Equal withdrawals expose both the remaining estate and the eventual shortfall Assumption. Start a separate portfolio at age 65 with S$330,100. Credit a smooth constant net return every month at an annual effective rate of 0%, 2.5% or 4%, then withdraw S$1,780. There are no additional flows, fees beyond the stated net rate, taxes or market shocks. The portfolio cannot become negative; its final payment is reduced when available funds are insufficient. Positive returns extend the funding period but do not create a lifetime promise ... ... 0 100 200 300 65 70 75 80 85 90 95 100 0% net 2.5% net 4% net S$000 Portfolio balance, SGD, after matching S$1,780 monthly withdrawals. Constant net nominal scenario rates. This is a deterministic comparison, not a market simulation or product forecast. Net annual return Last full monthly payment First payment with a shortfall 0% Age 80 years 5 months Age 80 years 6 months 2.5% Age 84 years 5 months Age 84 years 6 months 4% Age 88 years 9 months Age 88 years 10 months CPF LIFE illustration Pays for life while the member lives Payout amount may be adjusted under CPF rules The constant net annual return needed to pay S$1,780 monthly indefinitely while preserving S$330,100 of nominal principal is (1 + 1,780/330,100)^12 − 1 = 6.6662%. This is a mathematical perpetuity hurdle. It is not an available risk-free product rate, and preserving nominal capital would still leave inflation risk. An invested portfolio has advantages the CPF LIFE premium does not: remaining market value can support emergencies or heirs, subject to the asset's liquidity and market risk. It also leaves the household responsible for sequence risk, reinvestment rates, fees and withdrawals. A constant-return illustration omits those uncertainties. CPF LIFE reduces the risk of outliving the payout stream, while its refund declines and its money is less flexible. 9. Inflation and longevity change the planning question A level dollar payout buys less over time Fact. Standard Plan payouts are level in design. Escalating Plan payouts begin lower and rise by 2% annually on the payout anniversary. A fixed 2% increase does not track actual CPI exactly. [S03] [S04] Future age S$1,780 in age-65 dollars at 2% inflation At 3% inflation 75 S$1,460 S$1,324 85 S$1,198 S$986 95 S$983 S$733 Calculation. Purchasing power equals S$1,780 / (1+inflation)^(years after 65). These scenarios isolate inflation. They do not assume that CPF will index the Standard payout to prices or that future inflation will follow either path. Fact. Singapore's 2025 resident life tables report remaining life expectancy at age 65 of 19.9 years for males and 23.1 years for females. Those are population averages conditional on already reaching 65. They are not a deadline or a personal forecast. The data describe the 2025 mortality environment; a person turning 55 in 2026 reaches 65 in 2036. [S14] A survival-weighted expected present value would require age-specific survival probabilities, treatment of the refund in each death month, a discount curve and a clear population basis. It would also need assumptions about future mortality improvement. This report does not claim to reproduce CPF 's actuarial pricing or publish an actuarial “fair value”. Putting average life expectancy into an IRR calculator does not produce an expected IRR. The distribution of possible lifespans matters, especially the long-lived tail. Judgment. Plan essential spending beyond the average lifespan and stress late-life costs. Keep an explicit inflation budget. A person with a strong estate objective or a need for substantial accessible capital may prefer a different mix of lifetime income and investments even when the headline payout is lower. 10. Standard, Escalating and Basic need different models The Standard refund shortcut cannot be applied indiscriminately Plan Premium and payout structure Modelling consequence Standard All RA savings become the premium. Payouts are level in design. One quoted premium, a monthly payout path and the residual premium refund. Escalating All RA savings become the premium. Payouts start lower and rise 2% yearly. Use the actual initial quote and anniversary steps. The first increase follows twelve payments. Basic About 10% to 20% of RA becomes the premium. Payouts first draw from remaining RA savings until age 90. Track the remaining RA and premium separately, including interest and the actual payout schedule. Fact. Under Basic, the RA portion continues earning interest. As combined balances fall below S$60,000, extra interest declines and monthly payouts progressively reduce. CPF identifies age 90 as the transition from RA-funded payouts to CPF LIFE premium-funded payouts. [S05] Method. With initial Escalating payout W₀ and monthly payment number k, a simple anniversary model uses Wₖ = W₀ × 1.02^floor((k−1)/12). This formula models the announced escalation feature, subject to any actuarial adjustments. Its cumulative cash total and IRR depend on the actual initial quotation. [S04] For Basic, subtracting every payment from the small 10% to 20% premium would falsely exhaust the premium while ignoring the remaining RA. A sound model needs the allocation, RA cash-flow path, extra-interest rules, premium payout path and death-benefit schedule. No current personalised Basic or Escalating quotations were supplied, so this report does not invent their yields or rank the three plans numerically. Judgment. Standard favours higher initial income than Escalating. Escalating shifts income toward later years. Basic requires close attention to lower and potentially declining payouts as well as bequest. The relevant question is how each actual quotation meets spending needs and estate preferences, rather than which plan wins at an arbitrarily selected death age. 11. Deferral and top-ups require incremental comparisons A larger payout is not the same as a higher investment return Fact. CPF allows payout deferral up to age 70. It describes the increase as up to 7% for each year deferred and up to 35% for deferral to 70. This is an uplift in the later monthly payout, not a guaranteed 7% annual investment yield and not five years of compounding at 1.07. [S12] The published reference case shows S$1,780 monthly from 65 or S$2,380 from 70. The increase is S$600 a month, or 33.71%. Deferral also forgoes the first 60 monthly payments, a total of S$106,800 in this constant-payout illustration. [S02] Calculation. Ignoring bequest and discounting, it takes S$106,800 / S$600 = 178 months after age 70 for the higher payout to catch up with the foregone income. That is age 84 years 10 months. This limited cash-income calculation does not determine which choice has the better household return or insurance value. The source table does not supply the age-70 premium or full refund path. Reusing S$330,100 as the age-70 premium would manufacture a result. A full deferral comparison needs the actual premium and cash-flow schedules for both start dates. The next dollar can behave differently from the first dollar Fact. The 2026 ERS is S$440,800, double the current FRS. That multiple changed from 2025, so the older article's ERS description is historical. [S20] Calculation. Comparing the published FRS and ERS examples adds S$220,400 at age 55, S$320,000 of estimated premium at 65 and S$1,660 monthly payout. The incremental annual payout ratio is S$19,920 / S$320,000 = 6.225%. It differs from the 6.47% average ratio in the FRS case. Extra-interest caps and quotation assumptions make simple proportional scaling unreliable. [S02] For an incremental IRR, subtract the two complete cash-flow schedules. Incremental refund equals B_ERS,n − B_FRS,n, rather than mechanically applying max(extra premium − extra payouts, 0). Each policy can exhaust its premium at a different time. Tax relief and any eligibility-dependent benefits should be added only when verified for the person and decision being compared. 12. Comparing CPF LIFE with other products Align the funding date, income objective and terminal value Product Useful return measure Material differences CPF LIFE IRR by death age, with and without refund; lifetime income coverage Lifetime duration. Premium refund declines. Limited access to committed savings. Actual payout can be adjusted. SGS bonds and T-bills Yield to maturity plus the actual purchase price and cash-flow dates Fixed maturities. Bond prices can change before maturity. A ladder requires reinvestment and planned sales or redemptions. Singapore Savings Bonds Return for the actual holding period, interest received and redeemed principal Up to ten years. Monthly redemption feature. S$200,000 individual holding cap, so one person cannot place the full S$330,100 case in SSBs. Private annuity Separate guaranteed and illustrated IRRs with death and surrender values Term or lifetime structure varies. Participating bonuses are not guaranteed. Early surrender can cause losses. Investment portfolio Net total return, matched withdrawals, terminal value and shortfalls Market and sequence risk. Fees, FX and tax can reduce spendable SGD cash. Remaining assets may be accessible or inheritable. Source basis: CPF rules [S03] [S06] [S11] , MAS government securities comparison and SSB FAQ [S16] [S17] , and MoneySense annuity guidance [S15] . No current private-product benefit illustration or executable bond quotation was supplied. The report therefore provides a comparison method and transparent scenarios, not a named-product league table. Fact. CPF LIFE exemption is conditional. A qualifying pension or private annuity must meet the relevant lifelong guaranteed payout requirements. CPF says investments such as endowments and bonds are not accepted for this purpose. Prior top-ups remain in the RA and cannot be withdrawn as a lump sum, and the qualifying annuity cannot secure a loan. A spreadsheet comparison cannot make restricted retirement savings freely withdrawable. [S13] Method. Use the same initial date and the same money available to invest. Match monthly spending, even when coupons arrive only every six months. Record any shortfall explicitly. At death, use the relevant death benefit; while alive, use an actual sale or surrender value if liquidation is assumed. Never add both death and surrender proceeds for the same termination event. For foreign-currency products, convert every payout and terminal value into SGD at an explicit FX path or hedge cost. A foreign coupon rate is not an SGD return. For callable bonds, distinguish promised maturity cash flows from cash flows under a call scenario. For participating insurance, keep guaranteed and non-guaranteed amounts in separate columns rather than quietly combining them into a certainty claim. 13. Requirements for a reliable CPF LIFE builder An article-led interface can expose the calculations without overwhelming the reader Inputs and provenance Member profile and quote: quotation date, birth cohort, sex where used in pricing, plan, start age, exact premium, first payment date and payout schedule. Accumulation: starting RA and date, later contributions and withdrawals, current rate assumptions, extra-interest eligibility and a separately identified official projected premium. Comparison: funding date, actual purchase cost, currency, cash-flow dates, fees, taxes, guaranteed benefits, illustrated benefits, death values and surrender or market values. Scenario controls: death or review age, inflation, opportunity-cost rate, investment-return path and whether any income is reinvested. Outputs that should stay separate Output Required label or behaviour Monthly payout and annual payout rate State the premium denominator and payout start date. Cumulative income and remaining refund Show them separately, then optionally combine them as total cash delivered. Four IRR views Age-55 and payout-start clocks, each with income-only and household returns. Nominal and discounted recovery State the threshold and first crossing month. Portfolio comparison Show surviving capital, every income shortfall and depletion timing. Plan comparison Require real quotations. For Basic, require a suitable schedule or a separately validated account model. The article should explain the three stages first, then let readers change a few assumptions and inspect the cash-flow table. Use “remaining premium refund” rather than an unqualified “account balance” after annuitisation. Explain that the refund is payable on death and that lifetime coverage has already started. Validation should reject negative premiums, duplicate months and missing schedules. A model with no elapsed time should display IRR as undefined rather than forcing 0%. Where cash flows change sign more than once, the calculator should flag possible multiple IRRs and favour NPV comparisons. Monthly data should be downloadable with their input assumptions and source dates. 14. Strategy, counterarguments and next actions The conclusion depends on the risk the household wants to reduce A defensible planning sequence Quantify essential monthly spending in SGD and the income already available for life. This identifies the longevity-income gap. Decide how much capital must remain accessible for emergencies and known expenses. A death refund cannot serve that purpose while the member is alive. Obtain actual CPF quotations and alternative benefit illustrations using the same person, dates and capital. Compare guaranteed cash flows first. Test several survival ages, including late life, and show inflation and adverse investment paths. Use household and income-only results side by side. Evaluate the incremental top-up or deferral decision separately from the existing CPF commitment. Recheck withdrawal rules and the value of liquidity before acting. The strongest counterarguments deserve space Against an overly favourable CPF LIFE framing: zero nominal household growth over many early payout years has a real opportunity cost. The declining refund limits estate value. Level payouts lose purchasing power. Long-term payout adjustments remain possible. A household with ample independent lifelong income may place a higher value on flexible assets than on another unit of longevity cover. Against an overly critical investment framing: the payout rate is supported by returning capital and pooling longevity risk. A separate portfolio must either accept depletion risk, reduce spending, commit more capital or earn sufficient returns. The insurance protects against a difficult late-life outcome that a return calculated at one assumed death age cannot describe fully. Judgment. CPF LIFE can provide a foundation for essential lifetime spending, with other assets addressing liquidity, inflation and estate goals. The appropriate split depends on the actual income gap and available capital. The research does not establish that everyone should maximise CPF top-ups, select the same plan or choose the same payout start age. The useful question is: how much dependable income will the household receive, for how long, with what access to capital and what value remaining for beneficiaries? 15. Method, limitations and audit notes Reproducible arithmetic does not remove uncertainty in the inputs Item Treatment in the central case Currency and basis Nominal SGD. No personal tax relief, fees or outside CPF assets included. Initial cash flows −S$220,400 at 55 for the full-period view; −S$330,100 at 65 for the payout-period view. Monthly timing First S$1,780 payment one month after 65. Death occurs just after the selected month’s payment. Payout changes Held constant for analysis. Actual CPF adjustments and subsequent contributions would change results. Premium refund max(S$330,100 − cumulative payouts, 0), for this Standard case. IRR Monthly discounted cash-flow root, annualised as (1+i)^12 − 1. Separate income-only and household series. Portfolio scenarios Smooth net annual effective rates, monthly equivalent growth before withdrawals, no borrowing after depletion. Precision Exact arithmetic uses the published inputs. Those reference inputs themselves are rounded illustrations. Display precision is not quotation accuracy. The model has no mortality probabilities and is not an expected-value or actuarial-pricing model. It does not estimate individual health, predict lifespan, reproduce unpublished CPF pricing assumptions, or guarantee future payouts. The population life-expectancy statistic supplies context only. The calculator distinguishes financial arithmetic from those unanswered questions. Two independent numerical implementations were used for the central monthly cash flows. Their headline results, zero-IRR identity, recovery months, discount-rate comparisons and portfolio shortfall months were reconciled. Independent validation checks the arithmetic under the assumptions; it cannot validate assumptions as future facts. No personalised payout quote, full Basic/Escalating death-benefit schedule, age-70 premium, or named alternative-product benefit illustration was supplied. Those gaps limit product-specific rankings. The report deliberately leaves them visible. Source dates below are publication or update dates where displayed. All web sources were reviewed on 5 November 2026. Current rules can change, so a live comparison should retain its quotation date and refresh its official references. entries.title: CPF OA and Temasek 2070 | Independent research
entries.text: CPF OA and Temasek 2070 | Independent research ← Market Intelligence Hub · Research library My thoughts · 4 November 2026 CPF OA and Temasek 2070 Spend the income. Leave the capital. Testing the “2× income, 2× capital” idea with S$200,000, seven USD/SGD scenarios, verified bond terms and evidence from CPF, GIC, MAS and Temasek. Latest research papers Static research explained Five takeaways Price drives the pitch: a 2.5% coupon at price 50 is a 5% cash yield on clean cost. Same S$200,000 budget: the lot-sized illustration pays S$9,945 a normal year versus S$5,000 OA base interest, before unknown costs. FX matters: every requested 1.20–1.35 scenario stays ahead on gross income and par-redemption capital; this is not a forecast or an FX floor. Family inheritance is market value: nearly 2× capital requires full par payment in 2070 at unchanged FX, not an early sale. Different protections: CPF is Government-backed in SGD; Temasek’s corporate guarantee does not protect the bond’s market price or SGD value. entries.title: Diversification, made simple · Market Intelligence Hub · 6 Nov 2026
entries.text: Diversification, made simple · Market Intelligence Hub · 6 Nov 2026 Skip to report MARKET INTELLIGENCE HUB Independent educational research Research explained ↗ The simple idea See the mix Watch Client explanation Go deeper Sources Portfolio essentials / 6 November 2026 Diversification. Made simple. Give your money more than one job. Build a portfolio that depends on several sources of return, so one disappointment has less power over the whole. the project maintainer · Independent educational report Sources checked to 6 Nov 2026, 16:02 SGT (UTC+8) Diversification Equities Bonds Sharpe ratio Analysis One portfolio · different purposes ↗ Grow Participate in long-term business growth ≈ Generate income Meet part of your planned cash needs ○ Stay ready Keep money available when you need it A planning framework, not a suggested allocation. Each purpose can need more than one investment. [2] 01 Spread the dependence One holding should not decide everything. Spread exposure across businesses, markets and asset types. 02 Look for real differences Different names can hide the same risks. Check what the investments actually own. 03 Expect some trade-offs A diversified mix can still lose money. It may also trail the investment that wins most. Principles: MoneySense [2] , SEC [3] , FINRA [4] . All numerical examples below are hypothetical teaching examples, not market data. 01 / The one-minute idea Prepare for more than one kind of weather. Think sunglasses and umbrellas. A shop selling only sunglasses depends heavily on sunshine. Adding umbrellas gives it another source of sales when the weather changes. Your portfolio can follow the same principle. Own investments with different underlying drivers, so you depend less on getting one forecast right. The analogy explains dependence, not a perfect hedge. A quiet shopping day can hurt both businesses. Sunny days Sunglasses have a job Rainy days Umbrellas have a job Different conditions. Different strengths. Original illustration adapting the SEC’s umbrellas-and-sunglasses analogy, 27 Aug 2009. No prices or return data. [3] 02 / See it in action The combination changes the journey. Watch what happens when the investments behave differently. Each line starts at 100. The mix starts with half in A and half in B, then holds both without rebalancing. Different moves Same moves Both fall Hypothetical portfolio value · index starts at 100 Different moves: same finish, smaller swings for the mix Investment A: 100, 120, 108. Investment B: 100, 90, 108. Initial half-and-half mix, no rebalancing: 100, 105, 108. Two invented periods, no calendar dates. 120 110 100 90 80 Start Period 1 Period 2 A · 120 B · 90 Mix · 105 All finish at 108 A · solid B · dashed Half-and-half mix Index Start P1 P2 A 100 120 108 B 100 90 108 50/50 mix 100 105 108 Read left to right. The vertical axis runs from 80 to 120 to show the changes clearly; it does not start at zero. The exact values are available below. Different moves Same finish. A steadier path. +8% Total gain for A, B and the mix over both periods A rises first, then falls. B falls first, then rises. The mix spreads the dependence across both. Diversification helped the journey in this example. It did not need a higher final return to be useful. Author’s synthetic teaching example · prepared 6 Nov 2026 · index units, no currency · two invented periods · no fees, taxes, borrowing or external cash flows. Inputs represent hypothetical total returns; no separate dividends are added. A and B are not actual assets or forecasts. See the exact values for this scenario Portfolio value Start Period 1 Period 2 All in A 100 120 108 All in B 100 90 108 Initial 50/50 mix 100 105 108 Initial weights are 50% / 50%; the holdings are not reset between periods. Lines connect the stated observations and do not imply a path within either period. At each observation, the mix equals ½ × A’s index + ½ × B’s index. This is valid because both component indices have the same starting value. Full workings ↓ 03 / A common trap Three products can still contain the same bet. Count the underlying exposures, not just the statements. A technology share, a technology fund and a broad equity fund may all expose you to the same companies. Look inside each fund before adding more. The names on the packaging can differ while the drivers of gains and losses overlap. Direct share Company X Sector fund Company X Other holdings Broad fund Company X Other holdings Shared company → repeated exposure Conceptual example. Blocks are not portfolio weights. Actual overlap requires the current holdings and your allocation to each product. FINRA, “Concentrate on Concentration Risk”, 15 Jun 2022. [4] 04 / Put the idea to work Decide what each part is there to do. JOB 01 Long-term growth Broad equity exposure participates in business growth. Spread it across companies, industries and markets. Risk to remember: share prices can suffer large falls, and markets can fall together. JOB 02 Planned income Suitable bonds can contribute contractual cash flows. Match credit quality, maturity and currency to the purpose. Risk to remember: issuers can default; prices can fall when yields rise. Bond funds carry credit and interest-rate risk too. JOB 03 Near-term needs Accessible cash helps you meet upcoming spending. Match it to the currency and timing of those commitments. Risk to remember: inflation erodes purchasing power; deposit terms and access conditions matter. The right proportions depend on the person. Time horizon, ability to absorb losses and cash needs come before a fixed allocation. Adding a highly risky asset can increase the risk of an otherwise cautious portfolio. Planning framework based on MoneySense [2] and the SEC [3] ; bond-fund risks: Investor.gov [7] . No product selection or allocation is prescribed. 05 / The video connection Start with the journey. Learn the ratio later. ▶ The Sharpe Ratio Explained Wall Street Quants · published 22 Aug 2024 Loads YouTube only when you choose to play. Watch the diversification chapter ↗ Open the original video on YouTube ↗ The video’s sequence is a useful teaching route: first look at returns and fluctuations, then ask how combining investments changes the outcome. 00:33 Why returns alone are incomplete ↗ 06:26 Diversification and hedging ↗ 03:48 The Sharpe formula, when ready ↗ Chapter times and metadata verified from the creator’s published description. Full transcript could not be retrieved independently. This report’s examples are original, not reconstructions of the video’s charts. [1] 06 / Say it simply A client explanation you can use. Let’s give your money different jobs. Some can work towards long-term growth, some can provide income, and some can stay accessible for your spending needs. The aim is to reduce how much your whole portfolio depends on one investment doing well. We should check that the investments really bring different exposures. Diversification can help make the journey easier to stay with. It still allows losses, and it will not beat the best-performing investment every time. Copy client explanation Original explanatory wording, based on the principles in sources [2] – [4] . General education; allocations require a review of the individual’s circumstances. Make the next review about the whole portfolio. List it Bring holdings, amounts, funds and liabilities onto one page. Look through it Group repeated companies, sectors, currencies and risk drivers. Match the needs Keep near-term spending and emergency access in view. Set a rule Agree the intended mix and when to review or rebalance it. Start with the largest shared exposure. Review whether it is intentional, affordable and consistent with your goals before adding another investment. Author’s practical framework using MoneySense [2] , SEC [3] and FINRA [4] . 07 / Optional detail The workings, when you want them. Open all details The core message is already above. Open the sections below for the calculation method, the role of correlation, what the Sharpe ratio measures and the limits of diversification. 1. Exactly how the example is calculated Both components finish at 108 from 100. A earns +20% then −10%; B earns −10% then +20%. The two periods are fictional and have no stated calendar length. A: 100 × 1.20 × 0.90 = 108 B: 100 × 0.90 × 1.20 = 108 Mix after period 1: 50 × 1.20 + 50 × 0.90 = 60 + 45 = 105 Mix after period 2: 60 × 0.90 + 45 × 1.20 = 54 + 54 = 108 The mix is only 50/50 at the start. After the first period it holds 60 in A and 45 in B. We leave those holdings alone. Its second-period return is exactly (108 ÷ 105 − 1) × 100% = 20/7%, not 5%. What if we reset the mix? Rebalancing changes the strategy and the result. Resetting the 105 portfolio to 52.5 in each asset produces 52.5 × 0.90 + 52.5 × 1.20 = 110.25. The extra 2.25 index points arise from the rule and this deliberately alternating path. They are not a guaranteed diversification bonus. Scenario A: start → P1 → P2 B: start → P1 → P2 Mix: start → P1 → P2 Different moves 100 → 120 → 108 100 → 90 → 108 100 → 105 → 108 Same moves 100 → 120 → 108 100 → 120 → 108 100 → 120 → 108 Both fall 100 → 80 → 88 100 → 90 → 99 100 → 85 → 93.5 All chart scenarios use initial 50/50 weights and no rebalancing. In “Both fall”, A loses 20% and B loses 10%, then each rises 10% from its reduced value. Author’s exact arithmetic, 6 Nov 2026. Zero fees, taxes, financing and external cash flows are teaching assumptions. No live asset, price series or historical backtest is represented. Two periods cannot establish a reliable long-term volatility or Sharpe estimate. 2. Why how investments move together matters Correlation describes how returns move together. A value of +1 means perfect positive linear co-movement in the measured returns. Zero means no linear correlation; it does not guarantee independence. A negative value means a tendency to move in opposite directions, not a promise that every loss is offset. Negative correlation is not required for diversification to help. With ordinary positive portfolio weights, imperfect correlation can reduce portfolio volatility relative to the weighted average of the component volatilities. That does not guarantee less risk than the safest component on its own. σ² portfolio = w² A σ² A + w² B σ² B + 2w A w B ρσ A σ B Here w means portfolio weight, σ means volatility (standard deviation of returns), and ρ means correlation. Volatility measures fluctuations around the average return; it is not a maximum-loss estimate. A separate mathematical illustration Hold the expected return constant and change only the correlation. Assume each fictional asset has expected annual return 8% and annual volatility 20%. The mix starts 50/50; the illustrative risk-free rate is 2%. These are assumptions, not current market estimates. Assumed correlation Portfolio volatility, exact Expected return Sharpe , exact +1 · together 20% 8% 3/10 +0.5 · partly together 10√3% 8% √3/5 0 · no linear correlation 10√2% 8% 3√2/10 −0.5 · tend to offset 10% 8% 3/5 Volatility bars share a zero-to-20% scale. Square-root notation keeps irrational results exact. All returns and volatility use the same annual horizon; no costs. A mathematical illustration, separate from the two-period chart above. The last row halves the volatility without changing the assumed expected return. In decimals, variance = 0.5² × 0.20² + 0.5² × 0.20² + 2 × 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.20 × 0.20 × (−0.5) = 0.01; volatility = √0.01 = 0.10 = 10%. Original derivation of the standard two-asset variance identity, 6 Nov 2026. Real expected returns and correlations are uncertain and can change. Correlation interpretation: [2] , [5] and [6] . 3. Sharpe in plain English, then the correct formula The Sharpe ratio compares excess return with the fluctuations that came with it. “Excess” means above the chosen risk-free reference. It is a measure of return per unit of volatility, not an interest rate or a safety score. x t = portfolio return t − risk-free return t Historical Sharpe = mean(x t ) ÷ standard deviation(x t ) Same reward, more fluctuation In the annual model above: (8% − 2%) ÷ 20% = 0.3 Same reward, less fluctuation In the annual model above: (8% − 2%) ÷ 10% = 0.6 A higher ratio can come from an improved combination. But reducing volatility does not guarantee a higher Sharpe if expected excess return also falls. An investment with a lower standalone ratio can still help the whole portfolio if it contributes sufficiently different exposure. For a fair comparison What to keep consistent Return series Total returns, including distributions; the same fee basis and time window. Currency One reporting currency and a suitable benchmark in that currency. Frequency Matched daily, monthly or annual observations. Do not mix units. Interpretation Separate historical results from expected future returns. Show how many observations were used. Use arithmetic excess-return observations for the standard historical ratio. Compounded growth is a different measure. A bond’s coupon or yield to maturity is not a total-return history. Sharpe leaves important questions unanswered. It treats upward and downward fluctuations alike, does not describe every severe-loss possibility, and does not by itself tell you how a holding fits your other assets and liabilities. Definition and limitations: William F. Sharpe, “The Sharpe Ratio”, Fall 1994. [5] No real product or portfolio Sharpe has been calculated for this report. The earlier full Sharpe and financing report provides the separate technical treatment. 4. When the argument helps—and when it needs qualifying The main counterargument is real. A concentrated winner can outperform a diversified portfolio. Holding several exposures means some will lag. Diversification seeks a more manageable range of outcomes; it does not promise the highest possible return. What can happen Why it matters What to check Several assets fall together A shared inflation, interest-rate or liquidity shock can overwhelm differences. Stress the whole portfolio and keep cash needs separate. A new holding raises risk A volatile addition can increase total risk even if its correlation is low. Compare the complete mix before and after, including position size. Currency dominates Foreign assets can gain locally but lose value in your spending currency. Measure the result in the currency of the goal; review any hedge costs. Liquidity disappears A quoted value may not be available when you need to sell. Check dealing frequency, redemption terms and independent accessible cash. Rebalancing costs too much Fees, spreads and applicable taxes can erode the benefit. Use a considered review rule and account for costs. Qualitative risk scenarios, not forecasts or assigned probabilities. Framework informed by sources [2]–[6]. History shows that shares and government bonds can fall together. BIS authors documented the US stock–government-bond return correlation turning positive in mid-2021 as inflation became more influential. Their December 2023 analysis is historical evidence of a changing relationship, not a reading of today’s correlation. [6] What would change the proposed mix? Change the mix when its purpose or risk has changed. New spending needs, shorter time horizons, larger repeated exposures, changing asset relationships or higher implementation costs can all justify a review. A new holding should earn its place by improving the overall fit. The case for diversification is strongest when one outcome dominates your finances. If the existing portfolio already spreads risk well, adding another product may accomplish little. Review exposures first, then decide whether any change is needed. Author’s analysis and review framework, informed by MoneySense, SEC, FINRA and BIS. [2] [3] [4] [6] 08 / Evidence and scope Follow the explanation back to its sources. This is a concept report, not a market-timing call. Its original charts use disclosed fictional inputs. Market prices, FX rates, yields and forecast targets are not needed for this explanation and are not represented as live data. The creator’s written explanation also describes different paths and combining investments; its exact original publication date was not independently established. Neither source supplies the report’s invented data. MoneySense · Managing investment risk Page updated 19 Oct 2026. Checked 6 Nov 2026. Investor education, not a market dataset. entries.text: Gold buying and your return | XAU client brief Research Explained Dashboard XAU / GOLD · Q3 2026 IN BRIEF Central banks bought more. Gold prices still fell. Central-bank demand can support gold, while your return still depends on the market price, currency movements and costs. Three things to know Official buying increased. The World Gold Council estimated 321.2 tonnes of net buying in Q3 2026. Net buying means purchases less sales by central banks and other official institutions. [1] Some buyers remain unidentified. Public disclosures accounted for 120 tonnes within that total estimate. The estimates can be revised as more information arrives. [1] Your spending currency matters. For a holding without currency protection, gold’s USD price and the USD-to-SGD exchange rate both affect your SGD return. A stronger SGD can reduce or even erase a USD gold gain. The same quarter, two different directions Q3 versus Q2 2026 · percentage changes as published Measure Change Official gold demand [1] +8% Gold price, World Bank review [2] -5% Report interpretation Other investors also influence the price. Their selling and changes in market conditions can outweigh official buying. This comparison alone cannot show what caused the price move. Gold and official-sector demand; Q3 versus Q2 2026, changes in percent. Read each row separately; this is not a causal estimate. Full research and dated methodology Risks and your next step Gold can fall alongside other investments. Higher bond returns after inflation and a stronger US dollar can pressure gold prices. Physical gold pays no coupon, and dealing, fund or storage costs reduce returns. [3] Decide the purpose before buying. Consider how long you can hold gold, cash you may need in SGD, and the product’s costs and how it handles currency risk. Data date · Research cutoff 6 November 2026, 16:40 SGT. Q3 data cover July-September 2026. Historical data cutoff: 2026-11-06T16:40:00+08:00. Key sources · [1] WGC Q3 data / central banks (3 Nov 2026). [2] World Bank outlook (Oct 2026). entries.title: Historical Market Events | Chart-Ready Research Atlas
entries.text: Historical Market Events | Chart-Ready Research Atlas ← Research Explained · Market Intelligence Hub · Download the complete PDF Historical Market Events Contents Event tree Sources RESEARCH ATLAS • 05 NOVEMBER 2026 History belongs on the chart, not in an unstructured list Historical market events | A source-linked tree for rates, bonds, FX and portfolio context CENTRAL CONCLUSION Build one reusable event library, with a hierarchical tree for browsing and independent tags for filtering. Keep each dated milestone connected to its source and to an honest data frequency. The architecture is simple; the evidence discipline is the work. The architecture is simple; the evidence discipline is the work. Design recommendation. Counts describe this report’s selected starter catalogue, not the universe of historical crises. ONE LIBRARY 26 selected historical episodes MANY VIEWS Tree, period, region, asset and institution TRACEABLE CHARTS Evidence, units and date precision travel with each marker ONE LIBRARY 26 selected historical episodes MANY VIEWS Tree, period, region, asset and institution TRACEABLE CHARTS Evidence, units and date precision travel with each marker Design recommendation. Counts describe this report’s selected starter catalogue, not the universe of historical crises. Group by mechanism, not by headline alone. A primary folder helps navigation; it is not proof that an event had only one cause. Keep episodes and milestones separate. A multi-year crisis is not a one-day announcement. Use more than one time scale. Monthly averages explain context; daily observations expose abrupt moves. Show facts, interpretation and gaps separately. A marker beside a price move does not establish causation. Implement in stages. Start with verified records and source links before adding rankings, filters or portfolio simulations. Scope: selected episodes from 1929 to April 2025. This is a historical research and design report, not a current market bulletin, trading recommendation or deployed chart feature. No client information is used. Home Contents Report section 1 / 31 READER MAP Read the report in three passes Start with the tree, inspect the evidence, then use the implementation blueprint. A report that can become a maintainable feature A report that can become a maintainable feature Design map, not a delivery timetable. UNDERSTAND Pages 3–8: hierarchy, tagging and time COMPARE Pages 9–22: catalogue and worked cases IMPLEMENT Pages 23–27: chart rules, schema and controls UNDERSTAND Pages 3–8: hierarchy, tagging and time COMPARE Pages 9–22: catalogue and worked cases IMPLEMENT Pages 23–27: chart rules, schema and controls Design map, not a delivery timetable. Architecture and style 3–8 Verified historical catalogue 9–12 Comparisons and worked cases 13–22 Chart and implementation blueprint 23–27 Official source register 28–31 The report contains real historical observations, not invented market paths. Four monthly windows, one daily FX zoom and one policy-rate step chart illustrate the annotation method. Other diagrams describe mechanisms and are explicitly non-numerical. The companion files make the work reusable. The HTML is an offline, responsive reading version; the JSON is a research starter; the CSV retains source precision. They are not integrated into an existing website or connected to a live feed. EVIDENCE KEY REPORTED = source-backed historical statement. ANALYSIS = interpretation or design recommendation. MISSING = unavailable observation, never zero. A source link is evidence for the stated claim, not a blanket endorsement of everything written nearby. Home Contents Report section 2 / 31 01 • INFORMATION ARCHITECTURE Use five levels, but store each fact only once The tree is the route into the library, not the database itself. From broad grouping to a defensible chart marker From broad grouping to a defensible chart marker Illustrative hierarchy using a sourced milestone [S30]. Family and mechanism placement are editorial recommendations. 1 FAMILY Funding, leverage & liquidity 2 MECHANISM Margin calls and forced deleveraging 3 EPISODE UK gilt / LDI crisis, 2022 4 MILESTONE 28 September: temporary gilt purchases announced 5 ANNOTATION + EVIDENCE Chart marker, short explanation, exact source and date basis 1 FAMILY Funding, leverage & liquidity 2 MECHANISM Margin calls and forced deleveraging 3 EPISODE UK gilt / LDI crisis, 2022 4 MILESTONE 28 September: temporary gilt purchases announced 5 ANNOTATION + EVIDENCE Chart marker, short explanation, exact source and date basis Illustrative hierarchy using a sourced milestone [S30]. Family and mechanism placement are editorial recommendations. A level-five annotation should reference a milestone ID, not copy its facts. The same policy decision can appear on a gilt-yield chart and an FX chart, while its date and source remain maintained in one place. Correct the underlying record once and every linked view can update. One episode can contain different kinds of milestone. Trigger, market dislocation, institution failure, policy announcement, policy effective date and programme end are separate types. Do not force a “recovery” marker unless recovery is defined for a particular series and horizon. Sources: S30 . Design interpretation is this report’s recommendation. Home Contents Report section 3 / 31 02 • EVENT TREE, PART A Group financial stress by its dominant mechanism The six families are proposed navigation categories, not new colour assignments. Rates & monetary regimes Level 2: mechanism Level 3: historical episode Currency-regime changes ↳ End of dollar–gold convertibility (1971) ↳ Sterling leaves the ERM (1992) ↳ Swiss franc floor removal (2015) Monetary tightening and inflation ↳ Volcker operating-framework change (1979–1982) ↳ Fed tightening cycle (2022–2023) Policy communication and term repricing ↳ Taper tantrum (2013) Credit, banks & sovereign stress Level 2: mechanism Level 3: historical episode Bank runs and deposit confidence ↳ US banking panics (1930–1933) Asset–liability mismatch ↳ Savings and loan crisis (1980s–early 1990s) Foreign-currency debt and rollover stress ↳ Asian financial crisis (1997–1998) Housing losses and funding contagion ↳ Global financial crisis (2007–2009) Sovereign–bank feedback ↳ Euro-area sovereign stress (2010–2012) Duration exposure and concentrated deposits ↳ Silicon Valley Bank failure (2023) Confidence and bank funding ↳ Credit Suisse rescue (2023) WHY THE UK GILT EPISODE SITS HERE The fiscal announcement is a trigger; margin calls and forced deleveraging describe the amplification. Keep both in tags, but keep only one canonical episode record. Proposed classification. Detailed evidence and dated anchors follow in the catalogue. Family labels remain neutral; approved entity and asset colours retain their existing meanings. Browse the research tree Interactive report navigation only. No live prices or website integration. Rates & monetary regimes Currency-regime changes End of dollar–gold convertibility | 1971 Reported fact: The US suspended dollar convertibility into gold on 15 August 1971. Chart analysis: Separate the announcement from the wider transition away from Bretton Woods. Canonical ID: US-1971-GOLD · Date precision: day S03: official source Sterling leaves the ERM | 1992 Reported fact: The UK suspended sterling’s ERM membership on 16 September 1992. Chart analysis: A defended exchange-rate arrangement should not be treated as an unconditional floor. Canonical ID: GB-1992-ERM · Date precision: day S09: official source Swiss franc floor removal | 2015 Reported fact: The SNB discontinued its CHF 1.20 per euro minimum exchange rate on 15 January 2015. Chart analysis: The policy instrument was EUR/CHF; a USD/CHF chart measures a different cross. Canonical ID: CH-2015-SNB · Date precision: day S21: official source S22: official source Monetary tightening and inflation Volcker operating-framework change | 1979–1982 Reported fact: On 6 October 1979 the Fed changed operating procedures in its anti-inflation effort. Chart analysis: Mark the regime change separately from later interest-rate peaks or recession dates. Canonical ID: US-1979-VOLCKER · Date precision: day S05: official source Fed tightening cycle | 2022–2023 Reported fact: The Fed announced the first increase of this tightening sequence on 16 March 2022. Chart analysis: Keep announcement dates, effective dates and the plotted rate boundary explicit. Canonical ID: US-2022-HIKES · Date precision: day S28: official source S29: official source Policy communication and term repricing Taper tantrum | 2013 Reported fact: May 2013 testimony and subsequent June communication were interpreted as signalling future asset-purchase tapering. Chart analysis: Market expectations can move before the operational policy change. Canonical ID: US-2013-TAPER · Date precision: day S20: official source Credit, banks & sovereign stress Bank runs and deposit confidence US banking panics | 1930–1933 Reported fact: The national banking holiday began on 6 March 1933 amid the banking crisis. Chart analysis: Use a broad episode plus specific policy milestones; the holiday is not the start of the whole Depression. Canonical ID: US-1930-BANKS · Date precision: day S02: official source Asset–liability mismatch Savings and loan crisis | 1980s–early 1990s Reported fact: Savings institutions faced serious funding and asset-side vulnerabilities over a multi-year crisis. Chart analysis: Do not invent a 1 January trigger. Use sourced resolution milestones when expanding the catalogue. Canonical ID: US-1980-SL · Date precision: period S06: official source Foreign-currency debt and rollover stress Asian financial crisis | 1997–1998 Reported fact: Thailand changed the baht exchange-rate regime on 2 July 1997 as regional financial stress developed. Chart analysis: Study currency denomination, maturity mismatch and refinancing together. Canonical ID: ASIA-1997-AFC · Date precision: day S10: official source Housing losses and funding contagion Global financial crisis | 2007–2009 Reported fact: Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on 15 September 2008 during the wider financial crisis. Chart analysis: Separate institutional failures, emergency support and subsequent policy easing. Canonical ID: GLOBAL-2007-GFC · Date precision: day S16: official source S17: official source Sovereign–bank feedback Euro-area sovereign stress | 2010–2012 Reported fact: The ECB announced the technical features of conditional Outright Monetary Transactions on 6 September 2012. Chart analysis: An announced conditional backstop is not the same thing as a completed purchase programme. Canonical ID: EU-2010-DEBT · Date precision: day S19: official source Duration exposure and concentrated deposits Silicon Valley Bank failure | 2023 Reported fact: SVB failed on 10 March 2023; the Fed’s review describes management and supervisory weaknesses. Chart analysis: Analyse interest-rate exposure, liquidity and depositor concentration together. Canonical ID: US-2023-SVB · Date precision: day S31: official source Confidence and bank funding Credit Suisse rescue | 2023 Reported fact: The UBS takeover and SNB liquidity support were announced on 19 March 2023. Chart analysis: Keep the Sunday announcement distinct from the next trading session and later acquisition completion. Canonical ID: CH-2023-CS · Date precision: day S32: official source Funding, leverage & liquidity Leveraged convergence trades Russia shock and LTCM | 1998 Reported fact: A private-sector recapitalisation of LTCM was arranged on 23 September 1998 with New York Fed facilitation. Chart analysis: Forced liquidation can overwhelm apparently diversified positions; facilitation is not a Fed-funded bailout. Canonical ID: US-1998-LTCM · Date precision: day S11: official source Short-term funding scarcity US repo-market stress | 2019 Reported fact: Repo-market stress intensified on 17 September 2019 and the Fed intervened. Chart analysis: Money-market stress is not automatically a sovereign credit event. Canonical ID: US-2019-REPO · Date precision: day S25: official source Margin calls and forced deleveraging UK gilt / LDI crisis | September–October 2022 Reported fact: The UK fiscal statement on 23 September preceded severe gilt-market dysfunction. Chart analysis: The primary folder describes amplification through leverage, not an exclusive explanation of the trigger. Canonical ID: GB-2022-LDI · Date precision: day S30: official source Crowded funding trades and deleveraging August carry-trade unwind | August 2024 Reported fact: BIS identifies early-August turbulence and the 5 August peak, amplified by carry-trade unwinding. Chart analysis: Do not attribute every move to one trade or treat uncertain total positioning as measured fact. Canonical ID: GLOBAL-2024-CARRY · Date precision: day S33: official source Valuation & market structure Equity repricing and trading stress Wall Street crash | 1929 Reported fact: The late-October stock-market crash preceded the banking crises of the early 1930s. Chart analysis: Link related episodes, but do not collapse the crash and every later bank failure into one daily marker. Canonical ID: US-1929-CRASH · Date precision: day S01: official source Mechanical selling and market structure Black Monday | 1987 Reported fact: Black Monday occurred on 19 October 1987; the Fed issued a liquidity-support statement the next day. Chart analysis: Display the crash and response separately; a crash is not automatically a banking collapse. Canonical ID: US-1987-CRASH · Date precision: day S08: official source Valuation and earnings expectations Dot-com reversal | 2000–2002 Reported fact: Major US equity indexes reached peaks in March 2000 before the subsequent reversal discussed by the Fed. Chart analysis: Use source-appropriate month precision unless a chosen index’s exact peak is separately verified. Canonical ID: US-2000-DOTCOM · Date precision: month S12: official source Real-economy & external shocks Energy supply shocks Oil embargo and supply shock | 1973–1974 Reported fact: The October 1973 oil shock is a supply-side episode, not a single universal market-close event. Chart analysis: Pair commodity, inflation and activity charts; do not assume all asset prices respond in the same direction. Canonical ID: GLOBAL-1973-OIL · Date precision: month S04: official source Domestic economic adjustment Singapore recession | 1985 Reported fact: Singapore’s 1985 recession reflected external weakness and domestic structural pressures. Chart analysis: A year-level label is more honest than a fabricated daily market trigger. Canonical ID: SG-1985-RECESSION · Date precision: year S07: official source Operational and payment disruption September 11 disruption | 2001 Reported fact: The attacks disrupted financial operations and payment flows, prompting emergency liquidity support. Chart analysis: Distinguish exchange closures and operational liquidity from normal traded price observations. Canonical ID: US-2001-911 · Date precision: day S13: official source Public-health disruption SARS | 2003 Reported fact: WHO issued a global alert on 12 March 2003. Chart analysis: This alert is an annotation milestone, not the first infection or a universal start date for economic damage. Canonical ID: ASIA-2003-SARS · Date precision: day S14: official source S15: official source Public-health shock and demand for cash COVID-19 market crisis | 2020 Reported fact: The Fed announced a 0–0.25% target range on Sunday, 15 March 2020. Chart analysis: Separate the health shock, market dysfunction and policy actions inside the same episode. Canonical ID: GLOBAL-2020-COVID · Date precision: day S26: official source Fiscal, trade & political policy Trade-policy announcements April tariff shock | April 2025 Reported fact: The 2 April tariff announcements formed a major part of the IMF’s April 2025 risk assessment. Chart analysis: Policy-announcement, implementation and revision dates belong in separate milestones. Canonical ID: GLOBAL-2025-TARIFFS · Date precision: day S34: official source S35: official source Home Contents Report section 4 / 31 03 • EVENT TREE, PART B Separate forced liquidation from valuation repricing These branches focus on transmission: how a market disturbance becomes harder to absorb. Funding, leverage & liquidity Level 2: mechanism Level 3: historical episode Leveraged convergence trades ↳ Russia shock and LTCM (1998) Short-term funding scarcity ↳ US repo-market stress (2019) Margin calls and forced deleveraging ↳ UK gilt / LDI crisis (September–October 2022) Crowded funding trades and deleveraging ↳ August carry-trade unwind (August 2024) Valuation & market structure Level 2: mechanism Level 3: historical episode Equity repricing and trading stress ↳ Wall Street crash (1929) Mechanical selling and market structure ↳ Black Monday (1987) Valuation and earnings expectations ↳ Dot-com reversal (2000–2002) A price fall does not identify its own mechanism. A valuation reset can occur without a funding run. A financing constraint can force a sale even when an investor continues to believe the asset is worth more. The catalogue should make those questions visible rather than assign every episode a generic crash label. KEEP SECONDARY PATHS SEARCHABLE An episode placed under liquidity can still carry equity, FX, policy and regional tags. The primary path is an editorial route into the evidence, not an exclusion of other channels. Home Contents Report section 5 / 31 03 • EVENT TREE, PART C Keep external shocks and political policy visible A long list becomes useful when the branches answer different questions. Real-economy & external shocks Level 2: mechanism Level 3: historical episode Energy supply shocks ↳ Oil embargo and supply shock (1973–1974) Domestic economic adjustment ↳ Singapore recession (1985) Operational and payment disruption ↳ September 11 disruption (2001) Public-health disruption ↳ SARS (2003) Public-health shock and demand for cash ↳ COVID-19 market crisis (2020) Fiscal, trade & political policy Level 2: mechanism Level 3: historical episode Trade-policy announcements ↳ April tariff shock (April 2025) Link neighbouring episodes without merging them. The 1929 crash and the early-1930s banking panics are related but distinct records. Likewise, COVID-19 is a broad episode with a market-liquidity phase; it does not need a duplicate copy in every branch. Coverage should expand without breaking the IDs. Japan’s asset-price collapse, the 1994 bond sell-off, the 2010 flash crash and Brexit are sensible future additions, but are not presented as source-audited entries in this starter catalogue. PRACTICAL RULE Every episode has one primary path. Secondary mechanisms and related episodes are links or tags. A search result must deduplicate by the canonical episode ID, not by the visible title. Home Contents Report section 6 / 31 04 • COLOUR, TAGGING & TYPOGRAPHY Use the tree for browsing and tags for comparison One entity keeps one approved colour, even when it appears in several analytical views. Independent axis What it answers Example Region Where is the exposure or event? Singapore / US / Switzerland Person Who made the statement? Only a verified named person Institution Who acted? Federal Reserve / SNB / MAS Asset What instrument or currency? US Treasuries / USD/CHF Sector What activity is exposed? Banks / energy Company or ticker Which issuer or security? Resolve identity before tagging Macro indicator What is measured? Treasury yields / credit spreads Event What happened? Policy decision / liquidity stress Editorial status What is the evidence state? REPORTED / ANALYSIS / UNVERIFIED Follow the workbook’s actual matching order. Validate context first, choose the longest valid whole phrase, then use priority for a genuine equal-span conflict. Do not match “US” inside “USD” or “ Fed ” inside “FedEx”. Ambiguous aliases remain unresolved until the context establishes identity. Keep direction separate from identity. A bond term can remain Bonds Green while its price falls. A yield statistic uses Rates Blue rather than automatically inheriting the bond-instrument colour. Evidence uncertainty uses Status Gray, not a loss signal. FONT AND LAYOUT APPLICATION This report uses DejaVu Sans and DejaVu Sans Bold, matching the fonts embedded in the supplied visual guide. The guide requires readable hierarchy rather than prescribing a named family. The HTML uses a system fallback and 16px body text; PDF tables retain labels and units. Style authority: Market_Colour_Tag_Master_v1_2_Merged.xlsx; Colour_Tag_Visual_Design_Guide_v1_2_Merged.pdf, especially pages 6–8, 17 and 22–23. No new keyword-to-colour mappings are introduced. Home Contents Report section 7 / 31 05 • DATE AND EVIDENCE DISCIPLINE A historical event has more than one relevant date A precise-looking timestamp is not useful when it describes the wrong thing. Date field Meaning Example or rule Event / announcement When the development was announced or occurred Fed decision: 16 March 2022 Effective date When the operational change took effect Target range: 17 March 2022 Market observation When the displayed price or rate was observed H.10: New York noon, not session close Publication date When the source was released SVB review: 28 April 2023 Retrieval date When the source was checked for this report 5 November 2026 Date precision Day, month, year or broader period S&L crisis: multi-year episode Display / study window Chosen analytical period around an anchor 12 months before and after, where available Preserve local time and the trading calendar. Store an exact time and time zone only when supported. A Sunday announcement can influence Monday trading; after-close announcements can belong economically to the next session. Date-only records should remain date-only, not silently become midnight UTC. A monthly label is not an executable price at the start of the month. FRED’s monthly Treasury observations are averages. The month label should be displayed as a period, and an event-month band should not pretend to identify the announcement-day reaction. Do not shift an event to make the chart look more convincing Do not shift an event to make the chart look more convincing Reported policy dates [S28–S29]; observation rule is a design recommendation. ANNOUNCED 16 March 2022 EFFECTIVE 17 March 2022 OBSERVED Use the chosen market’s actual observation time ANNOUNCED 16 March 2022 EFFECTIVE 17 March 2022 OBSERVED Use the chosen market’s actual observation time Reported policy dates [S28–S29]; observation rule is a design recommendation. Sources: S23 , S28 , S29 , S31 , S36 . Home Contents Report section 23 / 31 18 • EVENT-STUDY METHOD Measure changes honestly before discussing causes A before/during/after panel should answer a defined question, not choose the most dramatic endpoints. Measure Calculation or rule Do not confuse it with Yield change (Ending yield % − starting yield %) × 100 = basis points Bond price return Price return (Ending price / starting price − 1) × 100 Total return including distributions Total return Use a valid total-return series or include cash-flow reinvestment explicitly A price-only line FX translation Write units first; invert the quote where necessary Symmetric percentage changes Study window Default context: 12 months before / after where available; add daily zoom A claim that the event caused the entire window Benchmark comparison Use aligned periods and define the comparator in advance A controlled causal estimate There is no single clean “event effect” in these descriptive charts. Expectations can change beforehand, other news arrives during the window, and policy responds to the same deterioration affecting prices. A descriptive overlay is valuable precisely when it makes these limitations visible rather than dressing them up as a model result. Do not fill a long data gap just to complete the picture. DGS10 does not provide a 1929 daily history. DGS30 was discontinued in February 2002 and reintroduced in February 2006. Missing observations should remain gaps, with an alternative series introduced only under a separate label and methodology. Point-in-time analysis needs point-in-time information. A historical backtest should use information available then, not revised macro data or an ex-post list of winning events. Forty sections connect equity valuation, AI earnings, the economy and fixed income to practical portfolio decisions, using selected facts from the J.P. Morgan Guide to the Markets, U.S. 4Q 2026.
