[14] 12:44 • Roughly 73 cents per $100 delinquent at regionals versus $8 in CMBS. Not comparable The 0.73% research figure is a mean across regional banks in the Sep 2024 table. CMBS is a different, balance-weighted loan universe and period. The difference cannot establish hidden loss equivalence. [9] [3] 13:17-14:23 • Floating-rate payoff cohort and 42% liquidation losses. Unresolved evidence gap The exact vendor cohort and loss-severity calculation were not independently substantiated. Even if correct for resolved loans, selection makes it unsuitable as a loss rate for all outstanding bank CRE. 15:02–15:26 • CMBS losses imply similar hidden regional-bank losses. THE REFINANCING TEST · 8 NOV 2026 12 / 16 12 / DEFINITIONS AND METHOD A report built to be checked Facts are sourced observations. Research findings are attributed. Causal interpretation and scenarios are explicitly the report's analysis. Definitions and analytical conventions Term Plain-English meaning CMBS Bonds backed by commercial mortgages. Loss allocation follows the security structure; loan trouble does not imply the same loss for every bond tranche. Delinquent / noncurrent A payment-status measure. Exact rules vary. Bank noncurrent generally means 90+ days past due or nonaccrual; Trepp's headline CMBS measure has a broader 30+ day and workout-status scope. Criticized / classified Supervisory or internal credit concern. Criticized is broader than the more adverse classified categories; neither is the same as a realised loss. NOI / DSCR / LTV Net operating income; income divided by debt service; loan balance divided by property value. Each measures a different part of repayment capacity. Provision / allowance / charge-off Expense for expected credit losses; the associated balance-sheet reserve; removal of an amount judged uncollectible. Timing differs and double-counting should be avoided. Basis point (bp) One hundredth of a percentage point. A yield moving from 4.19% to 4.86% rises 67bp. Read each technical term with its limited plain-language meaning. Definitions prevent mixing payment status, accounting recognition and realised losses. Three client talking points Coverage limits Results window: 11 Nov 09:03–13 Nov 09:03 SGT · Next 48h: through Sunday 15 Nov 09:03 SGT US Equities · AI infrastructure · Earnings · Credit and rates TODAY’S LEAD DEVELOPMENT Three AI earnings beats, three different market reactions Cisco, Applied Materials and Cerebras delivered encouraging results or guidance, while Nebius cut its revenue outlook despite beating quarterly estimates. The divergence shows that demand for AI is still strong, but commissioning delays, margins and financing are becoming decisive for share prices. entries.text: Own the Assets. Understand the Borrowing. | Full Research ← Market Intelligence / Research Sources Print / Save PDF New visual companion: charts & exact-value tables ↓ Added 4 November 2026 · original report retained MARKET INTELLIGENCE HUB / RESEARCH Own the Assets. Understand the Borrowing. Wealth, portfolios and disciplined carry Research note | 4 November 2026 | Core dataset: Q2 2026 U.S. Distributional Financial Accounts Prepared for the Market Intelligence Hub. Independent educational research, not an official bank publication or a personalised recommendation. The evidence supports a positive case for owning a portfolio and understanding secured financing, not a blanket instruction to borrow. Wealthy households own a disproportionate share of financial assets. Portfolio-backed credit is a well-established wealth-management tool. A carry trade can add value when its income and expected return adequately compensate for financing, market, currency and liquidity risks. These are three related propositions, but they are not interchangeable. [ 1 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] Central message: Build assets that can compound and produce income. Understand the liquidity those assets may support. Use borrowing selectively, at a size that allows the portfolio to survive stress. How to read this report The U.S. ownership figures below come from the five-page FRED snapshot dated 3 November 2026, cross-checked against the linked live table. Global family-office surveys, bank disclosures and product documentation provide separate evidence about borrowing. Algebra and interpretation are explicitly identified. Source figures retain their published precision; calculated additions and differences use those displayed figures. Rounded source data can produce totals of 99.9% or 100.1%. No client portfolio, current financing quote or expected return has been invented. [1] TOP 10% NET WORTH 68.9% U.S. households · Q2 2026 TOP 10% EQUITY / FUND CATEGORY 88.1% Category caveats in section 2 SURVEYED LOMBARD USERS 75% Includes rare use · DB 2025 Derived from the displayed shares in source 1 and survey categories in source 4. These are different populations and measures. Five key takeaways Ownership is concentrated. The top 10% held 68.9% of U.S. household net worth in Q2 2026. See the wealth chart . Financial assets matter. The same group held 88.1% of the broad equity-and-fund category, not 88.1% of its own portfolio. Compare asset ownership . Borrowing is a choice. Family-office surveys establish use of secured credit, not a rule that every wealthy household should borrow. See the survey chart . Positive carry is not total profit. Asset-price losses, FX changes and fees can outweigh coupon income after interest. Follow the calculation . Portfolio first, financing second. Keep stressed collateral headroom and a credible repayment route. Use the decision framework . Two five-slide presentations Summaries of the public wealth and Sharpe research. Historical ownership figures and invented teaching examples are labelled separately. Observed wealth patterns do not establish that borrowing causes wealth. Financial briefing (PowerPoint, 42 KB) Clear visual story (PowerPoint, 50 KB) Prepared 5 November 2026. Every slide includes formatted speaker notes and source references. Diagrams, charts and tables are editable. Educational research, not personal investment advice. Inside the research 01 The ownership evidence: financial wealth is highly concentrated 02 What the wealthy own: shares, debt securities and liquidity 03 Debt is not one thing: distinguish what households own from what they owe 04 Direct evidence: wealthy families do use portfolio-backed borrowing 05 Why a portfolio matters even before leverage 06 Secured lending, investment leverage and FX carry are different decisions 07 The carry arithmetic: cash income is not total return 08 Margin of safety: borrowing capacity is not a borrowing target 09 CHF, USD and carry: keep the currency risks separate 10 The Singapore application: portfolio first, financing second 11 The macro implication: asset prices and financing can reinforce each other 12 Research library: what the papers actually contribute 13 Related reporting: the market is expanding, but headlines need denominators 14 Practical framework: turn fear into a financing plan 15 Data audit and limitations 16 Sources and direct reading links 1. The ownership evidence: financial wealth is highly concentrated The wealthiest 10% held 68.9% of total U.S. household net worth in Q2 2026, while the bottom half held 2.3%. The top 1% alone held 32.5%, up from 31.1% one year earlier. The next 9% held 36.4%, unchanged at the displayed precision. The middle 40% saw its share fall from 30.1% to 28.8%. These are shares of net wealth, not income, spending or the number of people who invest. [ 1 , PDF p. 5] Wide table: scroll sideways to compare all columns. Household wealth group Q2 2025 Q1 2026 Q2 2026 Annual change Top 1% 31.1% 31.7% 32.5% +1.4 percentage points Next 9% 36.4% 36.4% 36.4% 0.0 percentage points Middle 40% 30.1% 29.5% 28.8% −1.3 percentage points Bottom 50% 2.4% 2.4% 2.3% −0.1 percentage points Top 10%, calculated 67.5% 68.1% 68.9% +1.4 percentage points Calculation: Top 10% share = 32.5% + 36.4% = 68.9%. Top 1% annual change = 32.5% − 31.1% = 1.4 percentage points. The top 10% row overlaps with the first two rows and must not be added to them. [ 1 ; author arithmetic] Wealth concentration increased over the year Q2 2025 Q2 2026 Top 1% Q2 2025: 31.1% Q2 2026: 32.5% Next 9% Q2 2025: 36.4% Q2 2026: 36.4% Middle 40% Q2 2025: 30.1% Q2 2026: 28.8% Bottom 50% Q2 2025: 2.4% Q2 2026: 2.3% 0 20 40% Share of total U.S. household net worth (%) Source 1. Categories are mutually exclusive. Top 1% rose 1.4 percentage points; a falling share does not necessarily mean falling dollar wealth. Read source 1 . Even within the top 1%, ownership is concentrated. The top 0.1% held 15.0% of net worth, compared with 14.1% a year earlier. This is a subgroup of the top 1%, not an additional group. A falling share does not, by itself, mean falling dollar wealth: the denominator may be growing faster than the group's holdings. [ 1 , PDF p. 5; interpretation] Layman story: Imagine dividing all net household wealth into 100 units. The wealthiest tenth receives 68.9 units, the next four-tenths receives 28.8, and the bottom half shares 2.3. The lesson is not that everyone can become wealthy by copying one trade. It is that participation in asset ownership is economically important. Takeaway: The portfolio discussion belongs at the centre of wealth planning, not at the edge of a deposit discussion. Section sources: [ 1 , 2 ] 2. What the wealthy own: shares, debt securities and liquidity The top 10% held 88.1% of the DFA category “corporate equities and mutual fund shares” and 79.3% of the displayed debt-securities category. Their ownership of financial assets was more concentrated than their ownership of real estate. This supports the argument that substantial wealth is associated with a financial portfolio, rather than property or cash alone. It does not reveal the ideal allocation for an individual investor. [ 1 , PDF pp. 1–3] Wide table: scroll sideways to compare all columns. Share of the specified household asset category Top 1% Next 9% Top 10%, calculated Middle 40% Bottom 50% Financial assets 36.5% 37.3% 73.8% 24.0% 2.2% Corporate equities and mutual fund shares 50.9% 37.2% 88.1% 11.4% 0.6% Debt securities 38.6% 40.7% 79.3% 20.2% 0.6% Money-market fund shares 38.3% 40.6% 78.9% 20.0% 1.1% Deposits 23.4% 35.3% 58.7% 35.8% 5.5% Real estate 13.4% 30.3% 43.7% 46.6% 9.7% Defined-contribution pension entitlements 11.6% 43.3% 54.9% 39.7% 5.3% Calculation: 50.9% + 37.2% = 88.1%; 38.6% + 40.7% = 79.3%; 23.4% + 35.3% = 58.7%. These are ownership shares within each category, not portfolio allocation percentages. “The top 1% owns 50.9% of this category” does not mean “50.9% of the top 1%'s portfolio is invested in it.” [ 1 ; author arithmetic] Ownership and consumer debt have very different distributions Wealthiest 10% Bottom 50% Corporate equities & mutual funds* Wealthiest 10%: 88.1% Bottom 50%: 0.6% Debt securities Wealthiest 10%: 79.3% Bottom 50%: 0.6% Financial assets Wealthiest 10%: 73.8% Bottom 50%: 2.2% Deposits Wealthiest 10%: 58.7% Bottom 50%: 5.5% Real estate Wealthiest 10%: 43.7% Bottom 50%: 9.7% Consumer credit owed Wealthiest 10%: 13.5% Bottom 50%: 51.6% 0 50 100% Share of the specified household asset or liability category (%) Source 1. Q2 2026. Top 10% calculated from the top 1% plus next 9%. *Broad category includes holdings described in section 2. Consumer credit is a liability, not an asset. Read source 1 . The equity label needs care. The Federal Reserve's 18 September 2026 announcement says hedge-fund and private-debt-fund holdings remain inside the DFA corporate-equities-and-mutual-funds category, although the aggregate household accounts now identify them separately. Corporate equities also cover publicly traded and privately held corporations. Pension entitlements appear separately. Consequently, 88.1% is not a clean measure of the top 10%'s ownership of all listed U.S. stocks, nor a measure including every household's indirect pension exposure. [3] The bond evidence is narrower than the everyday word “bonds.” The supplied table displays 79.3% for the top 10%'s debt-securities share, but the corporate-and-foreign-bonds rows are missing, shown as dots. Those dots are not zeros. Do not claim this file independently proves the same percentage for every corporate bond or every bond held through funds. [ 1 , PDF p. 2] Layman story: One household owns its home and bank deposits. Another also owns interests in companies, lending instruments and funds. The second household has more routes through which business profits, interest payments and asset revaluations can affect its wealth. Those routes can generate gains or losses. Takeaway: The defensible message is “own an appropriate mix of assets,” not “put everything into the asset class that rich people dominate.” Section sources: [ 1 , 3 , 8 ] 3. Debt is not one thing: distinguish what households own from what they owe The top 10% held 64.8% of household assets but 26.7% of household liabilities. The bottom 50% held 5.0% of assets and owed 29.5% of liabilities. This does not calculate either group's loan-to-value ratio, because total assets and total liabilities have different dollar denominators. It does show why the type and size of a balance sheet matter more than the mere presence of debt. [ 1 , PDF pp. 1, 4] Wide table: scroll sideways to compare all columns. Share of the specified category Top 1% Next 9% Top 10%, calculated Bottom 50% Total assets 29.9% 34.9% 64.8% 5.0% Total liabilities 5.9% 20.8% 26.7% 29.5% Home mortgages owed 4.0% 24.4% 28.4% 22.6% Consumer credit owed 3.2% 10.3% 13.5% 51.6% Other loans and advances owed 43.5% 32.8% 76.3% 6.8% The table does not identify a clean “carry-trade borrowing” category. The top 1%'s 43.5% share of other loans and advances is not equivalent to a 43.5% share of Lombard loans. These broad balance-sheet rows do not identify each loan's collateral, funding currency, investment purpose, term or interest rate. They cannot establish how many households borrow to buy bonds. [ 1 ; scope limitation] A particularly easy error is to confuse mortgage assets with mortgage liabilities. On page 3, the top 1%'s 49.4% share of mortgages appears under loans owned as assets. On page 4, its share of home mortgages owed is 4.0%. One is a claim on a borrower; the other is a debt obligation. Reversing them would reverse the economic story. [ 1 , PDF pp. 3–4] Layman story: Owning a mortgage claim resembles being the lender collecting payments; owing a mortgage means being the borrower making them. Both use the word “mortgage,” but they sit on opposite sides of the balance sheet. Takeaway: Productive assets and manageable financing can coexist. The FRED data does not support the claim that maximum borrowing is how the wealthy became wealthy. Section source: [1] 4. Direct evidence: wealthy families do use portfolio-backed borrowing Deutsche Bank's 2025 survey provides direct evidence of Lombard-loan use. Among 209 family offices surveyed from 9 May to 14 July 2025, the reported usage distribution was: [ 4 , printed pp. 4, 27] Wide table: scroll sideways to compare all columns. Lombard-loan use Respondents Extensive 7% Frequent, with low loan-to-value 12% Frequent, focused on leveraged returns 5% Opportunistic 30% Rare 21% None 25% Adding the categories gives 75% reporting some use, including rare use, and 54% reporting opportunistic or more frequent/extensive use. That supports “a recognised tool among surveyed family offices,” not “75% of all wealthy people run currency carry trades.” It is a selected global survey, not a population census. [ 4 ; author arithmetic] Lombard borrowing is a recognised tool, not a universal rule Survey respondents Extensive use Survey respondents: 7% Frequent, low loan-to-value Survey respondents: 12% Frequent, leveraged-return focus Survey respondents: 5% Opportunistic use Survey respondents: 30% Rare use Survey respondents: 21% No use Survey respondents: 25% 0 17.5 35% Share of surveyed family offices (%) Source 4. Deutsche Bank 2025 survey of 209 family offices. Some use: 75%, including rare use. Selected sample, not all wealthy households. Read source 4 . Another major survey shows why the universal claim would be too strong. Citi's 2025 report, based on 346 respondents from 45 countries, records 50% using no leverage and 25% using less than 10%. The questions and samples differ from Deutsche Bank's, including its distinction between current leverage and frequency of facility use. The results must not be averaged into one adoption estimate. [ 5 , printed pp. 4, 49] Lender disclosures confirm that this is a substantial business, not a theoretical product. Julius Baer reported CHF 33.8 billion of Lombard loans at end-2025, separately from CHF 8.3 billion of mortgages. A loan-book total demonstrates scale at that bank; it does not disclose how many wealthy people borrow or what proportion invest the proceeds. [9] Layman story: Many experienced drivers use a gearbox; others do not need every gear on every journey. Knowing how to use financing is valuable. Keeping financing permanently engaged is not the definition of sophistication. Takeaway: Your strongest supported statement is that secured borrowing is an established part of sophisticated wealth management, used selectively rather than universally. Section sources: [ 4 , 5 , 9 ] 5. Why a portfolio matters even before leverage A portfolio can serve several distinct functions: participation in growth, contractual or discretionary cash income, diversification and potential collateral. These functions should be designed together, but not confused. Shares can participate in business profits; bonds provide contractual claims subject to their terms and issuer performance; selected investments may be accepted as collateral. Neither distributions nor collateral eligibility guarantee a positive total return. [ 6 , 7 , 20 , 21 ] Wide table: scroll sideways to compare all columns. Portfolio function Potential benefit Essential distinction Ownership Exposure to profits and long-term capital growth Market prices and business outcomes remain uncertain Income Coupons, dividends or distributions Cash distributions alone do not measure total return; changes in NAV and costs also matter Diversification Less dependence on one business, property or market Correlations can rise during stress Collateral Access to financing without an immediate asset sale Lending value is below market value and can change Optionality More choices about spending, rebalancing and timing A credit line is not equivalent to unencumbered cash Research supports the importance of portfolio composition, but not a simple causal promise. Richmond Fed analysis describes greater stock and business-equity exposure among wealthier households, compared with the central role of housing further down the distribution. Dallas Fed research links pandemic-period wealth-share movements to differing portfolios and asset prices. These findings support understanding the assets one owns; they do not show that buying shares or borrowing automatically produces wealth. [ 8 , 10 ] Wealth accumulation also reflects earnings, business creation, inheritance and unequal opportunities. A Cleveland Fed working paper identifies large earnings differences as a primary driver in its model, with bequests and return differences also important at the top. An IMF paper using Norwegian administrative data finds persistent return differences associated with wealth, risk, scale and other characteristics. These are not estimates of the return a new leveraged investor will earn. [ 11 , 12 ] Layman story: A salary is money earned through current work. A financial portfolio is a set of claims on assets and cash flows that can continue beyond that work. The aim is to build a second source of financial capacity, not to replace one uncertainty with an oversized bet. Takeaway: The case for owning assets is stronger and more general than the case for borrowing to own more of them. Section sources: [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 20 , 21 ] 6. Secured lending, investment leverage and FX carry are different decisions Secured lending describes the collateral; carry describes the economics of holding a position. A wealthy client borrowing against shares to meet a temporary liquidity need is not necessarily executing a carry trade. A loan used to buy additional assets creates investment leverage. Borrowing in one currency to hold assets in another adds a separate currency position. [ 6 , 7 , 13 , 14 ] Wide table: scroll sideways to compare all columns. Structure What it does Main issue to examine Unleveraged portfolio Buys investments with own capital Asset selection, valuation and risk capacity Portfolio-backed liquidity loan Raises cash while retaining pledged investments Repayment source, collateral stability and permitted use Same-currency investment financing Borrows to buy additional assets in the funding currency Asset return versus all-in loan cost, duration and margin risk Cross-currency carry Funds assets using a different currency All of the above plus FX changes and hedge costs Avoiding a sale can be economically useful when there is a credible repayment plan. A loan may bridge a timing mismatch, preserve an investment position or allow a different asset to be bought without first liquidating existing holdings. However, borrowing to finance ongoing consumption creates an interest obligation without necessarily adding an earning asset. Preserving a portfolio is not, by itself, proof that the loan is worthwhile. [ 6 , 13 ; interpretation] Facility rules are jurisdiction- and contract-specific. U.S. securities-backed lines of credit described by the SEC and FINRA are non-purpose loans that cannot be used to purchase or trade securities. By contrast, OCBC's Singapore wealth-financing page and UBS Singapore's Lombard guidance expressly describe investment uses. Do not transfer the rules of one product to another. [ 6 , 7 , 13 ] Layman story: Borrowing against a shop to cover a short payment gap is different from borrowing to buy a second shop. Funding either loan in a currency the shop does not earn creates another decision. The same collateral does not make all three plans equally sensible. Takeaway: Start with “What job must this loan perform?” before asking “What is the cheapest borrowing currency?” Section sources: [ 6 , 7 , 13 , 14 ] 7. The carry arithmetic: cash income is not total return Positive cash carry means income exceeds financing costs over the measured period, not that the overall investment has made money. A bond can pay its coupon while its market price declines. A fund can make distributions while its net asset value falls. A discounted bond's yield to maturity is not the same as the coupon cash available to pay a loan today. [ 21 ; financial identities] General identities, not a client simulation For unchanged principal in one currency, define own capital E, loan principal L, gross assets A = E + L, asset total return r_A, borrowing return-cost r_L and fees F, all over the same period. There are no intermediate external capital flows in this identity. Economic profit = A × r_A − L × r_L − F. Return on own capital = r_A + (L/E) × (r_A − r_L) − F/E. This algebra shows that leverage amplifies the difference between the asset's realised return and the financing cost. If that difference is negative, borrowing worsens the result. The identity does not supply a forecast for r_A. Cash income after financing = cash received − interest paid − relevant cash fees. Principal repayment is a cash outflow that reduces debt; it is not an additional investment loss. Loan proceeds are not income. Asset appreciation is not cash until monetised. Accrued costs must still be recognised when measuring economic performance. An actual bank's published illustration OCBC's public page illustrates how financing can raise net coupon income, and how a higher funding cost erodes that gain. The following reproduces its hypothetical dollar amounts, not live rates or an offered client structure. The page uses “$”; this report does not assign an unstated currency. [7] Wide table: scroll sideways to compare all columns. Published illustration No financing Financing at 2.50% Financing at 4.50% Own capital $750,000 $750,000 $750,000 Gross investment amount $750,000 $2,500,000 $2,500,000 Loan principal, calculated $0 $1,750,000 $1,750,000 Annual coupon cash $37,500 $125,000 $125,000 Annual loan interest $0 $43,750 $78,750 Net annual coupon cash $37,500 $81,250 $46,250 Increment over unfinanced coupon $0 $43,750 $8,750 Exact workings: $2,500,000 − $750,000 = $1,750,000. $1,750,000 × 2.50% = $43,750. $125,000 − $43,750 = $81,250. At 4.50%, interest is $78,750 and net coupon is $46,250. A 2-percentage-point increase in funding cost reduces net annual coupon by $35,000. [ 7 ; author arithmetic] These are coupon calculations, not total-return forecasts. No price loss, FX loss, tax or additional fee adjustment is included in the displayed arithmetic. The example uses the maximum borrowing supported by a 70% advance ratio; that is a mechanical illustration of capacity, not a suggested operating target. No rounded equity-return percentages are substituted for the exact cash figures. Layman story: A shop earns rent, and its owner pays loan interest. The difference can be positive even if the shop's resale value falls. An investor must monitor both the rental-style income ledger and the balance-sheet ledger. Takeaway: A carry strategy needs positive economics and the ability to stay funded. Income alone cannot answer both questions. Section sources: [ 7 , 21 ] ; formulas and differences are author derivations. 8. Margin of safety: borrowing capacity is not a borrowing target A collateral-backed loan is safer for the lender than an otherwise comparable unsecured exposure; it is not a guarantee of safety for the borrower. The lender's right to demand repayment or sell collateral can conflict with the investor's intended holding period. A sound asset held with fragile funding can still become a bad realised outcome. [ 6 , 13 , 22 ] The collateral ledger In a simplified single-currency structure, let a be the permitted advance ratio and V the collateral's market value. Lending value = a × V. Actual LTV = L/V. Headroom = a × V − L. Advance ratio, also called an allowed financing or lending ratio in some products, is a limit. Actual LTV is the borrowing already used relative to current collateral value. A haircut h corresponds to a = 1 − h in this simplified framework. Product names and calculation rules differ by lender. For a portfolio, calculate each asset separately: lending value = sum of a_i × V_i. Compare this with all relevant credit usage, including any contract-specific liability adjustments, accrued interest, derivative obligations and currency conversion. One high-quality bond does not make every pledged position equally financeable. The OCBC maximum-capacity illustration has no initial headroom under this simplified test: 70% × $2,500,000 − $1,750,000 = $0. A decline in collateral value or a cut in advance ratio creates a shortfall unless cash or additional collateral is available. This is why the maximum is not the same as a prudent target. [ 7 ; author arithmetic] Wide table: scroll sideways to compare all columns. Joint stress What changes What must be tested Asset prices fall Market value declines Headroom after repricing Lender reduces advance ratios Less lending value per dollar of assets Shortfall even without further market losses Funding currency strengthens Debt rises in the reporting currency FX-adjusted principal and interest Loan rate resets higher More cash required for interest Coverage from sustainable income and reserves Collateral becomes less liquid Sale proceeds or timing worsen Ability to repay without relying on a quick sale Facility is reduced or not renewed Funding is withdrawn A credible alternative repayment route Independent liquidity is more reliable than unused capacity against the same falling assets. Cash or other readily available resources outside the stressed collateral pool can meet calls without simultaneously reducing the pool's lending value. An undrawn, uncommitted line may be reduced when it is most needed. [ 6 , 13 ; interpretation] Layman story: A bridge's maximum load is not an invitation to park at its limit during a storm. The purpose of unused capacity is to absorb movement, not to make a spreadsheet look inefficient. Takeaway: Confidence should come from quantified headroom and repayment capacity, not from the word “secured.” Section sources: [ 6 , 7 , 13 , 22 ] ; equations are simplified author derivations, not a bank's proprietary margin model. 9. CHF, USD and carry: keep the currency risks separate Borrowing cheaply in CHF to hold USD assets is both an investment decision and a currency decision. A USD asset can perform as expected while a stronger CHF increases the USD cost of repaying the loan. A Singapore investor then has a further reporting question: what is the resulting wealth worth in SGD? The currencies must be tracked separately rather than buried in one “net yield.” [ 14 , 15 , 22 ] For a one-period position with unchanged CHF principal, let A_0 and A_1 be USD asset values excluding distributed cash, C be USD cash distributions, L_CHF be loan principal, and q be USD per CHF. Convert interest at the exchange rate applicable when paid. USD profit = (A_1 − A_0) + C − L_CHF × (q_1 − q_0) − USD interest cost − fees. If CHF strengthens against USD, q_1 is higher than q_0 and the loan-principal translation term reduces profit. The formula deliberately does not subtract the full loan principal as a new expense: principal already exists on the opening balance sheet. It assumes no changes in loan principal or other external capital flows. A full FX hedge is not a way to retain the entire quoted interest differential for free. Forward exchange rates reflect interest-rate differences; cross-currency basis, bid-offer costs, tenor and bank spreads affect the actual hedged funding cost. The relevant comparison is the quoted all-in hedged cost for the matching period, not the CHF interest rate in isolation. [ 15 ] History makes this distinction concrete. On 15 January 2015 the SNB ended its minimum exchange rate of CHF 1.20 per euro. In August 2024, BIS analysis documented how unwinding leveraged equity and FX positions, including yen-funded carry, amplified a market shock. Neither event proves that every carry position is inappropriate. Both show why funding-currency appreciation and collateral stress must be tested together. [ 14 , 16 ] Layman story: Receiving income in one currency while owing another is like running a shop whose supplier can reprice the debt in a different unit. The shop can trade well and still face a larger repayment bill. Takeaway: A lower nominal loan rate is a starting input, not the final measure of cheaper financing. Section sources: [ 14 , 15 , 16 , 22 ] ; the profit identity is an author derivation. 10. The Singapore application: portfolio first, financing second Portfolio-backed financing is an established Singapore wealth-management service. OCBC lists bonds, shares, unit trusts and other approved assets among eligible collateral, describes interest-only tenors of up to six months with principal auto-rollover, and lists multiple drawdown currencies. Those public features are not a guarantee of renewal, a client-specific advance ratio or a current financing quote. [7] The sensible sequence is to choose a portfolio that works without leverage, then test whether financing improves the plan. Start with liabilities, liquidity needs and investment horizon. Next select the asset mix and investment amounts. Only then compare funding currencies, total borrowing costs, collateral terms and stress outcomes. This is an analytical framework, not a fixed recommended allocation. [ 6 , 22 ; interpretation] The U.S. tax story should not be imported unchanged. IRAS says gains from selling shares and financial instruments held as personal investments are generally not taxable in Singapore. Trading or business circumstances and other tax jurisdictions may change the result. A Singapore client therefore should not assume that U.S. “borrow rather than sell” tax arguments create the same benefit for them. [ 17 ] Wide table: scroll sideways to compare all columns. Decision Better question Asset ownership Does this portfolio fit future spending and loss capacity? Income How much sustainable cash is actually available, and when? Borrowing purpose Is this temporary liquidity, added investment exposure or both? Currency What would a stronger funding currency do to net wealth and margin? Loan size What remains after prices, advance ratios and funding costs deteriorate together? Exit Which independent resources repay the loan if markets or renewal terms disappoint? Layman story: Owning a home does not require borrowing against every available dollar of equity. A securities portfolio deserves the same discipline: useful assets first, suitable borrowing second. Takeaway: Do not be afraid of a portfolio merely because prices fluctuate. Do not add leverage merely because the bank offers it. Section sources: [ 6 , 7 , 17 , 22 ] 11. The macro implication: asset prices and financing can reinforce each other The distribution helps explain why strong markets and household financial pressure can coexist. Ownership of financial assets and consumer debt are distributed very differently. Rising equity valuations therefore need not improve every household's finances equally. Equally, the table does not provide a direct estimate of consumption growth or the spending response of each group. [ 1 , 10 ] A potential feedback loop is visible when asset ownership is combined with collateralised lending. Higher market values can raise lending capacity, which may enable further investment. In reverse, falling values and tighter advance ratios can reduce that capacity together. This is an analytical mechanism, not a claim that the FRED table measures how much current market activity is financed this way. BIS research documents the amplifying role of leverage and margin adjustments in market stress. [ 14 ; interpretation] For an investor, this changes the monitoring dashboard. A market view should sit beside a funding view: asset valuations, issuer quality and concentration on one side; actual borrowing, loan resets, currency mismatches and available liquidity on the other. An attractive long-run investment thesis does not remove the need for short-run financing resilience. [ 6 , 14 , 22 ; interpretation] Layman story: When the value of a building rises, its owner may be able to refinance. When values fall across a whole district and lenders become cautious, refinancing can become harder precisely when cash is needed. Securities-backed lending can follow the same direction of pressure, often at a faster pace. Takeaway: The portfolio should be built to benefit from ownership without relying on permanently rising collateral values. Section sources: [ 1 , 6 , 10 , 14 , 22 ] 12. Research library: what the papers actually contribute The strongest research case combines measurement, portfolio behaviour and financing risk rather than looking for one paper that endorses leverage. The following primary-source reading list separates research findings from bank surveys and product descriptions. Working papers express their authors' analysis; they are not central-bank investment recommendations. Wide table: scroll sideways to compare all columns. Paper or report Date and type Contribution to this report Introducing the Distributional Financial Accounts of the United States Federal Reserve, March 2019; methodology paper Explains how survey distributions are combined with aggregate balance sheets. Essential for understanding what the FRED figures can establish. [ 18 ] Portfolios Across the U.S. Wealth Distribution Richmond Fed, November 2023; research brief Documents how housing, stocks and business equity differ across household wealth groups. Supports the portfolio-composition argument, not a universal leverage rule. [8] Wealth Inequality and Return Heterogeneity During the COVID-19 Pandemic Dallas Fed Working Paper 2114, posted 10 November 2021; PDF dated October 2021 Identifies portfolio composition and asset-price movements as key influences in that episode. The finding is period-specific. [ 10 ] Heterogeneity and Persistence in Returns to Wealth IMF WP/18/171, 27 July 2018; empirical working paper Uses twelve years of Norwegian administrative data to study persistent return differences and their association with wealth. Not a forecast for U.S. or Singapore investors. [ 12 ] Accounting for Wealth Concentration in the United States Cleveland Fed WP 22-28, 20 October 2022 Highlights earnings differences, with bequests and heterogeneous returns also contributing. An important counterweight to an overly simple “leverage creates wealth” narrative. [ 11 ] Capital Management and Wealth Inequality New York Fed Staff Report 1072, September 2023; revised January 2024 Models how incentives and scale in capital management can generate concentrated ownership. Theoretical mechanism, not an observed carry-trade adoption rate. [ 19 ] The market turbulence and carry trade unwind of August 2024 BIS Bulletin 90, 27 August 2024 Explains how leverage, margin adjustments and currency positions amplified a market disturbance. Useful for joint stress design. [ 14 ] Covered interest parity lost: understanding the cross-currency basis BIS Quarterly Review, September 2016 Explains why FX hedging and cross-currency funding must be priced using more than two headline interest rates. [ 15 ] Family Office Financing Report 2025 Deutsche Bank; bank-sponsored survey Provides directly relevant reported Lombard usage, with a selected sample of 209 family offices. [4] Global Family Office Report 2025 Citi; bank-sponsored survey Shows substantial unleveraged participation among 346 respondents, demonstrating that there is no single wealthy-investor borrowing model. [5] Reading order: Begin with the DFA methodology and Richmond Fed portfolio brief, then read the family-office surveys, then the BIS financing papers. This moves from what is owned, to how financing is used, to what can destabilise it. Takeaway: Evidence supports understanding and disciplined use of leverage. It does not turn leverage into a prerequisite for wealth. Section sources: [ 4 , 5 , 8 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 14 , 15 , 18 , 19 ] 13. Related reporting: the market is expanding, but headlines need denominators News reports are useful context, not a substitute for the ownership data or loan contract. The following items are dated explicitly; older reporting is included for background rather than presented as this week's news. 27 October 2026 SGT: securities-backed lending reaches a wider client base The Wall Street Journal reported a Deloitte estimate of $5.4 trillion in securities-based credit extended, versus roughly $1.6 trillion actually borrowed. The distinction matters: credit availability is not drawn debt. These are third-party estimates reported by the Journal, not a verified count of wealthy households using carry. [ 23 ] 30 July 2026: borrowing instead of selling investments Barron's described wealthy clients using appreciated assets to fund liquidity needs without selling. The relevance is retained ownership and flexible financing, not proof that borrowing is always cheaper after tax or suitable for a Singapore investor. [ 24 ] 10 September 2025: wealth lending becomes a strategic banking priority Reuters reported that Merrill was creating a team to expand credit for wealthy clients. Reported purposes included liquidity, taxes, purchases and maintaining investments. The variety of uses is precisely why wealth lending should not be equated with currency carry. [ 25 ] Interpretation: The coverage supports the proposition that wealth financing is mainstream and commercially important. It also highlights a bank incentive: lending earns revenue while allowing client assets to remain invested. That makes a separate client-benefit test important, rather than treating availability as endorsement. [ 23 , 25 ] Takeaway: “Banks do a lot of this” is evidence of an established product, not proof that every offered loan is a good investment decision. Section sources: [ 23 , 24 , 25 ] 14. Practical framework: turn fear into a financing plan The objective is not to eliminate risk, but to select risks that the household can understand and carry through adverse conditions. A conservative unleveraged portfolio can be appropriate. A modest secured facility can also be appropriate. The decision depends on the client's overall finances, purpose, currency exposure and ability to meet obligations, not merely their wealth percentile. [ 6 , 13 , 22 ; analytical framework] Wide table: scroll sideways to compare all columns. Test Evidence needed before borrowing Warning sign Portfolio quality Understood assets, issuer exposures, valuation and diversification The asset is attractive only because it supports a large loan Cash servicing Actual coupon/dividend schedule, interest dates and independent cash resources Dependence on capital gains to pay routine interest Economic return All-in financing, fees, hedging costs and realistic asset analysis Quoting yield-to-maturity minus a promotional loan rate as guaranteed profit Collateral resilience Current and stressed advance ratios, concentration limits and currency-adjusted usage Borrowing at maximum capacity with no outside liquidity Funding continuity Renewal, repricing, commitment and repayment provisions Assuming auto-rollover is permanent guaranteed funding Exit capacity Specific assets or external cash that can repay the loan The only plan is to wait for markets to recover A useful portfolio-financing dashboard needs four separate views. First, asset value and investment performance; second, cash income and cash expenses; third, loan principal and FX translation; fourth, lending value and margin headroom. Keeping them separate prevents coupons being mistaken for profit, loan principal being subtracted twice, or a positive income spread disguising a collateral shortfall. For client communication, lead with ownership and choice rather than prestige. “Wealthy people use this” can explain why a tool deserves consideration. It is not a suitability test. The more persuasive explanation is what the tool accomplishes for this client and how the plan survives a bad outcome. Final layman story A family has spent years building a set of income-producing assets. When a temporary opportunity or expense appears, it need not automatically sell those assets. A well-structured loan may preserve ownership and create flexibility. But the family still needs enough cash, collateral headroom and time to repay without being forced to sell during a downturn. Another family can build the same habit of asset ownership without borrowing at all. Both approaches can be sensible. What matters is that the financing serves the portfolio and the household, rather than forcing both to serve the loan. Final conclusion: Do not be afraid of owning a portfolio. Understand secured credit as a legitimate tool. Use carry only when the economics and the capacity to withstand losses make sense. Ownership is the foundation; leverage is optional. Section sources: [ 6 , 13 , 22 ] ; decision framework and story are author synthesis. 15. Data audit and limitations The DFA is an estimated distributional account, not a quarterly census of every household's brokerage account. It combines the Financial Accounts with the Survey of Consumer Finances, reconciles their concepts, interpolates between survey dates and estimates periods after the latest survey. Figures can be revised. The current methodology and classification notes should accompany any repeated chart. [ 2 , 3 , 18 ] This report keeps the uploaded Q2 2026 snapshot as its numerical anchor. Dollar totals from earlier conversation text are not reproduced because they are not contained in the supplied share table and have not been independently reconciled for this report. No same-vintage historical series back to 1989 was reconstructed, and no claim that the observed year-on-year change is unprecedented is made. Ownership concentration is not household behaviour or causation. A share table does not reveal the percentage of households with an account, how assets were acquired, which loans funded them, or whether borrowing generated their wealth. Households can also move between wealth groups. Rich people losing a wealth share and poorer people gaining one would not, by itself, establish better individual investment decisions. Global surveys are not directly comparable with U.S. population accounts. The bank surveys use selected family-office respondents, different questions and different reporting conventions. Lending balances measure amounts, not borrower counts or motivations. Corporate-and-foreign-bond entries are missing in the supplied file; broad fund classifications and separately reported pensions limit claims about underlying securities. [ 1 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] No personalised trade is proposed. Actual decisions require current facility documentation, collateral eligibility, loan quotes, tax circumstances and full household cash-flow information. This report contains no invented client financing terms, current market rates or probability of success. 16. Sources and direct reading links The links below identify the underlying documents consulted during preparation on 4 November 2026. Publication dates are shown in the relevant sections; undated product pages are not treated as binding offers. Full-text availability may vary, and some news articles require a subscription. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17. Choose risk efficiency. Then choose the exposure. Why a higher-Sharpe portfolio may be a better starting point for leverage than the investment with the highest headline return. The investment decision has two parts: Choose a portfolio that uses risk efficiently. Then decide how much exposure the household can finance and withstand. Improving the portfolio and increasing its size are not the same decision. This new chapter extends Own the Assets. Understand the Borrowing. The original sections 1–16 and their visual companion remain available unchanged. Their Q2 2026 wealth figures remain anchored to the supplied FRED snapshot; this addition does not update those statistics or convert them into evidence of widespread high-Sharpe carry trading. Public research edition: this chapter uses original explanatory text, author calculations and newly drawn hypothetical examples. It reproduces no lecture screenshots, publisher charts or private account information. Illustrations are teaching assumptions, not actual investment records or forecasts. Question What the chapter establishes What should we own? Assess the combined portfolio, including how holdings move together. How much exposure should we take? Compare alternatives at the same risk or return target, then allow for actual financing. What can leverage accomplish? It can scale a worthwhile strategy. It does not manufacture investment skill or remove losses. What must remain feasible? Cash servicing, collateral headroom, currency exposure and repayment through stress. Return versus journey Read the ratio Diversification Equal-risk comparison Leverage algebra Real funding costs Bank illustration Efficient frontier Research evidence Currency and debt Limits and traps Measurement protocol Client framework Client-ready conclusion New sources Reading rule: “Research finding” refers to a cited publication. “Derivation” means algebra under stated conditions. “Hypothetical example” uses invented teaching inputs, visibly labelled and unrelated to any client portfolio. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.1 Same destination. A very different journey. Same endpoint, different ability to stay invested Original hypothetical diagram · index starts at 100 · six invented observations, no calendar period Two hypothetical paths from 100 to 120 Path A values: 100, 105, 102, 110, 113, 120. Path B: 100, 112, 78, 100, 105, 120. Values are invented to illustrate path risk, not investment performance. 70 80 90 100 110 120 Start Finish Path A Path B Author illustration. No Sharpe ratio or margin-call probability is inferred from these paths. Exact values behind the hypothetical paths Observation Path A Path B Start 100 100 1 105 112 2 102 78 3 110 100 4 113 105 Finish 120 120 A final return does not describe everything an investor experienced. The original diagram above uses two invented index paths that both finish at 120 from 100. A financing obligation can interrupt a journey even when the asset eventually recovers. An unleveraged owner may have the option to wait. A financed owner must also meet interest and collateral requirements along the way. An asset recovering later does not undo a sale required earlier to meet a loan obligation. [ 6 ] Look at the endpoint Also look at the path How much did the asset gain? How much did its market value fall before recovering? What income did it pay? Could that income and outside cash meet obligations when due? Was the eventual outcome attractive? Could the investor maintain the position without a forced exit? Interpretation: a steadier historical path may be helpful for a financed portfolio, but the picture alone cannot establish a Sharpe ratio, future loss distribution or margin-call probability. Equal ending wealth also does not imply equal arithmetic average returns. Client explanation: “We are not only choosing a destination. We are choosing a journey that your balance sheet can afford to complete.” PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.2 What the Sharpe ratio actually measures The Sharpe ratio measures average excess return per unit of variability in that excess return . It can describe historical experience or a forecast; the two must be labelled separately. [ 27 ] x t = R portfolio,t − r f,t S = mean(x t ) / standard deviation(x t ) The benchmark, currency, return frequency and sample period must match. The benchmark is not automatically the investor’s loan rate. Read the ratio as efficiency, not as an interest rate. A Sharpe ratio of 2 is not a 2% return and is not “twice as safe”. In the model it represents two units of excess return for each unit of volatility, measured consistently. No particular Sharpe number is a universal target or borrowing trigger. Use total returns. Coupon or distribution yield omits market-value changes. A yield-to-maturity quote divided by a price-volatility estimate is not a properly constructed historical Sharpe ratio. A price-only series and a distribution-inclusive series must not be mixed. Working principle: do not rank investments by return alone, but do not replace one simplistic ranking with an unquestioned Sharpe leaderboard. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.3 Improve the combination before increasing its size Individual Sharpe ratios do not tell us how well assets combine. Correlation is an additional input. A holding with a lower standalone Sharpe can improve a portfolio when its returns offset other exposures. [ 28 ] σ p 2 = w A 2 σ A 2 + w B 2 σ B 2 + 2w A w B ρσ A σ B Two-asset variance identity. The covariance term, not the number of line items, drives diversification. Diversification is about the relationship between returns: combining imperfectly correlated assets can improve risk-adjusted performance. Sharpe ratios themselves are not additive. Correlation changes the risk of a 50/50 mix Model portfolio volatility (%) · common zero-based scale Correlation +1.0 10.00% Correlation +0.5 8.66% Correlation 0 7.07% Correlation −0.5 5.00% 0 10 Invented inputs: each asset has 10% volatility, 8% expected return, and 50% weight. Risk-free rate 2%; correlations are assumptions, not estimates. No fees. Values rounded to two decimals. Hypothetical diversification arithmetic Correlation Expected return Volatility Sharpe +1.0 8% 10.00% 0.60 +0.5 8% 8.66% 0.69 0 8% 7.07% 0.85 −0.5 8% 5.00% 1.20 PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.4 Compare at the same risk, not just the same cash outlay The relevant question is not simply “Which line finishes highest?” Ask whether a more efficient portfolio can meet the desired return with less volatility, or deliver more expected excess return at an equal volatility budget. That comparison requires reliable forward-looking inputs and feasible scaling. [ 28 ] At a common volatility σ*: expected excess return = S × σ* At a common positive excess-return target m*: volatility = m* / S Idealised mean–variance derivation: a common risk-free rate, frictionless scaling and positive expected excess returns. Actual financing is addressed next. Hypothetical comparison: portfolio A has expected return 8%, volatility 10% and a 2% risk-free rate, giving S = 0.60. Portfolio B has expected return 10% and volatility 20% with the same benchmark, giving S = 0.40. Scaling A to twice its exposure gives 20% volatility and 14% expected return only in the frictionless model. These are invented annual model inputs, not forecasts. Central argument: a lower-return portfolio is not necessarily inferior. Its return per unit of risk may leave more room for sensible exposure sizing. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.5 Why leverage can scale a higher-Sharpe portfolio Define own equity E, borrowing D and gross assets A = E + D. Let λ = A / E be gross exposure per unit of equity. Here D is loan principal; Part I used L for that amount. A 1× exposure is unleveraged. λ is not a loan-to-value ratio. R equity = λR p − (λ − 1)r f μ equity − r f = λ(μ p − r f ) σ equity = λσ p S equity = λ(μ p − r f ) / (λσ p ) = S p Model conditions: positive constant exposure per measurement period; borrowing at the same constant risk-free rate; no incremental costs, FX mismatch, nonlinear payoffs or forced liquidation. For a single period, the equation is a balance-sheet identity before any external capital flows. Multi-period statistics require consistent rebalancing and return construction. [ 27 ] Unchanged Sharpe does not mean unchanged risk. In this ideal model, both expected excess return and volatility rise in proportion to λ. Leverage scales efficiency; it does not improve the underlying ratio. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.6 The real-world hurdle: borrowing costs and fees A loan normally has its own price. Retain the previous one-period, single-currency structure, but set the borrowing rate r b = r f + s. Let c be incremental fees divided by opening own equity, over the same period. Asset return μ p already includes any asset-level fees; do not subtract them twice. μ equity = λμ p − (λ − 1)(r f + s) − c = r f + λ(μ p − r f ) − (λ − 1)s − c If funding and fees are deterministic in this simplified calculation, σ equity = λσ p . Dividing the excess return by that volatility gives: S equity = S p − [(λ − 1)s + c] / (λσ p ) Author derivation. With a positive borrowing spread and positive fees, the financed Sharpe is below the underlying Sharpe in this model. Variable rates or FX require a richer risk model. When can the higher-Sharpe choice still win? Let A be the lower-volatility, higher-Sharpe portfolio and B an unleveraged comparison portfolio. Scale A to B’s volatility with λ = σ B / σ A > 1. Then: μ levered A − μ B = σ B (S A − S B ) − (λ − 1)s − c Potential advantage Must exceed σ B (S A − S B ) Extra financing spread and fees: (λ − 1)s + c A stronger underlying return/risk trade-off The implementation costs required to reach the common risk level Decision rule, not a recommendation: higher Sharpe creates a potential efficiency advantage. Actual funding terms determine how much survives. Equal volatility still does not mean equal tail loss, liquidity risk or margin risk. The derivation is symbolic. The separately labelled example below uses invented teaching inputs; no client return, current borrowing quote or suitable leverage amount is asserted. Compare expected return at the same 20% volatility Expected annual total return (%) · hypothetical inputs · not a performance record Portfolio B · unleveraged 10% Portfolio A · 2×, risk-free borrowing 14% Portfolio A · 2×, borrowing at 4% 12% 0 16 Same model assumptions as the text. The third bar includes a 2-percentage-point borrowing spread above the 2% risk-free rate, with no incremental fees. Equal volatility does not imply equal tail, liquidity or margin risk. Hypothetical exposure and funding comparison Case Gross exposure Borrowing rate Return Volatility Sharpe A unleveraged 1× None 8% 10% 0.60 B unleveraged 1× None 10% 20% 0.40 A scaled, ideal 2× 2% 14% 20% 0.60 A scaled, spread 2× 4% 12% 20% 0.50 PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.7 Connect the theory to the existing bank illustration Part I reproduces OCBC’s public hypothetical coupon example. It provides actual illustration inputs, but not the return series needed to calculate a Sharpe ratio . The website was rechecked for this addition. These are not current loan quotations or actual portfolio results. [ 7 ] Input or result Published / exact derived value Own capital E $750,000 Gross assets A $2,500,000 Loan D = A − E $1,750,000 Gross exposure λ = A / E 10 / 3 Debt / own equity = D / E 7 / 3 Loan-to-value D / A 70% Coupon cash $125,000 Interest at 2.50% $43,750 Net coupon at 2.50% $81,250 Interest at 4.50% $78,750 Net coupon at 4.50% $46,250 Exact financing sensitivity: increasing the loan rate from 2.50% to 4.50% reduces annual net coupon by $35,000. Relative to own equity, that reduction is: $35,000 / $750,000 = 7 / 150 = 14 / 3 percentage points The fraction is left exact rather than rounded. This is the reduction in cash return on own capital, not a calculated Sharpe ratio. The published example uses an unnamed $ currency. Risk interpretation: for the same underlying portfolio and the ideal fixed-rate model, exposure of 10 / 3 scales its volatility by 10 / 3. The original maximum-capacity example also has zero initial lending headroom: 70% × $2,500,000 − $1,750,000 = $0 Important boundary: higher coupon cash does not establish a higher Sharpe ratio. Even a genuinely high-Sharpe portfolio should not be assumed safe at maximum lending capacity. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.8 Choose the portfolio. Then set the risk budget. Separate portfolio construction from exposure sizing. First, select a mix offering an attractive expected return for its volatility. Second, select the amount of exposure. Adding cash reduces risky exposure; borrowing increases it. Choosing a more volatile asset is not the only route to seeking a higher return. [ 30 ] The highest-Sharpe tangent-portfolio rule depends on its assumptions: a suitable mean–variance objective, a common risk-free rate, reliable expected returns and covariances, and feasible borrowing or lending. With costly or restricted borrowing, the attainable set changes. Household liabilities and non-volatility risks also matter. Recent research qualifies the simple rule. Moshe Levy’s 2026 study finds that realistic borrowing restrictions can substantially weaken the alignment between Sharpe rankings and investor welfare; it examines geometric-mean-based alternatives. This does not make Sharpe useless. It means the best feasible choice need not be the highest standalone Sharpe. [ 34 ] Use this workflow: construct → compare → size → finance → stress-test. Do not treat the tangent point as permission for unlimited borrowing. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.9 Research supports the principle, not a guaranteed outcome Leverage aversion: riskier assets are not automatically better Betting Against Beta studies leverage constraints and evidence across multiple markets. Its low-beta / high-beta strategy is not simply “buy any safe asset with debt”. It combines leveraged low-beta holdings with a short high-beta leg and finds vulnerability when funding constraints tighten. The relevance is that return-seeking demand can favour intrinsically risky assets, leaving opportunities in how risk is packaged. [ 29 ] Risk parity: balance risk before scaling it Leverage Aversion and Risk Parity considers allocations that spread risk more evenly and then scale exposure. Its evidence supports studying portfolio risk contributions rather than dollar weights alone. A bond-heavy allocation, however, is not automatically the highest-Sharpe mix, and risk parity is not synonymous with Sharpe maximisation. [ 30 ] Buffett: quality selection and funding structure together The published 2018 Buffett’s Alpha study reports a Berkshire Sharpe ratio of 0.79 and estimated average leverage of about 1.7 to 1 . Its interpretation links results to cheap, lower-risk, high-quality equities and leverage. Those are sample estimates, not a current allocation or a leverage recommendation. [ 31 ] Version discipline: AQR’s accompanying web summary quotes 0.76 and about 1.6 to 1, reflecting a different presentation of the research. This chapter uses the published article’s 0.79 and about 1.7 to 1, without mixing them with the earlier figures. [ 31 , 35 ] Funding is part of the strategy. The authors discuss low-cost insurance-float financing in their summary. A private investor’s callable portfolio loan is not equivalent to that corporate funding structure. Copying exposure without matching the resilience of funding would miss a central implementation difference. [ 6 , 35 ] The stronger lesson: select worthwhile assets and an effective combination, then use financing that permits the strategy to survive. The objective is not to copy somebody else’s leverage number. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.10 Measure the financed position, not just the bond or fund Three things must remain distinct: the asset’s standalone Sharpe; the financed investor-equity Sharpe; and lending headroom. The first can be attractive while the second is damaged by funding or FX, and the third can fail before a long-term thesis is realised. [ 6 , 27 ] CHF debt changes the USD investment’s return distribution For one period with unchanged principal and interest accruing to the end, let q be USD per CHF and i CHF the contractual period interest rate. The effective USD return-cost of the debt is: R D = (1 + i CHF ) × (q 1 / q 0 ) − 1 R E = λR A − (λ − 1)R D − c Author balance-sheet derivation. R_A is the USD asset total return. Costs c are measured against opening equity. Interim interest payments require their actual dates and exchange rates. Before additional random fees and capital flows, the corresponding variance identity is: Var(R E ) = λ²Var(R A ) + (λ − 1)²Var(R D ) − 2λ(λ − 1)Cov(R A , R D ) A negative covariance is dangerous here: the USD assets can fall while the USD repayment cost of CHF debt rises. A Sharpe ratio calculated from the USD bond alone misses that interaction. For an SGD-based comparison, translate the complete net position and cash flows into SGD and use a matching benchmark. A bond coupon is not a stable price Bond total returns incorporate market values, accrued interest and distributions. Maturity and issuer obligations matter, but the ability to hold until maturity is a separate constraint when collateral is marked along the way. A high advance ratio does not certify a high Sharpe. [ 6 , 21 ] Accounting control: use net investor equity after liabilities. If NAV is already net of the CHF loan, do not subtract that loan a second time. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.11 Do not mistake a smooth line for a safe investment Sharpe can miss or obscure Required additional check Rare, severe losses Drawdown, downside scenarios and loss concentration Illiquid or smoothed prices Reliable executable valuations and liquidation time Changing correlations Joint stress across the whole portfolio Funding and margin constraints Haircuts, loan terms and outside liquidity Short samples or selected backtests Out-of-sample results, robustness and estimation uncertainty Research warning: Getmansky, Lo and Makarov show how illiquidity and smoothed returns can distort measured risk and motivate smoothing-adjusted Sharpe estimates. A steady reported NAV is not sufficient evidence of a steady economic value. [ 33 ] Product boundary: a cap/floor payoff, an insurance illustration or a sequence of declared crediting rates cannot be assigned a superior investable Sharpe without comparable economic returns, fees, surrender terms, liquidity and liabilities. This chapter does not calculate a product-specific or client-portfolio Sharpe ratio. No universal threshold: a Sharpe of 2 or any other single threshold should not become an automatic borrowing trigger. A high historical number is a prompt for verification, not permission to increase debt. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.12 Calculate it consistently, then test its reliability A valid comparison needs comparable inputs. Use aligned total-return observations, one reporting currency, a matched benchmark and clearly defined fees. Distinguish an actual investor-equity series from a fixed-weight backtest. Do not reconstruct investment returns by tracing a picture. Historical period Sharpe = mean(x t ) / s x Under the usual independent-observation test: t = S period √n If simple annualisation is valid: S annual = S period √k Therefore: t = S annual √(n / k) n = number of observations; k = observations per year. Testing the mean excess return is not the same as testing raw return against zero unless the benchmark is zero. An exact classical t-test additionally assumes independent, identically distributed normal observations; large-sample approximations require suitable regularity conditions. Andrew Lo’s research matters here: Sharpe estimates have sampling uncertainty, and serial correlation can invalidate routine square-root annualisation. A smooth-looking series can therefore produce misleading confidence and rankings. [ 32 ] Reporting standard: show period, frequency, currency, benchmark, gross/net basis, observation count and valuation source beside every ratio. Show drawdown and margin stress separately. Use “not calculable from available data” where a required input is absent. Use arithmetic excess-return observations for the ratio. Report compounded growth separately; do not silently substitute CAGR into the standard Sharpe numerator. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.13 Turn the idea into a portfolio-financing decision The objective is a better feasible portfolio, not the largest obtainable loan. The following is a proposed decision framework, not a client allocation or a prescribed leverage ratio. Step Evidence required Decision implication 1. Establish the base portfolio Holdings, weights, market values, total-return history and liabilities Do not use financing to make an unsuitable asset appear attractive. 2. Compare combinations Return, volatility and covariance on the same basis A diversifying holding can be useful even with a lower standalone Sharpe. 3. Choose a risk budget Loss capacity, cash needs, horizon and downside scenarios Equal volatility is a comparison device, not a complete definition of equal risk. 4. Price financing Actual rate, spread, fees, FX and hedge terms Test whether the efficiency advantage survives the extra costs. 5. Test path survival Stressed collateral, lower advance ratios, adverse FX and renewal terms Keep repayment resources that do not depend on the same assets recovering. 6. Monitor and rebalance Net equity, cash servicing, debt and headroom Use actual results, not unchanged historical Sharpe, to reassess exposure. UBS’s Singapore Lombard guidance explicitly identifies diversification, unused lending capacity and additional liquid assets as risk-mitigation measures. Those controls address funding resilience; they do not convert a volatile portfolio into a guaranteed outcome. [ 6 ] Recommended dashboard separation Investment efficiency: total return, excess return, volatility, portfolio Sharpe and correlation assumptions. Loss capacity: drawdown, concentrated exposures and stress losses. Financing: actual interest, debt principal, loan currency and reset dates. Survival: lending value, utilisation, collateral shortfall and independent liquidity. Go / no-go principle: proceed only when the asset mix, after-cost economics and funding resilience work together. An unleveraged portfolio remains a complete and legitimate choice. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE 17.14 The message to retain The argument is stronger than “wealthy people borrow”. Asset ownership creates participation in financial returns. Diversification can improve how efficiently the portfolio uses risk. Suitable financing may then adjust the scale of that exposure without forcing the investor to choose intrinsically riskier assets. The benefit must still survive costs and real constraints. [ 29 , 30 ] Plain-language explanation “We should not automatically choose the investment with the highest advertised return. We should first examine how much risk is required to pursue that return, and how the investments behave together. A well-constructed portfolio with a stronger return-to-risk profile may be a better foundation. Where suitable, financing can increase exposure to that portfolio rather than pushing us towards a much riskier asset just to seek a higher number. Borrowing still increases the amount we can lose, and its cost and repayment conditions matter. We therefore assess the portfolio, the loan and the ability to remain invested as one complete plan. The aim is not maximum return at any cost. It is an appropriate return from a portfolio and financing structure that we can sustain.” Own the assets. Improve the mix. Size the exposure. Protect the ability to hold. PART II / SHARPE, PORTFOLIOS & LEVERAGE New research and source links New research and source checks for the Sharpe chapter, accessed 4 November 2026. Hyperlinked titles lead to the underlying material; some full articles require publisher access. The original 25-source list remains in Part I, section 16 . Numbering here follows the expanded research edition; reference 26 is not used in this public chapter. [27] William F. Sharpe. The Sharpe Ratio (1994) Author-hosted article. Excess-return definition, scale independence and limitations. [28] William F. Sharpe. Morningstar’s Performance Measures: Sharpe Ratios Author-hosted explanation of equal-risk comparisons, borrowing/lending and portfolio correlation. [29] Andrea Frazzini and Lasse Heje Pedersen. Betting Against Beta (2014) Journal of Financial Economics 111, 1–25. Author-hosted full paper; leverage constraints and funding risk. [30] Cliff Asness, Andrea Frazzini and Lasse Heje Pedersen. Leverage Aversion and Risk Parity (2012) Author-firm research summary. Risk allocation followed by exposure scaling; not a universal risk-parity endorsement. [31] Andrea Frazzini, David Kabiller and Lasse Heje Pedersen. Buffett’s Alpha (2018) Financial Analysts Journal 74(4), 35–55. Published abstract: Sharpe 0.79; estimated average leverage about 1.7 to 1. [32] Andrew W. Lo. The Statistics of Sharpe Ratios (2002) Financial Analysts Journal 58(4), 36–52. Sampling uncertainty, serial correlation and annualisation. [33] Mila Getmansky, Andrew W. Lo and Igor Makarov. An econometric model of serial correlation and illiquidity in hedge fund returns (2004) Journal of Financial Economics 74, 529–609. MIT-hosted full paper; return smoothing and adjusted Sharpe measures. [34] Moshe Levy. Mutual Fund Selection When Borrowing Is Restricted (2026) Published 6 January 2026. Research on borrowing constraints, investor welfare and geometric-mean alternatives. [35] AQR author summary. Buffett’s Alpha: version cross-check Web summary quotes 0.76 and about 1.6 to 1. Kept separate from the published article used in this chapter. Derivations: the equal-risk identities, financing-spread adjustment, exact OCBC arithmetic and cross-currency variance decomposition are author calculations under explicitly stated conditions. They do not use invented client inputs. Public chapter prepared 4 November 2026. Original diagrams and calculations are explicitly labelled. No current product Sharpe, loan quotation, personalised recommendation or guaranteed outcome is implied. Return to the complete original wealth report .
